authors: Jacqueline Thomsen, Alex Ebert, Jordan Fischer

text:
The midterms punched a Texas-sized hole in the GOP attorneys general coalition, creating leadership questions for red states and handing Democrats new players to challenge the Trump administration.

The Texas attorney general’s office — known for taking innovative stances in litigation, leading multistate actions, and incubating conservative talent — will be getting a Democratic makeover.

Add Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Kansas to the mix, and the blue wave is placing thousands of government lawyers under Democratic control.

“The red-state coalition has effectively been beheaded,” Michelle Kallen, a former Virginia solicitor general, said of Texas’ loss.

At the US Supreme Court, Texas led the red states’ amicus filing in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Org. opposing the constitutional right to abortion. And the Lone Star State’s top attorney has been one of the biggest thorns in the side of Meta and other tech giants.

“This completely shakes up the traditional multistate dynamics, and the state that has served a leading role, if not the leading role, is now going to be part of a different coalition,” added Kallen, a partner with Steptoe.

The upheaval has major implications for where high-impact litigation gets filed, which red states emerge as leaders, what matters reach the Supreme Court, and how much pressure corporate America feels to make deals before power shifts in January.

“If you see an AG that’s coming in and focusing on something that you have pending, you might want to resolve that ahead of time,” Foley & Lardner partner Siran S. Faulders said in a post-election training call for lawyers representing businesses facing state regulation.

Texas Turnaround

The blue wave in Texas will upend outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton’s playbook for scoring victories defending Texas laws or dealing blows to Democratic presidents by bringing suit in the state’s federal courts.

Paxton could rely on the state’s federal courts stacked with President Donald Trump‘s judicial appointees, and appeals bound for the Fifth Circuit controlled by a Republican-appointed super majority.

That roadmap is expected to be tossed out by Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson (D).

Johnson may try to file more actions in state courts, as Democrats were largely successful in the state’s judicial elections, said Judd Stone, a former Texas solicitor general.

“You would have a much more favorable audience and a much more favorable record going up through the state courts than through the federal courts,” said Stone, a partner with Stone Hilton.

The new Democratic attorney general could pursue cases against the Trump administration in federal court that had never been brought by the state before, as the Texas attorney general and Trump are typically aligned, said Paul Singer, who worked in the Texas attorney general’s office for over two decades.

“So it is going to certainly create a whole new level of scrutiny and question about some of these actions from the court,” Singer, now an attorney with Kelley Drye & Warren, said of the Fifth Circuit.

No Republican attorney general will serve in a southern border state starting next year.

That tees up Johnson and his Democratic colleagues to take a leading role in combating the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Still, as long as they’re in federal court, they’ll run into conservative judges on the Fifth Circuit, and potentially the US Supreme Court.

“The most important thing about the election results is they don’t change anything about the federal judiciary,” Stone said.

Private Challengers

Stone said he’d expect some outside conservative groups would “privatize some of the functions” that a Republican-controlled state would typically take on.

But that too comes with downsides: State litigation is funded publicly, while private groups would have to fundraise. And states have doctrines that make it easier to prove they’re injured by the action they’re going to court over, whereas private parties face a higher burden in establishing standing.

Private groups are going to keep picking favorable turf for their litigation, and the federal judiciary may see few changes over the next two years due to Democrats taking control of the Senate.

“Our public policy strategy regarding legislation will be affected and will require some adjustments. But the litigation strategy is not affected by this election,” said Mat Staver, founder and chairman of Liberty Counsel, a group that brings religious liberty cases.

States’ litigation strategy is another matter, said Jesse Panuccio, a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner and former acting associate attorney general in the first Trump administration.

“Texas was at the forefront of litigation you’d consider conservative. With that office and its significant resources gone, I think Florida will naturally emerge in that space, along with others like West Virginia, Alabama and Tennessee,” he said.

Supreme Court

The shift could also resonate at the US Supreme Court, where Texas and Iowa have taken leading roles in pushing red-state interests.

The Texas Attorney General’s office alone employs more than 4,000 people. Its 750 plus attorneys include 17 dedicated full-time to the solicitor general’s office.

“One of the things that Texas brings to the table in more complex areas like antitrust or DEI stuff is the sheer number of hours” they can muster, according to former Indiana solicitor general Thomas M. Fisher, now litigation director at the nonprofit EdChoice.

It will be difficult for any individual state to fill Texas’ manpower gap, Fisher said.

“Attorney general budgets don’t expand just because you want them to,” he said.

It was Texas that helmed Republican states’ amicus brief in the case that overturned Roe v. Wade, a generational fight for conservatives. And Iowa, alongside Tennessee, led the red states siding with the Trump administration over birthright citizenship.

Talent Pipelines

The Texas solicitor general’s office has also served as a key conservative legal talent pipeline. Former heads include Judge James Ho, who now sits on the Fifth Circuit, and Jonathan F. Mitchell, who argued successfully at the Supreme Court in 2024 against Colorado’s attempts to disqualify Trump from the ballot.

West Virginia, which is already an active player in energy litigation, is ready to step up and may seek to entice conservative attorneys who may soon be leaving other offices, Solicitor General Michael R. Williams said. He expects other Republican states to do the same.

Williams said the losses create opportunities for states like Montana or Kentucky in major Second Amendment, religious liberty, or immigration litigation. But Texas’ expansive portfolio alone may take several other states to cover.

Florida Focus

As the third-most populous — and largest GOP-controlled — state, Florida could become the leader of Republican coalitions, practitioners told Bloomberg Law.

Without Texas, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier emerges as an even more powerful player, said Ashley Taylor, Troutman Pepper Locke partner and co-leader of its state attorneys general practice.

“When there’s a political blowout, you are part of the team that got blown out, and you survive — that creates opportunities,” Taylor said. “He was well-positioned before this — now he’s one I’d expect to be very prominent.”

Uthmeier has been the second-most active Republican top cop, after Texas, in pursuing Big Tech. He’s also taken on culture war issues like abortion and parental rights, and leveraged state antidiscrimination and antitrust law to drag huge corporations — from Starbucks to pharmacy benefit managers — into state court.

The 450-attorney office has often relied on private firms for reinforcements in big cases.

It’s also the lone holdout seeking a big payday against Meta after 48 states signed an $18 billion settlement, and New Mexico won billions taking its social media cases to verdict.

“This office has been leading these fights since the day I took office, and we’re going to keep leading them,” Uthmeier said in a statement.

text:
Stephen Miller, the architect of Donald Trump’s mass deportation policy and hardline crackdown on immigration, took up his new role as White House chief of staff on Monday.

Miller, 41, began his new role serving as Trump’s right-hand man after Republicans suffered massive losses nationwide in the midterm elections. He was previously serving as a deputy chief of staff.

On Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Miller – his most controversial aide – would replace Susie Wiles, his former chief of staff.

The announcement came as a surprise, because members of the Trump administration had denied reports that Wiles was on her way out. In recent weeks, several top women in the administration have stepped down, including Harmeet Dhillon, a top justice department official, and Katie Zacharia, who spent just five days as press secretary after replacing Karoline Leavitt.

Miller’s promotion came just days after voters rebuked the US president’s agenda just two years into his administration in the midterm elections.

Democrats accused Trump of not listening to voters by elevating Miller to a top role – especially because Trump’s harsh anti-immigration crackdowns rocked the nation over the last year.

Trump said himself that his mass deportation policy was “too tough” in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes which aired over the weekend.

“I think it was too tough,” Trump said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

Despite that, Trump chose after the interview to elevate the man behind one of his most controversial policies to a larger role in the White House.

More administration staffing changes could be coming soon, in the wake of the midterm results and Miller’s appointment. Richard Walters, a White House deputy chief of staff who was one of Wiles’s closest allies, announced he would also be leaving the administration.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents showed up at a hospital in Los Angeles on Saturday and blocked off the ambulance entrance.

KABC-TV, a Los Angeles TV station, reports that ICE showed up at about midnight at Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center with a person in custody who needed medical treatment in the emergency room. A hospital spokesperson said federal agents blocked the entrance to the ER for two hours.

“When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely, respectful, and culturally sensitive care,” the spokesperson told NBC Los Angeles.

Protesters soon showed up to object to the presence of ICE agents at the hospital, and one of the demonstrators, a teenage girl, was reportedly pepper sprayed by agents and needed medical attention.

Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman showed up at the hospital as well. “What happened last night at this hospital was an affront to the wishes of the American people and to the people of Los Angeles,” she later said.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli (whose appointment was ruled illegal last month) attacked Raman in an X post.

“I know you’re new to this, but facts matter. ICE was there to get medical treatment for a detainee who requested to see a doctor. I assume you support federal agents providing medical care to illegal immigrants in custody?” Essayli wrote. “As a public official, you should know the applicable laws. Agents are enforcing federal immigration laws passed by Congress. As mayor, you have no say in federal affairs. It’s called the Supremacy Clause. I can send you a copy of the U.S. Constitution if you’d like to study up.”

The city’s outgoing Mayor Karen Bass also condemned ICE’s actions.

“A hospital should be the one place where people feel safe. No one should have to think twice about receiving care or fear that a loved one’s treatment could be interrupted because of their immigration status,” Bass posted on X. “I condemn ICE’s actions and call on the Trump Administration to stop all immigration enforcement in and around health care facilities. Hospital leadership also had a duty to step in right away to protect patients and neighbors, and by all appearances, that did not happen.”

Hospital president Daniel Fontura said that agents entered the hospital and wanted to be present when doctors were speaking with the patient in ICE custody. According to Fontura, hospital officials rebuffed the agents.

“There was a time when ICE actually wanted to break protocol and be present with the physician in that sacred physician-patient encounter and we said no,” Fontura said. He said that when ICE started to block access to ambulances and EMS vehicles, the hospital then contacted the Los Angeles Police Department for help.

President Donald Trump emerged Monday with muddled accusations of election fraud, nearly a week after saying he would accept the sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote.”

“It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” he added.

It was not immediately clear what polls Trump was referring to. Trump’s own personal pollster Tony Fabrizio had been warning since last year that Republicans would take a major hit in the midterms. In July, Fabrizio found that Republicans were lagging three percentage points on a generic ballot. Among 65 percent of highly motivated voters, a Republican would lag by seven percentage points.

Vice President JD Vance also disputed polls that showed a Democratic blowout, following his party’s disastrous midterm results. “There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up,” he wrote on X last week.

It’s possible that Trump’s expectations were simply being manipulated by his sycophantic staff. A White House source told the Daily Mail that former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles had been promising a win right up to the end, telling people as recently as September that Republicans would sweep in the midterm elections. Trump announced last week that Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as top aide.

Trump’s latest missive represents a shift in the president’s outlook on the election results. On election night, Trump told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the election results and was looking forward to working with Democrats. Now he seems to be reverting back to his old tricks by making broad, unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud.

This story has been updated.

MAHA stalwart Calley Means, who resigned from the Department of Health and Human Services two weeks ago, has accused former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her team of insiders of bowing to “unrelenting” pressure from industry lobbyists—and even profiting from it.

In a two-hour interview with pugnacious podcaster Joe Rogan Friday, Means claimed that Wiles had withheld support from MAHA policies in order to keep corporate cash flowing ahead of the midterm elections. He accused her team of bowing to heavy lobbying for fruit-flavored vapes and Kratom, also known as “gas station heroin.” Means also claimed that any corporation that hired her daughter, Katie Wiles, a partner at political lobbying firm Continental Strategy, received “high priority” at the White House.

Means’s accusations arrived as Donald Trump announced that Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as chief of staff, following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections. Means resigned as a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. last month, citing “a corrupt D.C. bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo.”

On Saturday, Means posted a public plea that Wiles and White House deputy chief of staff James Blair stop “harassing” him with texts and calls about his Rogan appearance. “If there is a factual inaccuracy in what I said, send it to me in writing and I will vigorously correct and apologize for any misstatements. I will note that everything I said is substantiated by other senior officials,” he wrote.

Behind the scenes, things quickly got ugly. “If you are gonna try to knife me, I’m happy to return the favor,” Blair told Means in a text message reviewed by The Wall Street Journal. Blair is reportedly considering suing Means for defamation.

Speaking on CBS News’s Face the Nation Sunday, Means accused Wiles of being part of a “close-knit crew” of former lobbyists in the White House who “explicitly catered to special interests against the will of the voters” without Trump’s full knowledge.

“I think [Trump] had severe poor advice from people, I think, who treated him like a baby in many respects, and used him,” Means said.

The group of insiders allegedly consisted of Wiles, Blair, Richard Walter (the deputy White House chief of staff who exited ahead of Miller’s appointment), and Walker Barrett, assistant to the president for policy.

Means claimed that the group was working on behalf of the industries Trump ran on fighting, including the vape industry, the ultraprocessed food industry, the pharmaceutical industry, and the pesticide industry. The president was unaware that some of his advisers were “directly” taking money from these industries, Means said.

Means also pointed the finger at Tony Fabrizio, the president’s personal pollster, for playing an outsize role in approving Trump administration policy while getting paid by companies such as Pfizer and Pepsi. “It’s a matter of record that Tony Fabrizio is in the pocket of big pharma,” Means told The Washington Post. Fabrizio told the Post that this was “not only ridiculous, but demonstrably false.”

The president is claiming he’ll take a softer tone on immigration now that Stephen Miller, his despotic deportation chief, is his chief of staff—and his longtime MAGA allies are not happy with the unexpected switch-up.

Donald Trump appeared decidedly more diplomatic as he plotted out his new position post-midterms during a sit-down 60 Minutes interview that aired Sunday. Speaking with host Ross Douthat, Trump singled out immigration as the one thing he’s looking forward to working on with the incoming Democratic majority in Congress, claiming that his previous positions were “too tough.”

“Do you think immigration hurt you in the midterms? Do you think the crackdown hurt you?” asked Douthat.

“I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said, adding that he believed his deportation policies “hurt” him.

Then, in an incredible policy reversal, the president suggested that he could see a potentially viable pathway in which working, taxpaying, undocumented immigrants are offered a separate legal status.

“But there’s a group of people that I would say on the sort of pretty far right that would like everybody taken out,” Trump said.

“Do any of those people work in your administration? Are they in the building with us right now?” asked Douthat, to which Trump simply responded, “Yes.”

The interview was filmed an hour before news broke that Trump had tapped Miller to replace his notorious “ice maiden,” former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Trump had reportedly decided weeks earlier that Wiles would play the fall guy for Republican’s seismic midterm losses.

“Stephen Miller needs to CLEAN HOUSE of advisors, because this is a HORRIBLE take,” wrote far-right commentator Nick Sortor. “WITHOUT DEPORTATIONS, OUR COUNTRY IS GONE. PERIOD. ICE IS NOT THE PROBLEM. THEY’RE THE SOLUTION.”

But it’s highly unlikely that Miller—the architect of some of Trump’s most horrific immigration policies—would actually bend to such an idea.

Miller was fundamental in crafting policies from Trump’s first term including separating families at the border, terminating the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program, and the executive orders that amounted to Trump’s Muslim ban. In May 2025, Miller issued a tyrannical order to his Immigration and Customs Enforcement underlings, directing them to arrest a minimum of 3,000 immigrants per day.

President Donald Trump had a tough time on CBS’s 60 Minutes trying to defend the massive increase in his wealth since the start of his second term.

In an interview that aired Sunday, interviewer Ross Douthat pointed out to the president that his net worth has gone up by $3 billion since January 2025, to which the president tried to argue that it was all because of his children. Trump then claimed that everyone’s wealth went up, prompting Douthat to note that he himself didn’t make $3 billion. Trump retorted, “You should have owned stock.”

“I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don’t care. I make, I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I’d have. And I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know. I have a son who’s a very straight, good guy. He watches over money. I don’t even talk to him about it. He watches. He gives, they gave my money, I have a lotta cash, have, had a lotta cash long before I came in here. I don’t take a salary, you know?” Trump said, trying to explain his newfound wealth.

Douthat also pointed out the apparent corruption from Trump’s cryptocurrency venture, World Liberty Financial, and how it took money from the United Arab Emirates. He pointed out that if President Joe Biden had done something similar, Trump would have called it corrupt. Trump tried to pin it all on his sons.

“I have, but you have sons where they go around and they build buildings. That’s what they do. That’s what I did long before I became president. I did it better than anybody. I was very good at real estate. I made a lotta money. But—but I have a company. My sons run the company. It’s hard to say to them, ‘Don’t do anything any more for four years because I’m president,’” Trump said.

In response to Douthat asking about outside forces who use Trump’s cryptocurrency for influence peddling, Trump tried to claim that every president has had a similar problem, “going back to George Washington.”

Trump has a lot to answer for with his business dealings, and seemed to crumble at the weakest amount of questioning over it. Douthat didn’t even mention the allegations of insider trading from within his administration, or the fact that Trump’s own Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has made suspicious stock trades as well. Here’s hoping that the pressure on Trump continues over the next two years, with more scrutiny, pressure, and revelations.

text:
☀️ Good morning from The Legal File! Here is the rundown of today's top legal news:

📑 Democratic attorney general wins could reshape US lawsuits on abortion, immigration and more

Democratic challengers beat incumbent state attorneys general in key races last week, taking over the AG offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas. Many lawsuits the outgoing Republicans championed could now be dropped, narrowed or left undefended. Here’s what to know:

Abortion rights

Mifepristone (FDA suit): If Texas withdraws, Florida would be the remaining plaintiff. Florida's Republican AG, James Uthmeier, won a new term.

Mifepristone (Kansas): Kansas's new AG could exit a separate challenge to rules expanding access to the drug. That would leave Missouri and Idaho as plaintiffs.

Texas suits against out-of-state abortion providers: Texas AG-elect Nathan Johnson told the Texas Tribune he won't file these suits, calling them "political showboating."

Texas abortion ban: Johnson could decline to defend the near-total ban in the suit brought by the family of Tierra Walker. She died of a pregnancy-related condition after doctors refused to perform an abortion.

Georgia abortion law: AG-elect Tanya Miller's win could affect the state's defense of HB 481, the 2019 six-week abortion ban. The Georgia Supreme Court revived it in 2024, and litigation is ongoing.

Immigration

Texas SB4: The law lets state authorities arrest and prosecute suspected illegal border crossers. The 5th Circuit let it take effect in April while the challenge continues. Johnson could drop the state's defense.

Iowa: The US Supreme Court is weighing Iowa's appeal of a ruling blocking a similar law. AG-elect Nate Willems could decline to defend it if the Court takes the case.

Mike Scarcella and Daniel Wiessner have more cases to watch here, including environment, voting rights and religious liberties.

⚖️ Justice Department joins Texas lawsuit against Planned Parenthood

The DOJ is stepping into Texas' years-old lawsuit accusing Planned Parenthood of Medicaid fraud, according to a court filing made days after voters elected Democrat Nathan Johnson as the state's next attorney general.

The DOJ move, in a legal filing on November 6, would give the federal government a direct role in a 2021 case championed by outgoing Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who lost his bid to become a US senator.

Paxton and an anonymous plaintiff are seeking to force Planned Parenthood to return money it allegedly collected from Texas' and Louisiana's Medicaid programs after the states cut off its funding, plus heavy additional penalties.

Planned Parenthood has said it would be forced to shut down in Texas if it loses the case.

The lawsuit accuses Planned Parenthood of violating the federal False Claims Act by having continued to bill and collect payments from the states' Medicaid programs after the initial termination decisions, and failing to repay what it received once the terminations eventually took effect.

Read more.

💼 Law firm Kirkland brings on 40-lawyer Weil team, including would-be leader

Forty lawyers from Weil, Gotshal & Manges are joining rival law firm Kirkland & Ellis, including private equity partner Ramona Nee, who was previously poised to take over leadership of Weil before its decision to wind down.

Kirkland said on November 6 that Boston-based Nee would join in January with Weil private equity and M&A partners Jakub Wronski, Emily Willey and Michael Messina, and debt finance partners Benton Lewis and Paul Overmyer.

Weil's leadership recommended to partners last week that the 95-year-old New York-founded law firm wind down, after months of mounting departures by key partners to rival firms and failed merger talks.

Weil announced in March that Nee would succeed its longtime executive partner Barry Wolf as leader of the firm. But Nee, who served as co-managing partner, recently decided not to take the position, a person familiar with the matter previously told Reuters.

Nee in a statement said the team is excited to join Kirkland. "The collegiality and collaboration extended by Kirkland during this period is very meaningful to me and the team," she said.

Weil's collapse has spurred a recruitment rush and a scramble by hundreds of Weil lawyers, including prominent partners and roughly 700 associates, to find new homes.

Read more.

🚘 Flock lawsuits test legal limits of license-plate reader networks

Does your right to privacy end when you back out of your driveway? That question is driving a flurry of lawsuits against Flock Safety and others over cameras that automatically read and record the license plates of passing vehicles.

Plaintiffs lawyers contend the technology enables police to conduct unlawful mass surveillance. Where they diverge is in identifying a viable legal theory for their challenges.

Jenna Greene digs into the litigation in On the Case.

👋 That's all for today, thank you for reading The Legal File, and have a great day!

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

November 9, 2026

Contacts:

Global Refuge: Timothy Young | Email | 443-257-6310

RCUSA: Meredith Owen | Email

IRAP: Spencer Tilger | Email

WASHINGTON – Global Refuge, the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP), and Refugee Council USA (RCUSA), issued a joint letter signed by 70 refugee-serving, faith-based, refugee-led, legal services, veterans, and community-based organizations today in calling on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to rescind an interim final rule that significantly cuts the time refugees have to contest the termination of their refugee status from 30 days to 10.

In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and USCIS Director Joseph Edlow, the organizations warn that the rule denies refugees any meaningful chance to defend themselves before termination of their status. That includes refugees with limited English, disabilities, or serious medical needs, and those in communities where immigration legal services are already stretched thin. DHS identified about 186,000 “unadjusted” refugees who arrived to the United States between fiscal years 2015 and 2025 who have not yet received their green cards (permanent resident cards). The rule’s own economic analysis concedes that some refugees “could reaffirm their status in 30 days but not in 10 days under this rule.”

At the same time, USCIS has continued its adjudication pause on over 155,000 pending refugee green card applications, leaving resettled refugees in a dangerous bureaucratic trap. In tandem with the frivolous “re-vetting” of already-arrived refugees, the administration is destabilizing decades of precedent and putting new members of our communities in harm’s way.

While the rule went into effect on October 14th, the day it was published, without a notice and comment period, a federal district court has since temporarily blocked the administration from implementing it, and from enforcing termination notices already issued under the shortened deadline. Despite court intervention, immediate executive action is necessary – and Congress should do everything in their power to hold the administration accountable to safeguard refugee communities..

The letter calls on DHS and USCIS to:

Immediately rescind the rule and ensure refugees have a meaningful opportunity to secure counsel, review the allegations against them, and submit evidence before any termination is finalized;

Fully resume processing refugee green card applications, and create a way for members of Congress to request expedited processing, particularly for people with severe medical conditions;

End the re-vetting of refugees who are already among the most thoroughly vetted people to enter the United States; and

Provide notice and comment before any future rule on refugee status termination or re-vetting takes effect.

“No one can mount a real defense of their legal status in ten days, especially in a second language, without a lawyer, and while potentially having to retrieve records from a country they were forced to flee,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, President and CEO of Global Refuge. “These refugees have already cleared the most rigorous vetting the United States requires of anyone. Being welcomed here should not be the start of an endless audit that treats lawfully admitted families as perpetual suspects. A government confident in its case has nothing to lose by giving people a meaningful opportunity to respond. We urge DHS to rescind this rule and restore a fair process for the families it puts at risk.”

“This rule is part of a wholesale attack on the integrity of the refugee system,” said Rricha deCant, Senior Director of Policy and Climate IRAP. “The Trump administration has banned non-white refugees from entering the country, prevented refugees who are already here from being able to obtain green cards, and is now trying to remove their refugee status without due process. These actions are cruel, unlawful, and must end immediately.”

“This rule is not only an affront to our constitutional ideals, but also another way for this administration to terrorize and endanger refugee communities,” said John Slocum, Executive Director, Refugee Council USA. “Time and again, this administration has sought to dehumanize individuals fleeing violence and persecution and destabilize thousands of families who found community through work, school, and volunteership across the U.S. Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. That requires holding the federal government accountable for its discriminatory and unlawful targeting of refugees. We must denounce any attempt to dismantle access to permanent protection. We urge the administration to rescind this rule, resume processing refugees’ green card applications, and end this wasteful refugee re-vetting effort. And Congress must do everything in its power to safeguard refugees who have been welcomed by communities across the country.”

The full letter and list of signatories is available here.

About Global Refuge

Refugee Health and Wellness Program (RHWP)

Through training opportunities and resource sharing, the Refugee Health and Wellness Program (RHWP) empowers community members to feel confident supporting refugees. From large private sector to local organizations the training offers information to build trusting relations with refugees and newcomers, in turn building resilience and encouraging clients and patients to seek help for physical and mental health challenges.

Trainings Opportunities: All program trainings are free and are offered virtually or in-person.

Trauma and Culture and working with Diverse Population

This is a one-hour, virtual training, offered on a monthly basis. Please follow our newsletter to receive the most up-to-date training schedule or reach out to ksimpher@refugees.org to book a training for your agency.

This training covers how trauma and stress are experienced differently through one’s culture, including understanding the intersection of culture and trauma and the foundations of cultural competence and cultural humility leading to improved trauma-informed care, trust building and respectful care.

Mental Health First Aid

The program officer is certified to teach Youth Mental Health First Aid, resulting in attendees being certified Mental Health First Aiders. If you are interested in attending a MHFA training, please subscribe to our newsletter for the most up-to-date trainings or reach out to ksimpher@refugees.org to book a training for your agency.

More information on MHFA can be found at Mental Health First Aid Missouri

Dropbox

Compiled in our Dropbox is a large collection of materials that may help both providers and clients. Information and materials are organized in folders and within our master list of resources. From health topics (measles, diabetes, covid-19) to child safety topics (such as car seat safety) to information on health systems (Medicaid, transportation).

This resource hub includes information in multiple languages, flyers, and short videos.

Resources and trainings are also consistently developed based on need and feedback from the community!

What information and trainings would be helpful for you? Please take a minute to fill out this quick questionnaire if you would like a topic to be covered, beyond what is currently being offered.

Please email Katie Simpher, Refugee Health and Wellness Program Officer at ksimpher@refugees.org to discuss any training needs.

Refugee Health Promotion (RHP)

Refugee Health Promotion (RHP) is a Refugee Support Services (RSS) set-aside program that promotes the health and wellbeing of refugees and other ORR-eligible groups for up to 5-years from date of arrival to the U.S. or date of ORR-eligibility by:

1) Providing opportunities to increase health literacy,

2) Coordinating physical and mental health care; and

3) Organizing wellness group activities.

RHP-funded organizations may provide services that fall under one or more of these categories, which is dependent on each individual agency’s annual proposal and program design. The nature of services provided can also vary by agency, even within the same category, so it is always best to reach out to them directly to obtain information and coordinate care.

Health Education Program (HEP):

Health Education Classes and Targeted Health Outreach to Individuals. Programs provide opportunities to increase health literacy for eligible populations, empowering clients to make informed health decisions.

Health Navigation Program (HNP):

Medical and Mental Health Navigation and Support. Programs coordinating health care for individuals and providing services to ensure individuals can navigate and access complex health care systems.

Wellness Program (WP):

Adjustment Groups, Skill-Building Networks, and Peer Support Meetings. Programs organize wellness groups to connect individuals with social groups and learning activities that promote their health and well-being.

Missouri Refugee Health Services subcontracts with a combination of community-based organizations, federally qualified health centers and local resettlement agencies to implement the above programs.

Refugee Medical Screening (RMS):

USCRI administers this program to provide domestic refugee physical and mental health assessment, identify communicable diseases of potential public health importance and referrals to primary healthcare providers.

The Refugee Medical Screening program conducts the domestic health assessment for new ORR-eligible arrivals, following guidance issued by ORR and Centers for Disease Prevention and Control (CDC), referring clients to primary care and specialists as needed.

The Refugee Medical Screening must be completed for each new ORR-eligible arrival within 30-90 days post arrival to the United States or from their date of ORR-eligibility.

Missouri Refugee Health Services subcontracts with four federally qualified health centers to provide complete domestic health assessment and vaccinations to new arrivals. Those clinics are located in Saint Louis, Kansas City, Joplin and Springfield:

Saint Louis – Affinia Healthcare at the South Broadway location.

Kansas City – Samuel U. Rodgers Health Center – Downtown Campus (Euclid Ave)

Joplin – Access Family Care – Joplin Medical and Dental Clinics and Pharmacy

Springfield – Jordan Valley Community Health Center – Tampa Clinic

It is important to note that immunizations given at or during Refugee Health Screening appointments are the same ones required for the Adjustment of Status (or “Green Card”) process with a Civil Surgeon. Initiating Medical Screening as soon as ORR-eligible individuals meet eligibility is very important and ensures that families are more prepared for Status Adjustment when they file for their I-693 application.

Refugee Medical Assistance (RMA):

USCRI administers this program to provide high quality, cost-effective health benefits to refugees and other ORR-eligible groups, who are ineligible for Medicaid in Missouri.

RMA provides up to 4 months of health insurance that mirrors the state’s Medicaid program for adults without children or others in special circumstances, such as adults 65+ or living with a disability who are pending SSI/Medicaid.

In Fiscal Year 2027, with H.R.1 (“OBBA”) ending decades of Medicaid coverage for refugees and other humanitarian parolees, Missouri’s RMA usage is expected to grow exponentially for newcomers. This program, however, will continue to only cover refugees for up to 4-months from their date of arrival to the United States, even with upcoming shifts in policy leaving many refugees uninsured for long periods of time until their status is adjusted to meet Medicaid program eligibility.

In response to the H.R.1, USCRI is creating a directory for low-cost and free healthcare providers in Missouri. To accomplish this goal, USCRI has created a form to gather health resources that currently exist in the major Missouri regions of resettlement. If you are aware of a free or an affordable healthcare service in your community, please take a few minutes to fill out the form, by clicking here or using the QR code.

MO RHS partners with local agencies in Saint Louis, Kansas City, Columbia, Joplin and Springfield to enroll eligible clients into the RMA program.

Zeze’s childhood dream of pursuing a career in electronics engineering took a turn towards helping disadvantaged refugees when he became a refugee. His personal journey as a refugee in 1995 ignited his passion for supporting refugees, leading him to accumulate extensive refugee services experience both within and outside the United States.

Additionally, he has contributed his expertise to the boards of several non-profit organizations, including the Unity Alliance of Southern Idaho, Culture for Change, and the Valley House Homeless Shelter

Annahi Ruano has over a decade of experience working in human services and the criminal justice system. In 2013, she became a Behavioral Health Therapist specializing in family therapy and individual therapy for children 5-17 in the foster care system. She began working at ORR shelters in 2017 as a Clinician in Arizona in a 400-bed shelter for Southwest Key Casa Kokopelli and transitioned to Lead Clinician/PSA Compliance Manager in California for Casa San Diego a 90-bed shelter with three locations/ licensees for boys and girls 5-17. She later became the Program Director/CA Program Administrator with Southwest Key Programs for Casa San Diego. She has a passion is helping children and families in need and her heart is with immigrants, as she comes from immigrant grandparents and parents who came to the United States for a better future for future generations. She holds a bachelor’s degree in criminal justice and a master’s degree in forensic psychology.

With over 25 years of dedicated experience in working with vulnerable youth, Alejita Rodriguez brings a wealth of experience to the field of social work. In 2021, Alejita joined USCRI as the shelter Director of Rinconcito del Sol, a role that highlights her unwavering commitment to improving the lives of children. Alejita earned her Master’s degree from Grand Valley State University where she developed a solid foundation of knowledge and skills to address the complex challenges faced by vulnerable youth. Throughout her career, she has demonstrated a profound commitment to program development, ensuring programs are both innovative and effective. This dedication extends to compliance, as she is well-versed in regulatory and legal requirements, ensuring the utmost safety and quality of care for the children under her supervision. Alejita has been a catalyst for youth development, using her experience to create supportive, nurturing environments that enable children to thrive.

Sam Udani has been involved with the immigration community in the USA for most of his career spanning three decades, involving immigration politics and immigration policy and covering all manner of immigration into the USA, including refugees. He has been a tireless advocate for enlightened immigration laws for the USA since ACWIA, AC21/ACTA and continuing from then on.

Mr. Udani currently serves as the Law Publisher and CEO of ILW.COM and Immigration Daily, a position he has held for over twenty years. As Publisher, he directs all activities of the website and newspaper with over 50,000+ pages of free information on immigration law that receives 250,000 visitors per month. Under Mr. Udani’s direction ILW has conducted 600+ CLE seminars, published over two dozen immigration law books and conducted hundreds of immigration events in over a dozen countries. Earlier in his career, Mr. Udani founded an advertising agency and a small company in international trade.

A hallowed name for refugees, and generally for the entire immigration field, is Edith Lowenstein who served as Editor of Interpreter Releases, the first (and for half a century the only) periodical reporting on developments in immigration/refugees – Interpreter Releases was housed within USCRI’s predecessor entity for its formative decades. Today’s Immigration Daily is in direct descent of Interpreter Releases, Mr. Udani is always reminded of this when before Edith Lowenstein’s image in USCRI’s board room.

Gabriel Lajeunesse is a financial advisor and former U.S. Air Force officer with over 30 years of experience in national security, wealth management, and community development.

He served for two decades in international security roles, including assignments advising the Joint Chiefs of Staff and supporting National Security Council committees at The White House. His final deployment to Afghanistan included leading a multinational team of over 600 personnel. He is a Bronze Star recipient for his service in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Following his military career, Mr. Lajeunesse transitioned into financial advising, specializing in portfolio strategy, business transitions, and real estate investments. He holds certifications as a Certified Exit Planning Advisor and Accredited Asset Management Specialist, and is admitted to the D.C. Bar.

He is the founder of Aacred Development Holdings, a real estate private equity firm focused on Smart Growth housing in Northern New England. He also serves as a planning commissioner and member of the Vermont Community Development Board.

Mr. Lajeunesse holds degrees from the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Naval Postgraduate School, Georgetown University Law Center, and an Executive MBA from the Quantic School of Business and Technology.

John T. Monahan, JD, is interim dean at the School of Nursing & Health Studies and senior advisor to Georgetown University’s President. A Georgetown community member for many years, he holds Georgetown academic appointments as Professor of Medicine, Senior Lecturer at Georgetown Law, and Senior Fellow at the School of Public Policy, and has taught courses at NHS, Georgetown Law, and the School of Foreign Service.

Over the course of his professional career, the core of Monahan’s work has focused on addressing complex health and social service programs affecting vulnerable populations in the United States and internationally.

In his varied career, Monahan has served as Legal Counsel to US Senator David Pryor; Law Clerk to US District Court Chief Judge John Grady; and is a veteran of numerous political races, including the Mondale and Clinton presidential campaigns. A member of the Council on Foreign Relations, he serves on the boards of the National Network for Public Health Law, US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, and Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless.

Monahan holds bachelors and law degrees cum laude from Georgetown University.

Regis G. McDonald is an accomplished social service executive with decades of experience in managing and developing cutting edge programs and services for youth and families involved with the child welfare, juvenile justice, child mental health and immigration systems.

Mr. McDonald at the time of his retirement was Senior Vice President for Programs at The Children’s Village in Dobbs Ferry, New York. The Children’s Village was founded in 1851 in Lower Manhattan as the New York Juvenile Asylum. Today, the Children’s Village is a nationally and internationally respected multi-service human service organization with a staff of over 1,500 and an annual budget exceeding $91M. Mr. McDonald’s work at CV positively impacted and enriched every aspect of the organization, including its work on Undoing Institutional Racism and providing shelter and staff secure care to unaccompanied immigrant children.

At the invitation of the First Lady of Guatemala Mr. McDonald participated in two Central America Regional Child Migration Forums. One in 2013 in Antigua, Guatemala and the second in 2016 in Washington, DC. He served as a member of the United States Department of Justice Interagency Working Group on Separated & Unaccompanied Children in 2014.

Mr. McDonald earned an Associate in Arts degree from Wentworth Military Academy & College. He is the recipient of the Ted Messmore Honor Graduate Award, Wentworth’s highest award. Mr. McDonald was awarded a Bachelor of Science degree from Central Missouri State College and a Master of Social Work degree from Adelphi University School of Social Work.

Katharine Laud’s path has combined finance and non-profit management to provide opportunities to under-served communities, including women, minorities, immigrants and people of color for wealth creation.

Ms. Laud is currently the President of Opportunities Credit Union, the 11th largest credit union in Vermont, which offers innovative and affordable financial services to Vermonters. Before assuming her current position, Ms. Laud was the Associate Vice President for Finance and Administration at the University of Vermont Foundation, a non-profit organization committed to serving the university community. She was the Chief Financial Officer of a non-profit that focused on affordable housing for low-income people. Ms. Laud has served on a number of corporate boards, including the Board of Directors for Provident Financial Services, a NYSE-trading bank holding company, a member of the Audit and Governance Committees and as Chair of the Wealth Management Committee. While serving on the Board of Directors of the First Morris Bank and Trust. She was instrumental in the founding of the Wealth Management Division.

Ms. Laud has used her extensive background in finance to build avenues to wealth creation and management for diverse and under-served communities in Vermont. She has brought corporate efficiencies to non-profit management to promote economic self-sufficiency among low-income people.

Katharine Laud earned a B.A. and an M.B.A. at Dartmouth College.

Jeff Kelley has spent his career both in public service and in the private sector, focusing on communications, public affairs and government relations. He has worked for both the U. S. government and the private sector in the U.S. and Europe.

Most recently, Mr. Kelley served in the Obama Administration as Director of Public Affairs for the Administration for Children and Families. ACF houses programs such as refugee resettlement (ORR), Head Start, child welfare and foster care, and the nation’s family assistance program (TANF).

Mr. Kelley owned Peer Communications LLC, where he organized conferences on communications strategy for the senior public affairs executives of more than 100 Fortune 500 companies. He worked for more than 20 years for the DuPont Company, first as executive speechwriter for the Chairman, then in several senior management roles, including more than a decade in Geneva, Switzerland, leading the company’s communications and government affairs teams in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Earlier he was press secretary to U. S. Senator Thomas J. McIntyre (D-NH) and in the Carter Administration he was special assistant and speechwriter for Health and Human Services Secretary Patricia Roberts Harris.

Mr. Kelley’s volunteer experience includes six years on the Board of Visitors of the Nelson A. Rockefeller Center for Public Policy at Dartmouth College, a nationally acclaimed institutional home for social science research, teaching and experiential learning. In that role he has sponsored and mentored undergraduate interns working for the USCRI. He taught English as a second language at a center for immigrants in Washington, D.C. and volunteers as a National Parks Service guide at Ford’s Theater.

Mr. Kelley earned an undergraduate degree from Dartmouth College and a master’s degree from the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University.

Kevin Bearden is an accomplished senior executive with more than 25 years of experience in strategic business growth, corporate operations and the management of large performance-based federal programs, including humanitarian solutions, cloud, cyber data analytics and intelligent automation systems.

Currently, Kevin leads the humanitarian solutions portfolio at Cherokee Federal serving as Vice President. His new organization provides influx facility wrap around and direct care services for unaccompanied children as well as refugee support services for newly arrived Afghan parolees. Mr. Bearden previously served in C-suite and other key senior executive roles at The Providencia Group (TPG), SOS International (SOSI) and General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT). Before entering the private sector, he was a Commissioned Officer in the U.S. Army Signal Corp and served both on active duty as well as in the Army Reserves.

Kevin is very passionate about supporting underserved and vulnerable populations. He’s traveled both domestically and internationally as part of humanitarian missions assessing the plight of unaccompanied Eritrean minors along the Ethiopian border, he’s visited urban refugee processing centers in Nairobi Kenya and has overseen numerous domestic immigration programs supporting HHS’s Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), DoS’s Bureau of Populations Refugee’s and Migration (PRM) as well as DOJ’s Executive Office for Immigration and Review (EOIR). In his spare time – Kevin volunteers and mentors aspiring young men in local DC based urban education centers.

Mr. Bearden holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from North Carolina A&T and a Master of Science in Systems Engineering from Johns Hopkins.

Jeffrey Metzger, an attorney who has worked in corporate, government, and private practice, brings to USCRI’s Board of Directors extensive legal expertise in ethics and compliance as well as a personal drive to serve the refugee and immigrant community.

Most recently, Mr. Metzger was Staff Vice President and Associate General Counsel of Unisys Corporation, where he was responsible for the company’s litigation, counseling the company’s government businesses, and directing the company’s federal government contracts organization. He also designed the company’s first ethics compliance program and then served as Corporate Ethics Officer.

Before coming to Unisys, Mr. Metzger served on the professional staff of the President’s Blue-Ribbon Commission on Defense Management, where he was principally responsible for making recommendations on defense industry compliance issues. He also served in the Civil Division of the Department of Justice for a number of years, representing the United States in procurement fraud and government contract litigation. Before joining Justice, he worked in private law practice in Washington, D.C.

He earned a B.A., magna cum laude, from Amherst College, and a J.D. from Georgetown University Law School.

Helen R. Kanovsky’s distinguished career in housing began with her interest in social justice. Ms. Kanovsky has served in the U.S. government, private sector and labor movement, bringing to USCRI’s Board of Directors a wealth of expertise and experience in housing across sectors.

She currently is General Counsel at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), where she oversees the association’s internal legal affairs, compliance and human resources operations.

Prior to joining MBA, Ms. Kanovsky was the General Counsel of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and had served as HUD’s acting Deputy Secretary. Previously, she was General Counsel and Chief Operating Officer at the AFL-CIO Housing Investment Trust. She was the General Counsel at both GE Capital Asset Management and Skyline Financial Services. Additionally, Ms. Kanovsky worked in private practice and on Capitol Hill, where she served as Chief of Staff to Senator John Kerry.

Ms. Kanovsky is a member of the District of Columbia Bar, the American Bar Association and the Federal Bar Association. She served for three years as the Chair of the National Housing Conference. She has spent her entire career working and advocating for stable affordable housing as a human right.

Helen holds an A.B. degree in government from Cornell University and graduated Cum Laude from Harvard Law School.

Gene DeFelice is an accomplished attorney as well as a seasoned corporate executive. His areas of expertise include business management, compliance and corporate governance.

Mr. DeFelice is currently the Managing Director of Novo Strategic Partners, a company specializing in legal and corporate management solutions including compliance; governance; human capital; licensing, mergers and acquisitions; regulatory issues; legislative affairs; and forensic services. Previously Mr. DeFelice served as the Senior Vice President and General Counsel for Rackspace, a global leader in cloud computing and IT infrastructure with approximately 6,200 employees and $2 billion in revenue. He was Executive Vice President, Corporate Counsel and Corporate Secretary for HMS, a $450 million public healthcare technology, healthcare data analytics and medical services company. He has extensive experience in management, compliance and governance in Fortune 500 companies across a number of industries, including medical technology, healthcare analytics, pharmaceuticals, cloud computing and IT infrastructure.

Mr. DeFelice has sat on the boards of a number of non-profit organizations, donating his time and expertise to improving non-profit management and operations. He served for many years as USCRI’s Board Chairman.

Mr. DeFelice graduated from Rutgers University, earned an M.B.A. with distinction from Webster University in Switzerland, and was awarded a Doctor of Law from Seton Hall University.

Katharine I. Crost brings to the organization wide-ranging experience in the field of securities and corporate finance as well as non-profit leadership.

Ms. Crost was a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, LLP for over 30 years. Her extensive portfolio at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP included serving on the Firm’s Executive Committee, establishing and chairing the firm’s Women’s Initiative and acting as a Practice Group Leader.

Ms. Crost has been a passionate advocate on behalf of immigrants, refugees and global citizens worldwide. She has served as a Board Member of the Women’s Refugee Commission and currently serves as a Member of the Emeritus Board of Indego Africa, a non-profit that works to provide artisan women and young people in Africa training for sustainable livelihoods and access to markets. Her commitment to empowerment and social justice has taken her to refugee camps in Ethiopia and Myanmar. She has represented pro bono clients in researching and preparing a report on shelters for unaccompanied minors and a training protocol for border patrol agents to screen for human trafficking victims. She currently volunteers at USCRI’s field office in Albany, New York.

Katharine Crost earned a J.D. from the University of Virginia School of Law and a Bachelor of Music degree from Michigan State University.

Earl Johnson serves as a Member of USCRI’s Board of Directors following a decades long career in public service at the federal and state level. Mr. Johnson has been a leader nationwide in promoting responsible fatherhood and economic security issues related to men and boys of color.

He was appointed by the White House to serve as the Director of the Office of Family Assistance (OFA) with the Department of Health and Human Services’ Administration for Children and Families (HHS/ACF). In this position Mr. Johnson oversaw an annual budget of $17.8 billion. In this role, he was the principle policy and administrative manager for the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program.

Before accepting his current position, he was the Senior Policy Advisor and Interim Workforce Investment Board Director for the City of Oakland and Mayor Ron Dellums. Prior to that he was the Senior Program Officer for the California Endowment and the Associate Director for the Rockefeller Foundation’s Working Communities Division. He also served as the Associate Secretary for Planning and Evaluation for the California Health and Human Services Agency.

Mr. Johnson has worked serving families and children for his entire career. He brings this passion to USCRI’s programs for refugee and migrant families and children.

title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185000 Times Since Trump Took Office
description:
It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.
Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool.
In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.
In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes.
"The numbers reported to EFF amount to a dragnet domestic surveillance program by Trump's Homeland Security Department,” says US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon.
text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

That, however, has changed. The Trump administration recently argued in court that because the Customs Service’s powers were transferred to DHS following the passing of the Homeland Security Act, it can use that power to tackle its “broad investigative portfolio,” which it says includes enforcing laws “beyond legacy customs and immigration enforcement.”

Advertisement

“When we give law enforcement agencies powerful investigative tools, even with the best intentions and purposes to try to go after legitimate investigations and crime, you have to be really careful,” says Mackey. The newly reported filing is part of an ongoing Freedom of Information Act lawsuit filed by the nonprofit against ICE and DHS.

"The numbers reported to EFF amount to a dragnet domestic surveillance program by Trump's Homeland Security Department,” says US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon.

ICE did not respond to questions about why there’s been such a huge increase compared to prior years, but Mackey speculates that it may be because there is virtually no downside to filing them.

“The worst thing that will happen to ICE is that the service that receives it says it's not going to respond,” says Mackey. If that happens, ICE can just take the company to court to force it to comply, as it recently did with Google, or withdraw it and try to get the information it’s after by issuing a grand jury subpoena, as the Intercept reported it recently did with Reddit.

“Congress desperately needs to pass my bipartisan legislation to drastically curb federal subpoenas, including consequences for officials who abuse surveillance authorities,” says Wyden, referencing his proposed Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act. “Next year, I plan to use the Senate Finance Committee gavel to get to the bottom of HSI's unprecedented misuse of customs law to target Trump's enemies.”

Even without exact details about the 185,000 subpoenas HSI sent out, Mackey says their prolific uses still raises “significant concerns about an agency potentially being out of control and not being subject to any sort of internal oversight that respects people's First Amendment rights and their rights to privacy.”

More ICE shootings

More than a dozen people have been shot by federal immigration agents since Renee Good and Alex Pretti were killed in separate shootings during Operation Metro Surge.

Recent shootings in Houston, Maine and New York have led to protests and demands for more transparency from the Trump Administration.

Pretti’s family amplified those demands at an emotional press conference late last month.

Pleas from Pretti family

What they're saying:

"We are here begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right," Susan Pretti said.

The federal government has repeatedly withheld key evidence from the fatal shootings of Good and Pretti, according to court filings.

The Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) revealed this fall that the agency still doesn’t have the gun used to shoot Pretti.

"This is not normal," said Michael Pretti. "This is not justice."

The Prettis accused U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney for Minnesota Daniel Rosen of "stonewalling" them for nine months.

"What we have been treated to is cruelty," Michael Pretti said.

DOJ responds

The other side:

DOJ attorneys argued in court records that it would be "inappropriate" if the federal government was forced to provide evidence.

Steve Schleicher, the Prettis' family attorney, told the FOX 9 Investigators that the family should not have to beg the federal government for basic information.

"They are asking for the names of the shooters to be officially confirmed, and they're asking the federal government to not block the state government from doing its work."

Some evidence released

The backstory:

The feds blocked state authorities from investigating the scenes after three shootings during Operation Metro Surge in January.

The feds eventually turned over evidence from the Good shooting months later, including the vehicle she was driving when she was shot through the driver’s side window, but only after the state filed a lawsuit.

Good family files lawsuit

Dig deeper:

Good’s family filed a separate lawsuit against the federal government in October arguing ICE officer Jonathan Ross and other federal agents violated the Fourth Amendment and mandatory DHS use-of-force policies, which prohibit shooting at moving vehicles.

The fatal shooting on Jan. 7 immediately drew comparisons to another shooting during an ICE operation in Chicago last fall.

Marimar Martinez survived being shot five times while driving her car.

"I was watching the news and I seen that I was getting charged for impeding, interfering," Martinez told FOX 32 as part of an interview for the new docuseries.

Like Good, the Trump Administration quickly accused Martinez of interfering with federal agents and engaging in an act of domestic terrorism.

However, the charges were later dropped when evidence undercut the border patrol agent’s claims of self-defense.

"It has destroyed the trust of the community in federal law enforcement," said Chris Parente, Martinez’s attorney.

Other evidence revealed agents bragged about the shooting in text messages and tampered with key evidence.

Watch "Thin I.C.E." documentary series

A Wisconsin State Trooper who was born in South Africa and came to the United States as a teenager will be released from federal custody after being detained by federal immigration authorities.

Carel Van Der Merwe, 21, has been a Wisconsin State Trooper since 2025, joining the department along with 26 other new recruits in a graduation celebration presided over by Gov. Tony Evers.

Immigration attorney Marc Christopher said Van Der Merwe works out of the Tomah office and lives in Onalaska.

According to Christopher, Van Der Merwe came to the country with his family in 2019 and filed for asylum. The attorney said he is included on his father’s pending asylum application and holds federal work authorization bearing an expiration date in 2030.

Van Der Merwe was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers Thursday at the Dane County Regional Airport. He’s being held at the Dodge Detention Facility in Dodge County, according to an online database.

“When you have somebody who has done everything absolutely correct — they enter the United States lawfully, they lawfully filed their asylum application, they lawfully applied for a work permit, they’re lawfully waiting for their asylum interview — for them to be detained after all of this time is … in my mind, unconscionable,” Christopher said.

A Friday afternoon statement from Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden said he had reached out to Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, about the case.

“The trooper will be released immediately and will be responsible for working with the appropriate authorities to resolve his outstanding immigration paperwork and address his legal status,” the statement said.

Christopher confirmed to WPR that Van Der Merwe is being released Friday.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Van Der Merwe was arrested Thursday during a “targeted enforcement operation at the Dane County Regional Airport in Madison, Wisconsin.”

In a Friday email, a U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Van Der Merwe came to the United States in March of 2019 “with legal permission to stay until September 2019.”

“In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission,” the spokesperson wrote. “This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

“To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States,” the spokesperson added.

But, Christopher said, “It is absolutely at the discretion of ICE, is whether or not to detain people like this.”

Christopher said he met with Van Der Merwe Thursday evening. He’s attempting to get him released on bond, a process he said could take a few weeks.

He said he also talked with Van Der Merwe’s father and that the family is in “disbelief.”

“I don’t know that anybody would be able to logically explain why they would want to detain a person like this,” Christopher said.

The Trump administration has focused the asylum system on helping white South Africans. Of people the 16,292 people admitted into the United States under asylum rules this year, all but five were white South Africans, according to Axios.

And the administration said it would focus on white South Africans claims in the coming year, planning to admit another 17,500 additional White Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees over the next 12 months, according to CBS News.

In a Friday afternoon email, the Wisconsin Department of Transportation Office of Public Affairs said the Wisconsin Department of Transporation and the Division of State Patrol “are aware of the situation involving Trooper Carel Van Der Merwe.”

“The trooper has been employed with State Patrol since July 13, 2025,” the email said.

text:
DENVER — The ACLU of Colorado alongside immigration attorney and law professor, Elizabeth Jordan filed, an amicus brief in Quintero Alvarez v. Baltazar, et al. on Saturday, November 7. The court document details how ICE gathered a group of men on October 27 and told them they were being released from the GEO detention facility in Aurora, but instead they were kept in ICE custody and then put back in detention shortly after their false “release.” The men, who had been ordered released by a federal judge, were forced out of the gates of the GEO facility and then immediately swarmed by ICE officers who told them they were once again under arrest. ICE repeated that same cruel sham many times between October 27 and November 3.

U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney ordered the ICE Field Office Director for Denver, Nathan Rasper, to appear in court on Monday, November 9, to address these violations. On Sunday, November 8, Judge Sweeney also granted the emergency motion for the ACLU of Colorado, and Jordan, to appear and argue at the hearing.

“These actions by ICE are appalling and yet another example of how ICE and the Trump administration are trying to skirt the system to defy court orders. ICE repeatedly violates court orders and continues to cause profound harm in our communities with its brutal tactics,” said Tim Macdonald, ACLU of Colorado legal director. “ICE must immediately release anyone subjected to these sham procedures and be held accountable for this brazen and unlawful conduct.”

Jordan and the ACLU of Colorado have identified at least 17 cases in Colorado where ICE has held people in detention who courts have ordered be released. In one case, a man who petitioned the courts for his release, and was granted it, described the terrifying moment when he was supposed to be released, but was arrested and taken back into detention. The petitioner in Lebrun v. Baltazar described ICE agents turning off their body cameras when he asked what was happening to him and then being threatened with criminal prosecution. In another case, the man described getting excited to see his family, then not even making it to the sidewalk outside the detention facility before he was taken back into custody.

“ICE’s actions are not only harmful to the court’s authority and rule of law, but they are deliberately traumatizing the people who should be released and their families. They have the anticipation of finally seeing their families again and their families expect them home, but ICE instead keeps them in custody,” said Conor Gleason, ACLU of Colorado staff attorney. “ICE has proved they will not stop these unlawful and cruel tactics without immediate court intervention.”

Across the country and here in Colorado, ICE has arrested people without warrants and without probable cause, in violation of the law and court orders, and now continues to hold people in detention when courts order they must be released. ICE has also conducted these sham releases in Minnesota.

text:
A federal prison medical negligence case could end up weakening one of the last avenues for seeking compensation from officials who violate constitutional rights.

The U.S. Supreme Court will examine a case on November 9 that could further limit lawsuits against federal agents, including ICE officials.

– Why it matters: A decision that eliminates the legal precedent known as Bivens could prevent victims of constitutional violations from seeking compensation directly from federal agents through this avenue.

Supreme Court May Limit Lawsuits Against ICE Agents

The case revolves around Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents, a 1971 decision that allowed lawsuits against federal officials for certain constitutional violations.

For decades, the Supreme Court has reduced the scope of that precedent, making it harder for people to obtain financial compensation for wrongdoing by federal employees.

Now, the court, composed of six conservative and three liberal judges, has the opportunity to review what remains of that protection.

– The fact: The Bivens precedent allows for monetary damages in certain cases, but does not guarantee that any accusation against a federal agent can become a lawsuit.

– The limit: The Court has already restricted lawsuits that present significant differences from the few previously recognized constitutional cases.

A $3 Million Lawsuit Could Change the Rules

The controversy began with Kekai Watanabe, who filed a $3 million lawsuit against a nurse at a federal prison in Honolulu.

Watanabe claims he received inadequate medical attention after being injured in a gang fight in 2021.

According to his complaint, he was given over-the-counter pain relievers and told to stop complaining, despite needing specialized care.

Months later, an X-ray revealed a fractured coccyx and displaced bone fragments in nearby tissues, according to the information presented.

– The process: An appeals court allowed the lawsuit to proceed, considering it coincided with a 1980 precedent on inadequate medical care in federal prisons.

– The dispute: The Department of Justice argues that the decision is outdated due to subsequent rulings that restricted these claims.

What Could Happen to Lawsuits Against ICE?

Although the lawsuit does not directly involve immigration agents, its consequences could extend to other federal institutions, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law, warned that eliminating Bivens would close a judicial avenue for holding federal officials accountable.

His warning takes on relevance amid questions about the actions of immigration agents, including the fatal shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

However, eliminating this precedent would not necessarily mean that all forms of legal accountability would disappear, such as criminal investigations or other claims authorized by law.

– What you can do: People who believe their rights have been violated can seek legal advice to determine what judicial resources are still available depending on the circumstances.

What's Next: A Decision with National Consequences

The Supreme Court will hear arguments on November 9, but that does not mean it will issue a ruling that same day.

The judges will have to determine whether Watanabe's lawsuit can continue under existing precedents or if it should be further restricted.

The outcome could establish how far people can go to federal courts to seek compensation for alleged constitutional violations.
