text:
Protesters gathered at Fruitvale Plaza Sunday to air their frustrations as federal immigration authorities continue deportations of East Bay residents.

Some attendees of the protest, which was organized by the Party for Socialism and Liberation, said they believe enforcement may have increased as retaliation for the results of Tuesday's elections.

"That's why we're here today," said protest organizer Aditi Varshneya, "to mobilize in Fruitvale, the heart of the immigrant community here, to really let the will of the people be known."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin reaffirmed last week that immigration enforcement would not be diminished, regardless of the election results, with a three-word post on X.

"Deportations will continue," he wrote, two days after the election.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed that at least five people were detained in the East Bay on Thursday. A rapid response group in Alameda County, called ACILEP, reports that four people were picked up in Oakland on Saturday.

"There's been this ICE surge for the last several days," said Varshneya.

The Alameda County Sheriff's office issued a statement on Sunday affirming its policy of not assisting ICE operations, but acknowledging that they, too, have seen increased immigration enforcement activity at their jail facility.

"More recently, the Sheriff's Office has observed federal immigration enforcement take place outside of Santa Rita Jail," the statement said. "We understand that maintaining contact with incarcerated loved ones is critically important and this is at the forefront as we determine next steps."

The sheriff's office said they are looking into what options they have for securing the jail area. Similar detentions were made outside of Monterey County's facility in October as well.

Protestors emphasized that the battle over ICE detentions would not end simply because votes were counted. But Mark Airgood, a member of the activist group By Any Means Necessary, said that while it might not happen immediately, he was still confident that the will of the people would prevail.

"When will we abolish ICE? I can't give a date, but I do think the movement adopts that as a central plank of our movement, which is happening," he said.

CBS Bay Area reached out to ICE for comment on Sunday and has yet to receive a response.

text:
A federal judge ruled that New York can continue enforcing its statewide ban on law enforcement working with federal immigration agents, despite a bid from New York county sheriffs for a preliminary injunction.

Albany-based Judge Mae A. D’Agostino ruled that New York can continue to enforce its statewide termination on 287(g) agreements — contracts between local police departments and Immigration and Customs Enforcement — in accordance with the “Local Cops, Local Crimes” Act, while the final decision on the constitutionality of the law is still being adjudicated.

In the 28-page decision, D’Agostino ruled that the sheriffs have not proven that they have the legal standing to bring their lawsuit against the state forward.

“Although some scholars have called for a reform of the legal landscape to allow local governments to sue their parent state, the current state of the law does not appear to allow for such a suit,” D’Agostino wrote. “Indeed, Plaintiffs have not presented a single case which states that an independently elected sheriff may indeed sue in his official capacity to protect the duties of his office.”

The lawsuit was filed on Aug. 25 by Broome County Sheriff Fred Akshar and 14 other county sheriffs against New York Attorney General Letitia James and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, claiming the ban violated the federal and state constitutions. The lawsuit sought declaratory judgment that “Local Cops, Local Crimes” was unconstitutional, a permanent injunction blocking the enforcement of the law’s provisions and a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction that preserve the “status quo” by prohibiting further enforcement of these statutes pending a final judgment.

D’Agostino also ruled that James is allowed to investigate sheriffs who have previously worked with ICE, rejecting the sheriff’s bid for an injunction on this part of the act.

“Local law enforcement should be focused on keeping New Yorkers safe, not carrying out the administration’s cruel mass deportation agenda,” Attorney General Letitia James wrote in an X post. “We will continue to defend our laws in court.”

Akshar was reelected for Broome County Sheriff last Tuesday and said that he planned to continue with the litigation during a press conference following the announcement of his victory.

“This case is less about immigration and more about preserving the independence of the office of sheriff. It’s the oldest office in the history of this nation,” Akshar said at the press conference following his reelection.

Broome County first signed an agreement with ICE in March 2025 to establish a Warrant Service Officer program which permitted state and local law enforcement “to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their agency’s jail.”

The agreement has received criticism since its implementation. In October 2025, several community members voiced opposition to increased funding for the Sheriff’s office by 15 percent in Broome County’s 2026 budget, citing the sheriff’s agreement with ICE.

Community members and other organizers rallied in February to protest ICE detentions at the Broome County Jail following the detention of Guan Heng, a Chinese whistleblower and asylum seeker. Heng, who was detained in December 2025, allegedly documented human rights abuses committed by the Chinese Communist Party.

In October 2026, 18 Broome County residents were detained by ICE, according to Humans of ICE, a humanitarian project supporting ICE detainees in the Binghamton area.

“In an environment where ICE agents are brutally attacking immigrant New Yorkers at home, on our streets, and in other public spaces, the ban on 287g agreements prioritizes the public trust that is needed to keep all New Yorkers safe,” said Christina Zawerucha ‘05, president of Humans of ICE, in a press release.

text:
Austin will change its rules for how police officers interact and cooperate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Mayor Kirk Watson said Friday.

Watson said he asked Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis to craft a new policy to be ready for when Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, an Austin Democrat, takes over from Gov. Greg Abbott in January.

“I’m asking Chief Davis to update her general orders so that they can be effective when the new Governor comes into office to make sure that our policies align with Austin’s values and that they do not become outdated,” Watson said in a statement on the Austin City Council message board.

Austin’s policies around cooperating with ICE have been in flux all year amid a nationwide crackdown on immigration in U.S. cities. The Austin Police Department has changed its policy on collaborating with ICE agents twice in the last year.

The city first tweaked its policy in March to reduce ICE intervention in local policing. That was spurred by local uproar after a Honduran woman and her five-year-old daughter were arrested and deported after interacting with APD.

After a threat to withhold state money from Abbott, APD tweaked its policies on cooperating with ICE. But following Abbott’s stunning loss to Hinojosa on Tuesday, APD is changing its policy again.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire made a similar policy change Friday.

Watson said he expects less oversight on Austin’s policies in light of an incoming Democratic administration in the Texas Capitol.

“With the change in state leadership, I anticipate being able to better partner with the state on issues and without threats and undue pressure on local decisions, including those related to civil immigration enforcement,” Watson said.

Austin’s strategy this year has been to tweak the department’s internal rules for officers cooperating with ICE agents. APD has always notified ICE if an undocumented immigrant has a warrant for — or if they’re accused of committing — a violent crime. But its recent policies have given more latitude to officers on when they can cooperate with ICE agents.

The latest rules say if someone has an ICE administrative warrant — a noncriminal charge — officers should contact ICE “when operationally feasible.”

A state law, known as Senate Bill 4, bans so-called “sanctuary cities” from stopping law enforcement from interacting with ICE outright. That law, Watson said, is still the law and the city will follow it — for now. He said the federal crackdown and state preemption has created “a policy of fear.” Watson hopes the new policy will change that.

“Many Austinites in our community live in real fear—fear created not by local government but by other levels of government,” he said. “Austin has worked to mitigate that fear, and wherever we can, eliminate it.”

President Donald Trump has admitted his federal crackdown on illegal immigrants went too far and may have alienated voters at last week’s midterms, which saw Democrats take back control of Congress.

Speaking to correspondent Ross Douthat for Sunday night’s instalment of 60 Minutes on CBS News – his first major interview since Tuesday’s crushing defeat for Republicans – Trump said of the crackdown: “I think it was too tough.”

“I think it might be too tough, yeah,” he continued. “And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

Despite the admission, the president appears unlikely to further rein in his approach now that he has appointed Stephen Miller to be his next White House chief of staff, with the immigration hardliner replacing Susie Wiles.

Officials at the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not received any instructions to revise their tactics in response to the midterms results, according to CBS, despite the outcome being widely interpreted as a sharp rebuke of Trump’s policies.

“I would count on the opposite,” one official told the network in light of Miller’s ascent, hinting that the round-up and arrest of undocumented migrants will continue at pace.

A key reason for Trump’s re-election in 2024 was voter discontent over Joe Biden’s perceived failures on immigration, with many Americans attracted by the Republican promising a mass deportation push to drive out people in the country illegally, whom he portrayed as a menace to society.

However, there was backlash when masked ICE agents began to surge into Democrat run cities like Los Angeles and Chicago and targeted migrant communities, raiding homes and workplaces, arresting people without criminal records and spreading fear.

The unease boiled over into anger when two U.S. citizens were shot dead in the snowy streets of Minneapolis in January while protesting their actions.

That culminated in the removal of DHS secretary Kristi Noem, her top adviser Corey Lewandowski and Customs and Border Patrol chief Greg Bovino from positions of power and a scaling back of federal agents’ activities as attention switched to the Iran war.

The president admitted to Douthat that his immigration strategy had “both helped and hurt” his administration, insisting he deserved an A+ grade for securing the southern border with Mexico.

Asked where his approach had backfired, Trump answered: “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.

“But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.

“Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there’s a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.”

Striking a more conciliatory tone than usual, Trump also entertained the idea of working with congressional Democrats on an amnesty for people who have been in the country for a long time without the proper documentation.

“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” the president suggested. “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

Elsewhere in the interview, the president conceded that the Iran conflict had also cost Republicans the support of many midterms voters, before pivoting back to blaming the media.

A longtime Democratic House member representing a southern border district said Immigration and Customs Enforcement is not going anywhere as "Abolish ICE" became a rallying cry for more than a dozen progressive Democrats elected or reelected in the midterms.

While the elections brought a new class of Democratic Socialists of America members to Congress, Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital that they make up just "one part of the spectrum" and that there are many "blue dogs" like himself who value strong border and immigration policies.

Cuellar, who is currently the ranking member of the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee, is poised to become chairman, giving him significant influence over how funding for ICE is allocated.

The congressman's district includes Laredo, where Border Patrol has a major presence. Cuellar has repeatedly broken with his party on immigration enforcement, including voting with Republicans in January to approve a DHS funding bill that included billions for ICE, though he later opposed a $70 billion Republican-backed enforcement package over concerns about oversight.

text:
While much of the florid, fashy antics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, has lingered long in the memory, there’s one thing the agency has been doing that’s largely flown under the radar—its efforts to surveil protesters using sophisticated tracking technologies. This represents a realization of warnings that privacy advocates have long expressed: the tools of the war on terror would be turned on Americans by an authoritarian. According to a recent report from Wired, during the unrest in Minneapolis last year, ICE utilized Reaper drones, Signal chat interceptions, financial tracking, license plate readers, and more to target activists.

The report focuses on how over 100 Homeland Security Investigations, or HSI, agents were deployed to infiltrate and monitor community meetings, marches, and general strikes in Minnesota. This was approved under a Trump directive from September of last year titled National Security Presidential Memorandum 7, issued after the assassination of Charlie Kirk. But this surveillance operation also relies on programs that date back to the early days of the PATRIOT Act.

This isn’t an isolated incident, either. Reporting suggests that ICE has been utilizing many of these surveillance tactics around the country, and there’s still much that is not known about these programs. Daniel Solove, a professor of intellectual property and technology law at George Washington University, tells The New Republic that he’s long expected these kinds of tools would eventually be used in the ways we are now seeing.

“The chickens have come home to roost,” Solove says. “We have an authoritarian government with all these surveillance technologies and minimal-to-no limits on what it can do with them. The legal controls are very weak, and now they’re abusing it. This isn’t a surprise. This is a disaster foretold.”

Solove says it’s still “outrageous” that it’s happening, but it’s not a shock to him. He says that warnings from privacy experts like himself have mostly “fallen on deaf ears among policymakers,” as they’ve chosen not to pass comprehensive privacy protections through Congress.

“This is exactly the type of scenario we’ve been warning about,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “The government has a very long history of surveilling people based on their political beliefs. In this new era, it’s not a surprise that the agency with carte blanche to buy and hoard as much surveillance equipment as possible, and that answers directly to the president, is the one being deployed to spy on protesters.”

Surveillance is “infrastructure,” Guariglia says, and whatever justification the government might give for buying all of these tools often isn’t the only thing they’ll use it for. They might argue it’s to fight crime or protect national security, but it can easily be turned against citizens practicing their First Amendment rights.

“At some point there’s going to need to be a huge accounting of what data DHS has collected in the last few years and what it’s been used for,” Guariglia says. “That includes data taken about protesters, any database that exists and how they’ve been using facial recognition. It also includes data they’ve been getting from other branches of government.”

The first Trump administration crossed a lot of lines and violated people’s rights, but it wasn’t known for deploying surveillance technologies at the scale we’re seeing today. The second Trump administration has far fewer guardrails and a clear focus on utilizing technology to help achieve its authoritarian aims.

“I don’t want to underplay the first Trump administration. There were terrible abuses,” Solove says. “But this one is different. It goes much, much further.”

It’s not just the government we need to worry about, Solove says. Private data brokers and other private interests are deeply entangled in ICE’s surveillance operation, and he says that if legislators are going to tackle this threat to privacy and civil rights, the private sector needs to be a major part of their focus.

“A lot of the tools, data and techniques the government uses are supplied by the private sector. That’s where the government gets the data,” Solove says. “This is a partnership, or collusion, between the private sector and the government. You can’t stop it by looking only at the government side anymore.”

Guariglia says that through the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill that passed last year, the Department of Homeland Security received roughly $170 billion in new funding. He says the department has so much money now that it can throw a lot of it toward “dangerous technologies.”

“What concerns me most right now is the interoperability of all these different devices and the capacity to fuse all of that data,” Guariglia says. “It’s not just license plate readers tracking where you move. It’s license plate readers tracking where you move, superimposed with information police get from protests and with social media posts, all of it digested and analyzed by AI.”

Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections tomorrow morning, but a growing number of GOP senators are calling for a delay to discuss how contenders plan to lead in the wake of historic losses among their ranks.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., wrote in a letter he plans to send today to Senate Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., that senators should meet tomorrow morning instead to hear “what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

The White House has mostly been without a press secretary since late August, after Karoline Leavitt left the administration. Katie Zacharia briefly replaced Leavitt, but she left after just five days.

text:
In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.

"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.

Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped.

"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."

The political fallout

Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling. Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."

That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.

"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.

In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.

"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.

Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.

"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.

What could the new Congress actually do?

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.

ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.

It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.

Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.

"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."

He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.

The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."

Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday, a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.

Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.

"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."

The Trump Administration vows that "Deportations will continue".

The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : "Deportations will continue."

Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.

He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.

Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."

Could we see more oversight on ICE detention facilities?

The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.

The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.

The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?

CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."

text:
Donald Trump has admitted that his deportation policy was “too tough” and has offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in a concession after the Republicans’ disastrous defeat in the midterm elections.

In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.

Trump was asked by the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

The president’s comments were an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis this year.

The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”.

Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years.

“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

Trump suggested Democrats were receptive to a compromise, saying some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.”

Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance, that the conflict had been a significant factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel.

He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”

He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms.

In a separate interview with CNN, the president said a renewed assault on Iran was “highly unlikely” but warned that his decision “depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement”.

On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said.

Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, despite having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.”

The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House.

Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son.

Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial, in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.”

But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X, arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains.

Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case.

Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.”

He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, while declining to rule out other contenders.

The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military.

At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including the former FBI director James Comey and the former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.”

Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime, and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on, help me out here.”

But Trump remained adamant: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”

Douthat noted that many presidents were remembered with a single line, such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war”, and asked what line would Trump’s presidency be remembered with.

The president said: “That I made America great again.”

text:
Hearings commence Monday in a constitutional challenge to Canada’s inhumane practice of sending most refugees crossing the border into our country back to the United States — where they face abusive detention at the hands of ICE and other enforcement agencies and deportation to countries from which they had fled.

The plaintiffs in the case include Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees (CCR), and The Canadian Council for Churches, along with former refugee claimants whose humanrights were infringed because of Canada’s Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA) with the United States. Collectively, they will argue that Canada’s participation in the agreement unfairly discriminates against racialized women, LGBTQI+ people, and children and thus violates equality rights enshrined under Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Take action: Tell Canada to end the Safe Third Country Agreement with the U.S.

Learn more: Canada’s Safe Third Country Agreement with the U.S

“The United States is not a safe place for migrants and refugees, particularly those who are racialized women, children, or LGBTQI+ people,” said Ketty Nivyabandi, Secretary General of Amnesty International Canada’s English-speaking section. “The practice of sending some of the most vulnerable people in society back to the U.S. — right into the hands of ICE — is unjust and un-Canadian. And we are in court today to make it stop.”

Under the STCA, most refugee claimants who arrive at the U.S.-Canada land and water border seeking protection in Canada are denied entry and turned back to the U.S. First implemented two decades ago, the agreement is based on the false premise that both countries reliably respect people’s right to seek asylum.

“The evidence we present in this case, and the horrors of ICE that Canadians can see unfolding on their news screens, make it clear that the U.S. asylum system is broken and dangerous — particularly for racialized women, children, and LGBTQIA+ refugees,” said CCR President Asma Faizi. “Since the Canadian government is not acting on what is plain for all to see, we are asking the court to strike down the designation of the U.S. as a safe country for refugees.”

Janet Anstead, General Secretary of The Canadian Council of Churches, said: “The member churches of The Canadian Council of Churches are united in their commitment to the understanding that each person bears the image of our Creator and thus each and every person deserves dignity, respect, compassion, and peace. The treatment of individuals, especially the most vulnerable, under the U.S. asylum system is antithetical to our core Christian values. We are grateful to stand in solidarity with Amnesty International Canada and the Canadian Council for Refugees as we insist that Canada stay true to its ideals as enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.”

Multiple court challenges target Canada’s participation in Safe Third Country Agreement

In 2023, at an earlier stage in this legal challenge, the Supreme Court of Canada sent constitutional questions about the agreement’s compliance under s. 15 of the Charter back to the Federal Court for consideration.

Amnesty International Canada and the Canadian Council for Refugees are involved in an additional court case regarding the implementation of the STCA at the border. In this separate case, announced in June, the organizations argue that Canada has failed to make available constitutionally required “safety valves” that would stop deportation to the U.S. if a person was at risk of unfair detention or refoulement.

The practical effect is that, under the STCA, Canada is sending refugee claimants back to the U.S., where they face detention in inhumane conditions at the hands of ICE and deportation into danger in their countries of origin. This was true before U.S. President Donald Trump re-assumed office in January 2025. However, the human rights risks have skyrocketed since his administration embarked on a racist campaign of mass detention and deportation, in defiance of international law, on a scale unprecedented in modern American history. Widespread human rights violations documented by Amnesty International have led the movement’s global leadership to call for, among other urgently needed changes, the abolition of ICE.

Representing the three organizations in Federal Court are lawyers Kate Webster, Heather Neufeld, and Nadia Nadeem, with Prasanna Balasundaram and Jared Will representing the individual applicants.

“We are immensely grateful to our counsel team for devoting their time and talent to protect women, children, and LGBTQI+ people whose rights hang in the balance,” Faizi said.

title: 'Nuclear Option' Move Overrules Judges, Keeps Immigrants Jailed - Bloomberg Law
authors: John Holland, Owen Auston-Babcock, Andrew Wallender
description:

In at least 12 cases, judges questioned “the governmental interest in continued detention of these least-dangerous individuals,” using the exact language cited in previous rulings.

text:
She followed her parents across the US border, because that’s what 9-year-olds do.

In the three decades since, she graduated from high school, opened her own painting business, paid taxes, and raised three US citizen children. Teachers, parents, and church members raved about her contribution to the town of Olathe, Colorado, population 2,000.

Everything changed on July 29, 2025, when ICE agents pulled Maria Teresa Alfaro from her car and put her in a Colorado prison. That began a nine-month ordeal that continued even after an immigration judge canceled her deportation order, praised her “exceptionally fine” character, and ordered her free on bond.

Instead of letting her go, government lawyers invoked an obscure 9/11-era rule aimed at suspected terrorists — one federal judges have long found unconstitutional — to overrule the bond order. The tactic, called an automatic stay appeal, has been used more than 900 times in the second Trump administration, compared to a handful of times in the previous six years, Bloomberg Law found in analyzing government data and hundreds of habeas corpus petitions filed in federal court.

Judges are overwhelmingly rejecting the practice when detainees challenge it in habeas petitions. Out of 147 automatic stay decisions to reach a final opinion since Trump returned to office, judges ordered petitioners freed 128 times, most often on constitutional due-process grounds. Judges found the automatic stay legal only five times during that period, Bloomberg Law found. The remaining 14 didn’t reach a decision on the merits.

“Troublingly, the respondents do not even attempt to articulate a case for the automatic stay’s legality,” Sarah Evans Barker, senior judge in the US District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, wrote while granting a 2025 habeas petition. Barker, an appointee of President Ronald Reagan, also awarded $8,400 in attorney’s fees, writing that federal judges “unanimously” ruled against the government.

“In short, there is no legal authority—save for the existence of the regulation itself—to support the government’s position that the regulation was lawful,” Barker wrote.

The tactic is applied only to people immigration judges have already ordered released, usually after finding they pose no danger and aren’t likely to flee. The government doesn’t have to explain its reasoning when invoking the stay, which can keep immigrants behind bars for months or longer while their appeal plays out.

Government lawyers sometimes acknowledge in court pleadings that they will lose, but continue defending the stays anyway. Judges have responded at least seven times by taking the unusual step of awarding attorney’s fees, of as much as $40,000, to the petitioners.

In at least 12 cases, judges questioned “the governmental interest in continued detention of these least-dangerous individuals,” using the exact language cited in previous rulings.

“If enforced by the Court, the automatic stay regulation would destroy that due process by permitting unilateral governmental detention,” Judge Leonie M. Brinkema of the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton, wrote in a 2025 case. “In essence, the automatic stay provision renders the Immigration Judge’s bail determination an empty gesture.”

The Department of Homeland Security didn’t make an official available for an interview or answer detailed emailed questions. The agency said in a statement that the use of the automatic stay is a “tool” it’s legally entitled to use.

“We will never apologize for or hesitate to use legally available tools to enforce the law and defend the homeland,” the agency said.

The EOIR-43

Bloomberg Law reviewed thousands of pages of habeas petitions, immigration court rulings, photo exhibits, affidavits, and government responses from courts around the US.

The records reflect decades of ordinary life in America. Marriage certificates and birth announcements. Parents, children, and spouses of US citizens and military service members. Driver’s licenses and green cards. Even a photocopy of a Covid-19 vaccination card.

Petitioners came to the US as young as 3 years old. Sworn statements from church members, school officials, and bosses create a record that immigration judges rely on to grant bond, often at the minimum $1,500 level.

That’s when the government invokes the automatic stay appeal, known as a form EOIR-43.

The only criteria are that the form must be filed within one business day and be approved by a senior DHS official. That places a hold on bond payments and gives the government 10 days to file a formal appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals. The stay applies for up to 90 days, but DHS lawyers can and have invoked extensions that can keep the petitioners for months longer.

“In other words, the prosecuting officials who failed to convince the IJ to keep (my client) can unilaterally block the IJ’s order and force continued detention,” Colorado attorney Skylar Larson wrote in one habeas petition.

Federal judges are questioning the motives of some of the appeals.

The decision “is made by a senior DHS legal official who has necessarily adopted the losing position taken by their agency before the Immigration Judge,” Judge Susan M. Bazis, a Joe Biden appointee, wrote in a 2025 Nebraska district court case. “That does not inspire much confidence that every appeal really is meritorious.”

Avoiding Bad Law

In some cases, government lawyers argue that the automatic stay provision is legal because bond decisions aren’t final until the appeal is heard by the BIA, which is part of the Justice Department.

“Simply because an IJ has set a bond amount, does not mean that a final, operative decision on bond has been reached by the attorney general,” Special Assistant US Attorney Elizabeth Puskar wrote in a April 2, 2026, brief defending the practice.

Three of the five judges who called the automatic stay legal pointed to what they called an administration’s broad mandate to enforce immigration policy. The other two judges didn’t find the length of detention unconstitutional.

Courts should have a limited role in the process to “reflect Congress’s judgment that it is best to entrust the Executive with the responsibility of making the day-to-day determinations,” Judge Robert Jonker, a George W. Bush appointee on the US District Court for the Western District of Michigan, wrote in an April decision. He added that courts should “insulate those determinations from judicial second-guessing,” he added.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review, part of the Justice Department, declined Bloomberg Law’s request to expedite a Freedom of Information Act request seeking the total number of EOIR-43s filed in the last 12 months. DOJ last year did provide a snapshot of its use in response to a FOIA filed by Paul Moses, a former Brooklyn College journalism professor who writes for immigration news site Documented.

The response, provided by Moses to Bloomberg Law, showed the government filed 889 EOIR-43 appeals in the first eight months of the second Trump administration. The figure has since ballooned to more than 900, a Bloomberg analysis of court opinions found.

In court filings and in interviews, attorneys said the broad use of the appeals shows that the tactic is an expression of administration policy, rather than an assessment of the facts in individual cases.

“In the past, the DOJ was strategic in litigation to avoid making bad law,” said Jessica Dawgert, a former associate deputy attorney general who spent 15 years at DOJ, the last two overseeing immigration issues, before leaving last year. “Now, it seems like they just don’t care and will keep trying to get away with as much as they can.”

9/11 ‘Emergency’

On October 31, 2001, the Justice Department introduced the automatic stay appeal regulation “on an emergency basis and without public comment,” federal judges wrote at the time.

Previously, if an immigration judge granted bond, the government could file an appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals. But that took time, and in the frenzy after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, DOJ wanted to keep people locked up.

The tactic swiftly came under fire.

While the rule imposed time limits, in reality they were not limits at all, Judge William Alsup, a Clinton appointee on the Northern District of California, wrote in a 2005 opinion.

Two of the earliest cases involved not terrorists, but convicted child molesters granted bond by immigration judges. Even then, the practice was found unconstitutional by two judges.

By 2006, the newly created Department of Homeland Security introduced changes to increase accountability, including that use of automatic stays be approved by senior agency officials. If a habeas petition is filed in federal court, the Justice Department handles the defense.

“The automatic stay allows the Government to keep Petitioner detained indefinitely simply because it disagrees with what the IJ or BIA orders,” Judge Vernon S. Broderick, a Barack Obama appointee in the Southern District of New York, wrote in 2025.

Over time, the government essentially stopped using automatic stays — until President Donald Trump took office for a second time on January 20, 2025.

“We knew this tool existed, but the legality always seemed dubious so there was concern of using it, of course,” said Kerry Doyle, deputy general counsel for homeland security in the Biden administration, who later became an immigration judge. She is now a partner at Green and Spiegel LLP, a Toronto-based immigration law firm.

“It was like a nuclear option. It was in our tool box for the very worst cases, but I’m not sure we ever used it, because we didn’t want judges to take it away,” she said. “Now they are using it indiscriminately, and that’s why you are seeing so many judges reacting.”

Judges have become increasingly critical of how DHS is deploying the automatic stay.

The court “has no earthly idea what governmental interest could be served by Petitioner’s continued detention,” Judge Julie Rubin, a Biden appointee, said in a 2025 Maryland district court decision, one of the first and most cited calling the practice unconstitutional.

‘Literally a Nun’

If the government files the EOIR-43 but doesn’t make the appeal within 10 days, the person is supposed to be freed under the terms of the bond. But that isn’t happening in many cases.

One successful petitioner spent weeks in a Virginia detention center as her family was blocked from posting bond at Immigration and Customs Enforcement centers in Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. Similar scenarios have played out around the US, court records show.

“I had a case involving a nun, literally a nun,” said Jeremy Jong, an attorney with the immigration advocacy nonprofit Al Otro Lado. “I started drafting her habeas, and found out they hadn’t filed the appeal, but they still wouldn’t take the bond. She spent an extra month or two in detention when she should have been out.”

Court documents show that the number of cases involving automatic stay appeals is slowing in recent months, particularly in Colorado and Nevada, where federal judges have repeatedly rejected the practice. It’s not clear whether that’s because a new wave of immigration judges appointed under Trump is rarely granting bond — meaning there is no release order to stay — or because of the drubbing DHS has taken in court, according to attorneys and an analysis of records.

Habeas petitions are still being filed, both to enforce bond orders and to request bond hearings that never happened. In many of those, federal judges preemptively block the government from using automatic stays should bond be awarded — issuing more than 270 prohibitions on automatic stays.

“This Court has found that ‘the automatic stay provision imposed in immigration cases constitutes an unequivocal violation of due process,’” Judge Roderick Young of the Eastern District of Virginia, a Trump appointee, wrote in an October 29 order enjoining the government from using the automatic stay.

Nine Months Before Freedom

An immigration court judge spent pages outlining reasons Maria Teresa Alfaro, 42, shouldn’t be sent back to Mexico, a country she left 33 years earlier as a child and hadn’t seen since.

By the time of her first hearing, Alfaro had already spent three months inside the ICE detention center in Aurora, Colordao. The time “away from her children provides a clear picture of what life will be like for them,” Immigration Judge Alison Kane wrote.

The picture “will be academically and emotionally devastating,” she added in Nov. 8, 2025, order canceling her deportation.

Kane also pointed to Alfaro’s “unquestionably” fine character, integrity, and honesty, based on testimony from friends and family, and the judge’s own observations in court. She’d never been arrested, always paid her taxes, and ran a business. She lost her protections under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program only because of a technical mistake on an online renewal form.

“She is also not at fault for entering the United States as she did, since she was a child — only 9 years old — when her parents brought her to this country,” Kane wrote.

Kane set Alfaro’s bond at $1,500, and also cancelled her deportation order, putting her on a path to obtaining a Green Card. Government lawyers immediately appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals, invoking the automatic stay provision.

Five more months passed, until Judge Philip A. Brimmer in Colorado, a George W. Bush appointee, ordered Alfaro’s immediate release on April 7. But Alfaro’s ordeal wasn’t quite over.

Three times her family posted the bond, and three times ICE refused to accept it. That prompted yet more court filings. Finally, eight days after Brimmer’s order, and nine months after being swept up by ICE, Alfaro was released.

Methodology

The cases in this article are drawn from about 750 federal district court opinions in Bloomberg Law’s platform that were identified using keyword searches for immigration habeas cases that mentioned the automatic stay through Oct. 31, 2026. A large-language model categorized details from the opinions, such as when DHS invoked the automatic stay regulation after an immigration judge granted bond or when judges blocked the government from invoking it in the future. Reporters manually reviewed a random sample of the model’s outputs to verify their accuracy. When cases had multiple published opinions, the date of the most recent ruling was considered to group the cases by month and year.

LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC) - A former Forest Hill police chief and an Oakdale businessman are scheduled to be sentenced Monday for their connection to an immigration fraud scheme.

Former Forest Hill Police Chief Glynn Dixon and Oakdale businessman Chandrakant Patel are scheduled to appear at 3 p.m. in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana on Monday, November 9th, according to federal court filings. The two previously pleaded guilty.

Former Oakdale police chief, city marshal sentenced in immigration fraud scheme

Former Oakdale police chief, local officials plead guilty in immigration fraud scheme

Former La. public officials, businessman to plead guilty in immigration fraud scheme

Investigators say Patel paid law enforcement officials to make fake crime reports that listed foreign nationals as victims so they could stay in the U.S.

Dixon faces up to five years in prison. Patel faces up to 15 years.

Previous Sentencing

The pair are only two of the five total men who pleaded guilty in the federal court case. Court filings show Patel and Dixon’s sentencing was delayed from the original date of October 22nd.

text:
In the wake of the midterm elections, President Donald Trump acknowledged that he felt as if his deportation agenda had gone too far and hurt his party with voters.

"I think it was too tough," Trump said in an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" that aired Sunday night. "And I think -- I think ultimately, that hurt me," he added.

The acknowledgement from Trump comes as the president just elevated one of the key architects of that policy, Stephen Miller, to replace former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles on Monday.

While Trump said the overhaul of immigration enforcement was a factor in the Republican Party's losses across the country during the midterms, he stood behind his administration's decisions on border security and "getting the bad ones out."

He said the backlash came down to deporting immigrants who had "good jobs."

"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs," Trump said.

On the prospect of a possible immigration deal with Democrats following midterms, Trump acknowledged that he was open to negotiating with the opposition to try and strike a deal to create possible paths for some immigrants.

"I'd love to do something on immigration," Trump said when asked about something he thinks he can work with Democrats on.

"Well, the deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something -- I think that's something that's actually doable," Trump said.

Trump referenced immigrants who worked as cleaners, waitresses and landscapers. "When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's worked there as a, you know, as a maid, as a cleaner ... as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs. And all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country. It's tough. It's a tough thing."

"Let the people that are here and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them," Trump said.

On a potential deal, Trump asserted, "People have already called me," though he did not say who.

Asked if he could refrain from insulting Democrats for six months in order to strike a deal, Trump said that he could.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday said that his deportation policy for undocumented immigrants was "too tough" for voters and he can work with the Democrats in the new Congress to craft an immigration deal.

Speaking during his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm election, Trump said his deportation policy may have been part of the reason Republicans lost.

"I think it was too tough," Trump said. "I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough."

In his interview to CBS that aired on Sunday, Trump said that he can find a way to work with the Democrats.

"The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something — I think that's something that's actually doable," he said in the interview.

Trump did not share the details of what the immigration deal would look like but shortly after the interview he appointed Stephen Miller, who designed the Trump administration's hardline deportation policy, as his chief of staff.

In his tenure, Trump's administration has aggressively pushed to deport millions of undocumented migrants which drew widespread criticism.

text:
DES PLAINES, Ill. (WLS) -- The daughters of a suburban Chicago woman ordered released on bond are traveling to Kentucky as they wait to learn whether the Department of Homeland Security will challenge the decision.

A federal immigration judge ordered Beata Siemionkowicz released Friday, but she remained in custody because DHS has 24 business hours to challenge the order. Her daughters, Gabi and Claudia Siemionkowicz, planned to leave late Sunday with some of their mother's favorite foods.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

For the past 15 months, the sisters' contact with their mother has been limited to two 15-minute video calls each week.

"I feel like she's been still confused this entire time. She's like, I tried to come here legally, tried to come here the right way, the right paperwork," Claudia Siemionkowicz said.

Siemionkowicz, a green card holder from Poland, has been in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody in Kentucky since August 2025. Masked ICE agents detained her while at her eldest daughter's home in Des Plaines.

"I was at work, which is, like, 20 minutes away. She was here, gardening in my backyard," Claudia said.

DHS seeks to deport Siemionkowicz based on two misdemeanor shoplifting charges from 2005 and 2011. She was held without a bond hearing until last week.

"Both of those charges and convictions were contextualized by an immigration judge on Friday as a byproduct of a domestic violence abusive relationship she was in," said Hirsch Joshi, an attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union.

Officials also accused Siemionkowicz of using forged documents in Poland to obtain immigration benefits in the United States. Her daughters said a background check in Poland found no evidence supporting the allegation.

"There's nothing. There is no evidence. They didn't even bring it up once in court," Gabi Siemionkowicz said.

Gabi, who lived with her mother in Round Lake, dropped out of school and got a job to cover the mortgage after her mother was detained.

"I almost got evicted twice. And it was super scary, because I knew it was my responsibility now. And I had so much thrown onto me," she said.

The sisters remained cautious as they prepared for the trip to Kentucky.

"I feel like it's still kind of a shock. I'm not going to believe it until she's physically here with me," Claudia said.

DHS issued a statement on Siemionkowicz's case.

"ICE complies with all lawful court orders," the department said. Adding, "For decades, Siemionkowicz has made a mockery of our immigration system and our laws...She will remain in ICE custody pending her removal."

When pressed, DHS would not confirm whether it planned to challenge the order releasing Siemionkowicz on bond. The judge's decision does not change the deportation order against her, but release would allow her to continue fighting it from home.

An 8-year-old Haitian boy who lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year was taken into federal custody after an immigration check-in, according to local advocates and school officials.

The third grader, who attends Fay Elementary School in San Diego, was placed into government custody alone after attending an Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointment with his uncle on Thursday, according to his school district and an advocacy group.

“The eight-year-old received a letter to meet with an ICE agent,” the San Diego Unified School District said in a letter to DHS. “His uncle, with whom he’s been living since the child’s father was deported more than a year ago, took him to meet the agent because he did not want to break the law.”

Advocates and school officials said the boy had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year.

"They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance.

Cody Petterson, a board trustee with the SDUSD, told ABC News the uncle was designated on school records as an authorized caregiver.

A spokesperson for ICE told ABC News in a statement that because the uncle could not establish legal guardianship, agents treated the 8-year-old as an unaccompanied child under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, a federal law that provides protections for unaccompanied immigrant children.

The agency did not allege any wrongdoing or abuse by the uncle, but invoked the law to mandate the child's transfer after designating him as an unaccompanied minor.

"Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," the spokesperson said.

According to the school district and an advocacy group, the 8-year-old remains in ORR custody. It is unclear if he will be removed from the U.S.

Jozef called the detention "an excuse for [ICE] to remove the child and potentially put him in deportation proceedings.”

“He was dressed very well, and he is very well cared for,” Jozef added. “There's absolutely no reason for them to remove him from the care of his relatives without putting in place proper procedures for him, knowing very well that ICE already deported the father.”

In the letter to DHS, San Diego Unified School District officials said they have “witnessed situations in which children who should be attending school and participating in a supportive educational environment instead find themselves in government facilities.”

“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” the district said.

text:
US President Donald Trump has said his immigration crackdown was "too tough", marking one of his clearest public retreats from a defining plank of his political agenda, following his party's drubbing in the midterm elections.

In an interview with CBS' 60 Minutes programme, Trump said he believed he deserved an "A plus" for drastically limiting illegal border crossings, but he had been politically "hurt" by sweeping deportations.

His acknowledgement came despite his homeland security department insisting it was not backing away from the crackdown.

Election day polling indicated immigration was the third most important issue for midterm voters, after the economy and the state of democracy.

In historically conservative states like Texas, a swing of Latino voters towards Democrats helped seal the Democratic Party's landslide majorities in Congress.

The president told 60 Minutes that immigration "both helped and hurt" his fellow Republicans in Tuesday's midterms.

"I think I got an A plus for closing up the border," he said in the programme that aired on Sunday evening.

He added: "For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.

"But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

"I think it was too tough," the president said.

Trump also said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats, without offering details.

In a previous interview with 60 Minutes a year ago, a defiant Trump insisted his administraiton's immigration raids "haven't gone far enough".

His conciliatory words on Sunday were an abrupt change in tone from a White House statement earlier in the day to the BBC.

A spokeswoman vowed "the administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorise our communities".

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also showed no sign of a U-turn on Sunday.

"ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down," a DHS spokesperson told the BBC.

Following Tuesday's electoral losses, Vice-President JD Vance had appeared receptive to adjusting their immigration strategy.

"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance," Vance wrote in a lengthy online post reflecting on the results.

However, Trump's promotion on Friday of immigration hawk Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff signalled no climbdown from the administration.

Miller is widely seen as the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policy during the first and second Trump presidencies.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sources told CBS that in recent weeks officials have been instructed to aim for about 2,700 arrests of illegal immigrants per day, an increase from an earlier 2,000 daily arrest target.

text:
In an interview with 60 Minutes, President Trump said his administration's hardline approach to immigration enforcement around deportations may have been "too tough" in pursuing people in the country for a decade or more.

The president spoke with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat three days after Republicans faced jarring losses in the midterm elections. Support for the party plummeted in South Texas and other heavily Latino areas that trended toward the GOP two years ago — a reversal that many voters linked at least in part to Mr. Trump's immigration crackdown.

Mr. Trump said his immigration crackdown "both helped and hurt" him at the polls. He believes he "got an A+ for closing up the border," and got "very high marks for getting the bad ones out."

"But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally," the president continued. "Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

He continued: "I think it was too tough."

"A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough," he said.

The president also said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate starting next year.

It's unclear whether the Trump administration is planning to alter its immigration enforcement strategy. On Friday, Mr. Trump replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, a hardliner who is widely viewed as an architect of the Trump administration's immigration policies.

The president's 2024 victory was fueled partly by voters' discontent with former President Joe Biden's immigration policies, including the surge in unauthorized U.S.-Mexico border crossings.

Since Mr. Trump's return to the White House, illegal border crossings have fallen dramatically. Federal officials have also ramped up arrests and deportations in the interior of the country, with the number of people detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement charting record highs. Miller pushed the agency to aim for 3,000 arrests per day last year.

A large share of the arrestees do not have criminal records beyond immigration offenses. The Trump administration has long said its priority is to arrest the "worst first," while warning that anybody who is in the U.S. illegally can be arrested and deported.

And many of the administration's immigration tactics have drawn scrutiny, including its citywide crackdowns in Minneapolis and elsewhere, its vehicle stops, its detention practices and its practice of deporting some migrants to places other than their home country.

Some Republicans have pushed back, with Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar of South Florida warning in September that many Hispanics who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 "feel betrayed."

In exit polling, 58% think the Trump administration's actions on immigration have gone too far. Still, on the question of which party voters think is better able to handle immigration, voters trust Republicans (43%) slightly more than Democrats (41%).

The administration has defended its approach, saying it is targeting public safety threats.

text:
A Round Lake mother who has been held by ICE in a Kentucky jail for more than a year over two retail theft cases, the most recent from 15 years ago, is being detained in violation of her due process rights, a federal judge ruled.

Beata Siemionkowicz, 57, of Round Lake, has been held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for more than 15 months, mostly at the Campbell County Detention Center in Newport, Kentucky.

U.S. District Judge Karen K. Caldwell of the Eastern District of Kentucky granted Siemionkowicz’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus on Tuesday and ordered the government to give her an individualized bond hearing within seven days.

Caldwell said in her ruling that the government must show by clear and convincing evidence that Siemionkowicz’s continued detention is necessary.

Siemionkowicz, a native and citizen of Poland, was admitted to the United States on a visitor visa in November 1995 and became a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green card holder, in 2003, according to a petition filed on her behalf in federal court.

She raised two daughters, both U.S. citizens, and worked for many years as a caregiver, the petition said.

Siemionkowicz pleaded guilty in two misdemeanor retail theft cases in Lake County, including retail theft of less than $150 in 2005 and retail theft of less than $300 in 2011, court documents show.

She received court supervision in the first case and conditional discharge in the second, according to the petition, which noted that court supervision is not a conviction under Illinois law but may count as one for immigration purposes.

She has not been convicted of or arrested for any crime in more than 15 years, the petition said.

ICE agents arrested Siemionkowicz outside her daughter’s home on August 2, 2025.

She was served a notice to appear the same day charging her as deportable for having committed two crimes involving moral turpitude, court documents said.

Immigration Judge Kelly Johnson of the Memphis Immigration Court denied Siemionkowicz’s request for bond on August 26, 2025, determining she had not proved she was not a “flight risk,” court records show.

The burden of proof at that hearing was placed on Siemionkowicz rather than the government, the petition said.

Johnson denied Siemionkowicz’s application for cancellation of removal in December 2025 and ordered her removed to Poland, a decision she has appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Attorneys with the ACLU of Kentucky and the ACLU of Illinois filed the petition on September 10 in federal court in Covington, Kentucky, naming Campbell County Jailer James A. Daley and federal immigration officials.

The petition asks that Siemionkowicz be released or given a new hearing, at which the government would have to justify her detention.

The government argued that Siemionkowicz is subject to mandatory detention because she is deportable for two crimes involving moral turpitude, that she is not entitled to a bond hearing and that her due process rights had not been violated.

Caldwell found that the two retail thefts are crimes involving moral turpitude that make Siemionkowicz deportable, a point she did not dispute, and that she is held under the federal law requiring mandatory detention of certain non-citizens with no statutory right to a bond hearing.

Caldwell noted that the U.S. Supreme Court said in a 2003 case that most such detentions last less than 90 days.

Caldwell weighed the three factors courts use under a 1976 U.S. Supreme Court case, Mathews v. Eldridge, to decide whether due process requires more safeguards — Siemionkowicz’s interest in her freedom, the risk of an error under the procedures used and the government’s interest.

Caldwell said Siemionkowicz has been detained longer than the Supreme Court contemplated in the 2003 case and that the risk of wrongly depriving her of her liberty “is high if she does not receive a hearing.”

The judge said a hearing for Siemionkowicz “would not undermine the Government’s interest.”

“Finding that all three Mathews factors weigh in Siemionkowicz’s favor, the Court holds that her detention violates due process,” Caldwell said.

“My sister and I are grateful to the court. This ruling gives us hope that we might be able to hug our mother soon,” Gabi Siemionkowicz, Beata Siemionkowicz’s younger daughter, said in a statement Wednesday.

“All we want is a fair chance for our mother in the courts,” Claudia Siemionkowicz, Beata Siemionkowicz’s older daughter, said.

Claudia Siemionkowicz said the family hopes the ruling is a step toward getting her mother back to “the family that loves her.”

ACLU of Illinois Staff Attorney Hirsh M. Joshi said the court recognized that Siemionkowicz’s lengthy detention merits a new bond hearing with the burden on the government to show she should still be detained.

“Our client is a hard-working mother, someone who has cared for hospice patients. Her detention serves no purpose other than cruelty,” Joshi said.

ACLU of Kentucky Staff Attorney Bethany Baxter said the ACLU has maintained from the beginning that the government should bear the burden of justifying why someone should remain detained and is pleased the court recognized “the serious constitutional concerns at stake.”

“We hope this ruling brings Beata one step closer to returning home to the family that has fought so hard for her,” Baxter said.

The ACLU said Siemionkowicz has never been charged with or convicted of a violent crime and that her case drew attention from the office of U.S. Sen. Richard Durbin because of her daughters’ advocacy.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said that Siemionkowicz was twice convicted of retail theft and is “wanted in her home country of Poland for convincing individuals to forge documents.”

The spokesperson said Siemionkowicz’s green card was revoked following her convictions and that an immigration judge issued her a final order of removal on December 9, 2025.

The spokesperson said Siemionkowicz became a green card holder in 2000, while court documents and the petition said it was 2003.

The government must file a status report with the court by November 17 saying when the bond hearing was held, whether bond was granted and the reasons if it was denied.

Wisconsin state trooper Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe has been released from ICE custody after he was detained while attempting to board a domestic flight Thursday. The South African native moved to the U.S. aged 14, with his lawyers stating that—while having waited seven years and counting for his asylum case to be addressed—he has a valid work permit up until 2030. DHS owes this family more than silence.” Van Der Merwe graduated as a state patrol trooper in 2025, in a ceremony overseen by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers.
