text:
Donald Trump set the stage for his administration to lurch further to the right this weekend, claiming the US had taken a “giant step back” by widely rejecting his party.

The US president’s hardline aide, Stephen Miller, will begin as White House chief of staff on Monday. He will also meet with Dana White, CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, after offering him the job of press secretary.

“America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election,” Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, citing the sharp sell-off in global markets, fueled a rout of US tech stocks. “But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!”

Despite Republicans losing control of both chambers of US Congress in Tuesday’s decisive US midterm elections, and voters across the country expressing frustration with key pillars of Trump’s controversial agenda, from the Iran war to sweeping tariffs, the administration appears set to press ahead.

Miller’s promotion has stoked expectations that Trump is poised to double down on an aggressive immigration crackdown, stoke cultural war battles, and refuse concessions to the new Democratic majority in Congress. The move “signals the administration is going to ⁠have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years”, Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor and energy executive, told Reuters.

Trump abruptly announced on Saturday that he had offered White, whom he described as “a violent Fighter and Warrior”, the role of White House press secretary, which has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt departed the administration this summer. Leavitt initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, lasted five days in the job.

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” said Trump. “Dana, please take the job!”

After Trump also threatened Democrats planning to conduct oversight of his administration and family, announcing he had ordered the US Department of Justice to “look into” them, attorney general Todd Blanche told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that “there could be” investigations. Republicans have faced “dangerous” threats, Blanche claimed, without specifying what crimes he believed had been committed. “You have to draw the line.”

Democrats have made clear that Miller and Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and a close Trump ally, are likely to be targets of congressional investigations once the party retakes control of Congress in January.

Congressman Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, who is set to chair the powerful oversight committee in the House of Representatives next year, said on Sunday that investigations are set to explore Musk’s involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency’s mass firing of federal workers last year, and Miller’s role in Trump’s immigration crackdown. “I think there’s a lot ⁠of interest – not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress – to speak to Mr Musk,” Garcia told CNN.

Representative Jamie Raskin, poised to become the chair of the House judiciary committee, has also requested information on the business dealings of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.

With 33 of 35 Senate races called, the Democrats had won 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44. Votes are still being counted in Alaska, which had long been seen as a key battleground, and Mississippi, a previous Republican stronghold which remains too close to call.

Congressman James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky who currently heads the House oversight committee before his party cedes control to Democrats, told Fox News that the committee is going to dedicate the last two months of this congress investigating Alaska over the controversy surrounding its Senate race.

Trump has already threatened Democratic candidate Mary Peltola with criminal prosecution over reports that her campaign was linked to the recruitment of a second “Dan Sullivan” in Alaska’s Senate race, with the same name as the Republican candidate.

Democrats meanwhile embarked on a victory lap this weekend, celebrating their historic wins on Tuesday. Democratic candidates won after running on policies that would “change working peoples’ lives”, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani told Fox News on Sunday.

“We are seeing a moment in time where working class Americans have made very clear that they are tired of waiting,” said Mamdani. “They are tired of being told, again and again, that there is less for them to make ends meet, while we see the world’s first trillionaire emerge in Elon Musk.”

But there has been friction within the party regarding the incoming congressional leadership, with Chuck Schumer set to become the next majority leader in the US Senate Hakeem Jeffries widely expected to become House speaker.

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas – the first Democrat the state has sent to the US Senate in almost a century – told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday the Schumer is a “kind of polarizing figure” adding: “It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas, and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”

The celebrations continued, though.

During a Saturday Night Live skit this weekend, a member of the cast impersonated Trump attacking James Talarico, the Democrat who ran for US Senate in Texas, and called him “Talafreako” – only for Talarico himself to walk out on stage.

text:
At least two Afghan refugees have been detained by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Sacramento area of California, sparking concern among refugee advocacy organizations and the Afghan community. These detentions come amid a federal plan initiated under the previous US administration led by Donald Trump, aiming to deport nearly 150 Afghans held in immigration detention centers. Court documents reveal a plan to transfer these individuals to Pakistan and then to Afghanistan. Human rights groups have warned that returning them to a country controlled by the Taliban regime poses risks of retaliation and torture, especially for those who collaborated with US forces or Western entities.

Over 60 members of the US Congress have jointly sent a letter to the Secretary of State and Acting Secretary of Homeland Security, urging the cancellation of deportation flights targeting Afghan and Iranian refugees, including those deported through third countries. They emphasized that sending these individuals back to Afghanistan could result in abuse, torture, or even death.

Shawn VanDiver, head of the Afghan Evacuation organization, noted that this deportation plan includes individuals who served alongside US forces and trusted America. Democratic representative Doris Matsui expressed concern that Afghan families who supported US forces are among those at risk of deportation, with some losing their legal protections under new government policies.

Nazar Ahmad, a former translator for US forces and member of the Afghan-American coalition, also expressed dismay over the plan, warning that anyone on these flights could be personally at risk. He fears that Afghans who came to the US seeking security might be handed over to those who previously opposed US forces.

A federal court ruling in New York in early November has temporarily halted immediate deportations to Afghanistan or Pakistan and ordered that certain individuals must be notified prior to any deportations to these or other countries. However, this ruling does not constitute a general ban on ICE detentions or investigations, and it remains unclear whether the detainees in Sacramento are included in this protected group.

US Immigration and the Department of Homeland Security have told the media that they respect all legal orders. No additional information has been disclosed regarding the identity, immigration status, or current location of the two detained Afghan refugees in Sacramento.

These developments unfold as Afghanistan, under Taliban rule, faces extensive security and human rights threats, and forced returns of refugees could endanger their lives.

text:
The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.

Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.

"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."

A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.

Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."

The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.

Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.

That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Congress can also demand internal documents, like use-of-force reports.

"They can dissect these individual shootings, and really unravel the story of what happened," says Naureen Shah, who leads the ACLU's immigration policy work.

Democrats have already held shadow hearings on the ICE shootings, during which they've called in family members and witnesses to testify.

But Shah says now Congress can ask key questions of top decision makers: What orders were given to immigration officers in the field? What was training like for these officers?

Who made the decision to paint Good and Pretti as threats, including calling Pretti a "would-be assassin" and a domestic terrorist, when video showed otherwise?

"It's like we can turn the faucet on and actually find out so much more," Shah says. "There's an aspect of this that is really about a kind of reckoning with how it's possible that things that seemed unthinkable could happen on American streets. How do you have that reckoning if you don't actually have the ability to force people to explain themselves?"

Democratic leaders have already said that's the plan.

Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, told NPR in a statement that Congress will use "every tool" at its disposal to investigate ICE and that it is time for the agency to "start answering to the American people."

California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, vowed to take on DHS and ICE abuses in a two-word statement: "Lawyer Up."

Mississippi Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter on Wednesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, demanding the agency "comply with all document preservation requirements."

Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez wrote on social media that Noem, Miller, Homan, Bovino and Mullin should "clear" their schedules.

In response to that, DHS general counsel James Percival said Democrats are "more interested in political shenanigans than in governing" but said the agency is prepared to "deal with this nonsense."

There are key limitations to what Democrats in Congress can do with their majority when it comes to ICE accountability, says Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.

Major changes, like clawing back funding for the agency, would require a veto-proof majority, something the Democrats don't have.

"You still have a president who has shown a complete lack of interest in accountability for federal agents and in fact, a great deal of knee jerk defensiveness about their conduct," Moran says.

In a statement, a White House spokesperson told NPR "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Democrats, the statement added, "should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

But that's not true. Congress has its own powers, one of them being the ability to compel testimony. Moran says a deeper probe into the shootings could still serve important purposes, like making evidence available for states to use in their own criminal investigations.

Minnesota officials, for instance, have been fighting with the federal government to get evidence related to the Pretti and Good killings.

Brent Ganger, Renee Good's brother, says learning more information about his sister's death will be hard to hear, "but I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day. I don't want history to keep repeating itself."

It was painful, he says, to watch immigration agents kill more people after his sister. He thought her death would be a turning point. In a way, it might have been the start of one. After the surge in Minneapolis, most Americans said ICE had gone too far.

Ganger, who considers himself a moderate, was happy to see the Blue Wave this week. On election night, he was scrolling Instagram when he saw a photo of his sister's memorial site, with all the "I Voted" stickers.

"I was very grateful to see the repudiation of this administration from the country. It felt very supportive of my entire family," he says.

The next morning, in his home in Colorado, he got up and made biscuits and gravy, his sister's favorite breakfast.

Voters on Saturday rejected a measure that would have weakened California’s landmark environmental law by fast-tracking reviews for some projects.

With about 76% of votes counted, voters rejected Prop. 45 by 55.7% to 44.3%.

The vote maintains the status quo under the state’s Environmental Quality Act, which since 1970 has required public agencies to review project developments that could have harmful environmental impacts, and mitigate those harms.

“Californians have sent a clear message to corporate developers, utilities and data center builders that they will not stand for a broad assault at the ballot box on state law protecting our air, water and natural resources,” No on 45’s Woody Little said. “We were outspent but not outgunned.”

Supporters had said the changes would reduce building costs. The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored Proposition 45, the Building an Affordable California Act, which would limit the length of environmental reviews for projects deemed “essential” to 365 business days and require courts to resolve litigation in 270 calendar days. Those projects include housing, water, broadband and transit developments.

Proponents said the savings from building more quickly would pass to consumers and spent $41 million campaigning for the measure. The Building a Better California political action committee was the largest donor, giving $10 million to the campaign. The organization is funded partly by current and former Google executives Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt. Two of the largest investor owned utilities, Pacific Gas & Electric Company and Southern California Edison, together donated $4.4 million.

Environmental groups argued the measure would go too far in weakening a law meant to protect people from environmental harms. Opponents, including a coalition of environmental, health and union organizations, spent $30 million trying to stop it. Wendy Schmidt, a Democratic philanthropist, was the largest donor, giving $10 million to the campaign. The political action committee Clean and Healthy California Sponsored by Environmental Organizations contributed $7 million.

The California Democratic Party opposed the measure. The California Republican Party supported it, while county Republican groups were split.

Deborah Sivas, environmental law professor at Stanford University, said Prop. 45 would radically change current law. It would shift power “away from local governments and to developers by giving them some new tools … and limiting what courts can do in terms of reviewing decisions that agencies and local governments make,” she said.

CEQA and housing

California’s environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to assess the environmental impacts of developments and help mitigate them.

Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down construction.

State legislators have tried to fix the problem by passing laws that exempt or streamline certain projects from environmental review. In 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many urban housing projects from the full review process.

But some supporters of Prop. 45, including the California Building Industry Association and the California Council for Affordable Housing, say those changes don’t go far enough.

“It’s an important piece of the puzzle, but (that type of housing) does not produce quickly or at scale,” said Jennifer Hernandez, an attorney who helped write the measure. “We need quicker, at scale, affordable housing.”

Supporters say Prop. 45 would help California redevelop large, unused sites like malls and parking lots into housing and make it easier to build away from urban areas.

Pro-housing groups, public agencies divided

Pro-housing and local government groups usually support CEQA reform, but Prop. 45 has divided many of them.

Housing advocates in the Bay Area, including East Bay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance, oppose the measure. Other Yes in My Backyard groups are neutral, including Abundant Housing Los Angeles and both California YIMBY and YIMBY Action — the movement’s two flagship advocacy groups.

The split between pro-housing groups lies in whether California should keep building outward onto undeveloped land or promote construction in urban centers. Some supporters, including Oakland Democratic Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, have said the state needs all types of housing.

Others say building away from urban centers would make it harder to address climate change.

“We believe we can (and must) solve the housing and climate crises simultaneously. That means building communities with denser housing and alternatives to automobile dependence,” wrote Max Dubler of California YIMBY in a blog post explaining the group’s neutral stance on Prop. 45.

Public agencies and local governments that could benefit from the building rules were also divided.

The California Municipal Utilities Association opposes the measure. But most other groups representing local governments, including the League of California Cities and California State Association of Counties, remained neutral.

Financial impacts for Prop. 45

Prop. 45 supporters argued that streamlining development would make life more affordable for Californians, but the long-term financial benefits are unclear.

An analysis by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimated the measure would produce $1.5 billion in savings and additional revenues for public agencies over 10 years that would reduce overall housing costs.

But the measure would initially cost local governments and public agencies more as they adjust to the measure’s rules, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, a nonpartisan adviser to the Legislature.

Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.

It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.

But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.

How young voters powered Democrats to victory

Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.

However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.

The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points; however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.

Explaining the massive shift from 2024

When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.

But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.

Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18- to 29-year-olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.

The young voters Trump lost

Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.

Democrats made gains with some young voters who backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.

Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.

How the election results broke down by age

The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.

"The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."

Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.

"I also think we shouldn't overread what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."

By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.

"Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.

"They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

Abraham Zavala was born at Adventist White Memorial. So were his kids. So late Friday, when he heard federal immigration agents were at the Boyle Heights hospital, and that local youth were out blowing whistles to warn neighbors, he went.

“To me that’s sacred ground,” said Zavala, an organizer with Unión del Barrio.

“I’m a dad,” he said. “I wanted to be there to support the youth.”

He was among the Boyle Heights residents who converged on the hospital and stayed in a standoff with federal immigration agents into the early hours of Saturday. Agents detained at least two people, according to rapid response groups.

Neighbors alerted each other with noisemakers and fireworks. A woman pounded her pots and pans. Teenagers ran across Mariachi Plaza, shouting that ICE was in the area and urging residents to lock their doors.

“Even though we’re afraid, you know we’re still showing up,” said Myra Vasquez, a Boyle Heights resident who rushed to White Memorial after hearing reports of ICE in the area. “We’re not going to allow them to just come into our communities and terrorize us because they’re the real terrorists causing harm.”

The confrontation peaked around 11:30 p.m. Video shared with Boyle Heights Beat shows agents pushing back protesters who had moved toward them, and the two sides begin shoving. Agents appear to pepper-spray people on the sidewalk. One agent then tackles a man and pins him to the ground, while a second person is pulled from the crowd. Both were detained.

The standoff continued past midnight. Zavala said agents got out of their vehicles and formed a line in front of the parking lot where paramedics enter, blocking an emergency exit. “They literally became White Memorial’s private security detail,” he said. Zavala said he and another person were sprayed with Mace.

The Dept. of Homeland Security declined to comment about the incident in Boyle Heights, and, in a statement, the agency said they would “not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations.”

The spokesperson instead said that obstructing law enforcement is a federal crime.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” the statement said, despite the large turnout of protesters who encountered the masked agents at the hospital.

Father Brendan Busse, who pastors nearby Dolores Mission Church in Boyle Heights, rushed to White Memorial after seeing reports from the Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network of ICE at the hospital.

Busse, a Jesuit priest, said he witnessed people caring for each other and tending to those suffering from pepper spray. People there advocated for them to find treatment at White Memorial, Busse said. Community members, he said, “were obviously doing their best, not just to communicate their feelings, but to push, to instigate the dispersal of this ICE presence.”

As clergy, Busse said their presence can help combat a narrative of those advocating for immigrants as “somehow dangerous, or violent, or vulgar.”

“Just to be there is a sign that that’s not the only version of what this looks like,” he said.

Initially, Busse showed up wearing a hoodie, but he decided to change into his green stole he had in his car as things appeared to get tense. “Just try to do what I could to bring a presence of maybe a little moral authority,” he said.

“It’s bad enough that people have to lift up their voices to say something so obvious, that their lives matter, that our communities are sacred, that families belong together,” Busse said. “It’s bad enough that they have to be out at 3 a.m. in the morning to tell anybody that.”

“It’s even worse if they would have to suffer the consequences of retribution and violence that comes from speaking out in that way,” Busse added.

Expect silent nights in Naples’ channels this holiday season.

The Naples Improvement Association announced Saturday that this year’s Naples Island Holiday Boat Parade, a Long Beach tradition since 1946, has been canceled because of expected high tides and heavy surf that organizers said would make the event too unsafe for visitors and participants.

It’s the first time in six years — since the onset of the COVID pandemic — that the parade has been canceled. What began as a small procession of decorated barges filled with singing church choirs has grown into an institution in Long Beach with more than 100 entries, from Duffys to dragon boats, and 60,000 spectators.

Ben Fisher, the association president, said the decision came after weeks of deliberations and a 600-respondent poll that found most wanted the parade — and all holiday events in Naples — to be canceled this year.

Forecasters expect a powerful El Niño season that will raise tides 6 to 18 inches above typical levels. This is paired with a series of slow, very wide swells of warm water known as Kelvin waves expected to frequent Long Beach’s southern-facing coast this winter.

During the week of Christmas, tides are expected to reach 7.5 to 8.5 feet, with the highest forecast to arrive in the mornings and peaking around Christmas Eve.

Part of the decision was also tied to ongoing frustrations with the city, which Fisher said has failed to address the island’s deteriorating infrastructure, from its aging seawall to underperforming drainage systems, that make it “too unsafe to draw tens of thousands of people to visit Naples this holiday season.”

“The city has told us to sandbag everything (public and private property); docks and gangways are being dismantled and sawed off however each individual owner sees fit; and the seawalls themselves are crumbling with exposed, rusted and sharp rebar in many places along the canals where many families normally would sit on any given holiday evening,” Mr. Fisher wrote.

For decades, the seawall has shielded multimillion-dollar homes and fortified the man-made canal that loops around the island. The city evaluated the structure in 2009 and found it in significant disrepair. A six-phase repair plan is underway, but only two phases are complete.

City officials have said they need $125 million to finish replacing the aging seawall, and they have halted reconstruction amid shrinking oil revenue and an uncertain future for federal disaster aid. Among the options under consideration is a 30-year bond spread across the whole neighborhood that would cost $5,100 per property annually. If limited to homes along the seawalls, it would cost $48,000 per property.

In a statement Saturday, council member Kristina Duggan, whose district includes Naples, said she respected the decision and added that the focus this winter should be on preparing the island for the upcoming weather. While the seawalls are stable under high tidal pressure, she said, maintenance work will “start next week to seal cold joints and help reduce water seepage.”

“We are encouraging everyone to prepare, and we look forward to seeing the Naples Boat Parade return next year,” Duggan wrote.

When high tides arrive, water already spills over the seawalls in some spots, reaching nearly two feet deep, flooding sidewalks and threatening homes. Residents and officials disagree over whether to prioritize coastal protection or recreational amenities.

The money normally spent on the parade will go instead toward pumps, hoses, plugs and generators, Fisher said, “resources our waterways and neighbors desperately need.”

Whether residents decorate their homes this year, he said, is up to them.

title: Opinion – What the US Midterms Cannot Undo About Operation Metro Surge
description:
During Operation Metro Surge, in Minneapolis-St. Paul, one-in-four residents who interacted with federal agents reported physical assault.
They tend to implicitly attribute the cruelty of Operation Metro Surge to President Trump’s alleged authoritarian tendencies or the frequently discussed militarization of ICE.
Yet, Modi’s government has not carried out an immigration operation comparable to Operation Metro Surge.
This distinction helps frame both what made Operation Metro Surge possible and what needs to be considered to prevent similar operations in the future.
Taking Operation Metro Surge seriously suggests that preserving liberty may require not only eternal vigilance, but also the capacity to anticipate how existing capabilities can be harnessed by actors with particular intentions to erode protections once considered secure.
text:
The morning after the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, “I voted” stickers peppered the memorials of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota. The sticker-laden tributes serve as a stark reminder that although the cruelty of U.S. immigration enforcement operations in 2025 and 2026 have largely disappeared from the news cycle, their legacy remains. During Operation Metro Surge, in Minneapolis-St. Paul, one-in-four residents who interacted with federal agents reported physical assault. Federal agents drew weapons on approach in nearly 40% of interactions and just after approach in a further 30%. The majority of people arrested (64%) had no criminal history, and over 1,000 lawsuits challenging detentions have been filed with nearly 90% resulting in court-ordered releases. These excessive and unlawful uses of force also assumed an inhumane character at times: a five-year-old and his father with legal immigration status were arrested, and a U.S. citizen was taken from his home without a warrant, paraded unclothed in the freezing Minnesota temperatures.

The traditional American emphasis on freedom from government intervention – even at the expense of providing “positive freedoms” such as healthcare – makes those infringements of personal liberties particularly difficult to reconcile. The violation of foundational protections against arbitrary arrest and extrajudicial killing by the state are especially incongruous. That these events occurred in the name of border security, 1,520 miles from the Southern border, is another reason to consider how this could happen. The few explanations presented so far are generally underdeveloped, incomplete, or one-dimensional. They tend to implicitly attribute the cruelty of Operation Metro Surge to President Trump’s alleged authoritarian tendencies or the frequently discussed militarization of ICE. However, under scrutiny, these explanations alone prove insufficient.

Explanations centered on Trump’s alleged authoritarian tendencies do not account for why similar operations have not occurred under other governments also characterized as authoritarian. India under Narendra Modi provides a case in point: Modi declared that 1.9 million undocumented Muslims were ineligible for refugee status and faced imminent detention, and he has deployed the military against citizens in the Kashmir region. Yet, Modi’s government has not carried out an immigration operation comparable to Operation Metro Surge. This suggests that authoritarian tendencies, even in combination with aggressive anti-immigration policies and a willingness to deploy force against civilians, cannot fully account for the extent of actions in the U.S. Explanations centered only on the militarization of U.S. immigration enforcement are also incomplete. That militarization significantly predates both Trump administrations and therefore does not fully explain why Operation Metro Surge occurred at all, nor why it did not occur during the first Trump administration.

Considering those factors in combination with other key factors through a lens that takes into account both cultural and political-economic factors can offer a more comprehensive explanation. Specifically, multiple conditions seem to have converged: militarized immigration enforcement institutions, decades of cultural discourse that securitized and dehumanized immigrants, record levels of unauthorized border crossings, and the leadership of Trump and his loyalist appointees. The result was a perfect storm. Some of these conditions had developed gradually over decades and under both U.S. political parties; others were more recent developments.

There were several slow-forming conditions which evolved over decades but were accelerated by Trump. The discursive framing of immigrants as national security threats - particularly since the aftermath of 9/11 made otherwise extraordinary actions, such as the deployment of 4,000 heavily armed federal troops into Minneapolis suburbs, conceivable. The dehumanisation of immigrants weakened people’s moral constraints against using force on those targeted by immigration enforcement. At the same time, the institutional capacity to carry out such actions had developed over decades. Both ICE and CBP report directly to the President and are relatively insulated from congressional and public constraints. Both were also increasingly militarized over several years by Democratic and Republican administrations. With budgets that exceed those of most national militaries, these features have made it possible over decades for those enforcement agencies to function like an executive’s army.

What changed in 2025 was who was positioned to act on these pre-existing factors. Trump accelerated these conditions and, in his second term, appointed anti-immigration loyalists who often demonstrated a willingness to resort to force. It was the combination of these pre-existing factors and Trump’s willingness to mobilize them in pursuit of an exceptionally restrictive immigration policy that drove the violent and cruel implementation of Operation Metro Surge.

The significance of this convergence is not that liberal democracies are inevitably vulnerable to any single anti-democratic actor, but rather that rights protections can erode when multiple, mutually reinforcing conditions converge in particular ways. One could argue that, given his acceleration of these conditions, Trump was a trigger and therefore the causal factor, but such an argument ignores the fact that the institutional capacity to carry out such actions already existed, and it remains in place for a future leader to exploit.

This reality ties into a commonly discussed concept in security studies: a threat can be understood as a combination of both an actor’s capabilities and their estimated intentions. Intentions are inherently uncertain and changeable, and therefore impossible to ascertain with complete confidence. Capabilities, by contrast, are more observable and relatively stable. Regardless of an actor’s intentions, the institutional capabilities they help build and mobilize can outlast them, remaining available for future actors to exploit. This distinction helps frame both what made Operation Metro Surge possible and what needs to be considered to prevent similar operations in the future. Arguments centered solely on Trump’s intentions or his characteristics as a political actor, however accurate and well-founded, address only one side of the equation. The other is the domestic enforcement capability the U.S. had accumulated by 2025 through ICE and CBP, which any future administration will inherit.

Taking Operation Metro Surge seriously suggests that preserving liberty may require not only eternal vigilance, but also the capacity to anticipate how existing capabilities can be harnessed by actors with particular intentions to erode protections once considered secure. The voters who left their stickers at the memorials after casting their midterm ballots were expressing their opinion about who should and shouldn’t hold that capability next. Whether anyone should hold it in its current form, however, is a question the new U.S. Congress can not avoid.

text:
Immigration attorneys and advocacy groups raised the alarm in a legislative hearing Friday that local law enforcement agencies are assisting Immigration and Customs Enforcement despite state laws intended to limit such cooperation.

Since 2005, the state Legislature has passed laws to restrict formal agreements and law enforcement cooperation with immigration enforcement agents.

But during Friday’s meeting of the Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee, several examples were given of law enforcement personnel routing detainees to ICE agents after traffic stops and routine encounters.

Those examples included a Sandoval County deputy meeting ICE agents in a store parking lot to hand over a man the deputy had just pulled over, and another man released after a DWI charge who found ICE agents waiting for him.

Teague González, executive director of the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center, told lawmakers the agents “just happened to know the moment that he was walking out of the courthouse,” suggesting they had help from local law enforcement.

Advocates shared emails obtained through public records requests that appeared to show county officials — including the Eddy County warden — notifying federal agents when suspected noncitizens were booked and when they would be released.

“What do these all have in common?” González asked. “This, in each case, was a choice that someone made county by county, and there is no written policy prohibiting it.”

She said the groups presenting to the committee were grateful for the Immigrant Safety Act (House Bill 9) — particularly that it barred formal agreements allowing ICE to deputize local law enforcement. But it didn’t go far enough to bar “informal” cooperation, she said.

“It does not bar local city or county police in any city or county in New Mexico from informally calling ICE,” González said. “And I think that while HB 9 closed the paperwork pathway, not one of these handoffs that we described to you today needed paperwork.”

She said there needs to be one statewide rule that encompasses every jurisdiction, adding, “One county walks a man to a parking lot and hands him over. The next county doesn't. A patchwork cannot be reconciled county by county.”

Billy Massingill, Eddy County Detention Center warden, told the Journal he has been notifying the Department of Homeland Security of suspected noncitizens booked into the jail since he came on board in 2012 — regardless of “who is president.”

He said the only law against collaboration is the one restricting counties from going into a 287(g) contract with immigration enforcement. Massingill added, “But nothing that I know of says that you can't converse.”

Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, Massingill began tracking the number and said at least 202 people have been handed over to immigration authorities from Eddy County since February 2025.

“We would let them know, ‘Hey, this guy's getting out. … And if you want this individual, you got to be at the facility when they’re released,’” Massingill said. He emphasized that they do not house immigration detainees and, if the agents don’t show up when the person is released, they will not hold them.

Massingill said there have also been hundreds of instances in which they notified DHS of a suspected noncitizen but were mistaken — “either they were U.S. citizens or they had green cards or work visas or whatever.” He added that Eddy County has no plans to change the practice.

“I just think that our county is willing to work with the government the best we can. Obviously, within reason and our state laws,” Massingill said.

Collaboration

González said that of the more than 500 detainees attorneys have spoken with, at least 232 reported entering ICE custody “through transfer from local law enforcement” in arrests made since January 2025.

“Almost everyone that we meet inside the detention centers has lived here for years. They have jobs, families, children, often U.S. citizen children. They are people who own homes, have built businesses, and pay taxes here,” she said. Many have applied for citizenship status and “have done everything right,” she added.

The tactics are not the only thing that has changed, the groups said. Since the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown began, both the number of people detained and the speed of deportations have surged.

Gabriela Ibañez Guzmán, staff attorney with Somos un Pueblo Unido, testified that immigration arrests increased from 20 in July 2024 to 700 in July this year across New Mexico. She added that despite laws and policies limiting cooperation, “our state still has one of the highest arrest rates in the country.”

The Journal found that, even in jurisdictions with strengthened policies, like Albuquerque, ICE agents are scouring public jail rosters to find noncitizens. In those cases, the noncitizens had been booked on both low-level and serious offenses, from concealing their identity and DWI to drug trafficking and child abuse.

The groups said that on any given day, 1,500 people are being held on immigration cases in New Mexico. Some are transferred here from out of state due to the number of empty beds in facilities in Cibola, Otero and Torrance counties. Now, many are being transferred to Camp East Montana in El Paso, they said.

González described conditions inside the detention centers as “abhorrent,” with a “huge spike” in detainees needing emergency care, including a man with an untreated abscess in his mouth, a person with facial paralysis after a stroke and another with vision loss due to an untreated eye condition.

She said attorneys are often unable to see their clients or the visits are cut short, while removals to third countries — where detainees are not originally from — “follow no discernible process.”

González said the current environment has them on the defensive, launching a program to teach families how to navigate the system, and advising parents to have a plan for their child’s care should they be detained.

Guzmán said to drill down on cooperation with immigration agents, both formal and informal, they have requested records of communications from counties statewide. While dozens of jurisdictions have not responded or provided records, at least 10 “showed some level of communication or collaboration” with immigration enforcement.

The records showed “nearly daily communications” between ICE officials and employees of Lea and Eddy counties in southeastern New Mexico, she said.

For example, in November 2024, Lea County sent ICE a daily list “of foreign-born individuals who are brought to the Lea County Detention Center, regardless of reason for their arrest.” In Eddy County, detention center staff spoke with ICE almost daily to notify them of booked noncitizens, including at least one for an unpaid traffic ticket.

In multiple attached emails sent in September 2025, Massingill, the Eddy County warden, notified immigration enforcement when jail staff told him suspected noncitizens were booked, saying they only spoke Spanish or were born in Mexico. In one such email chain, an agent responded to Massingill, saying, “Someone will be en route shortly Sir. Thanks for the heads up.”

Guzmán said “a clear statewide policy” was needed to lay out rules for working with immigration officials and to ensure local law enforcement collaborating in federal immigration enforcement “could face liability under both the U.S. Constitution, New Mexico's Constitution, and a number of our state laws.”

Legislation

Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez, D-Albuquerque, said “it’s really shocking and upsetting” when legislation that was passed is not followed, particularly by law enforcement. She said it was important to seal the “gap” allowing county employees to volunteer information on bookings to ICE, calling the practice “despicable.”

“Reading these emails, it's so upsetting to see this inhumane practice against our own people. I'm just very, very disappointed to see this,” Sedillo Lopez said.

Rep. Andrea Romero, D-Santa Fe, said she was concerned it would be hard to target informal assistance through phone calls or in-person meetings but hoped a renewed call for oversight, amid Democrats’ success in the midterms, could help address the issue.

“The fact that you have to prepare for your disappearance for any family member is just unheard of,” Romero said.

Rep. John Block, R-Alamogordo, asked if there was a draft of proposed legislation and questioned if it would prevent someone charged with a serious crime from being turned over to ICE.

He said he was thankful the Otero facility was open, calling HB 9 “the most ineffective piece of legislation ever passed in the history of time. … Thank you to the incompetence of this Legislature. I appreciate it.” Block said the facility was extremely clean, with a barber’s shop, kitchens serving halal and kosher food and “beautiful” murals of the Maldives.

“They literally have a phone line that has different phone numbers for the people being detained for them to access legal services, including from your organizations,” he said to the groups.

Block closed by saying, “Hopefully we can continue to deport criminal illegal aliens who are in this country. … I will continue to be a big supporter of that because our country needs to be safe.”

After Block’s statements, Rep. Marianna Anaya, D-Albuquerque, felt the need to address the advocacy groups and the families and children seated in the chambers.

“I'm really glad you're here, first of all, and I also just want to apologize for my other colleague’s words earlier. … Because one, you or anybody else or your families, are not illegal. Nobody's illegal. You should know that. Also, I don't think you guys are aliens, right?” she said.

Applause broke out, and there was a call for order to return to the chamber.

Anaya, referring to the outcome of the election, added, “The majority of this country believes in compassion and justice, and absolutely stands with you. And I hope that you saw that on that map across the United States.”

text:
Abraham Zavala was born at Adventist White Memorial. So were his kids. So late Friday, when he heard federal immigration agents were at the Boyle Heights hospital, and that local youth were out blowing whistles to warn neighbors, he went.

“To me that’s sacred ground,” said Zavala, an organizer with Unión del Barrio.

“I’m a dad,” he said. “I wanted to be there to support the youth.”

He was among the Boyle Heights residents who converged on the hospital and stayed in a standoff with federal immigration agents into the early hours of Saturday. Agents detained at least two people, according to rapid response groups.

Neighbors alerted each other with noisemakers and fireworks. A woman pounded her pots and pans. Teenagers ran across Mariachi Plaza, shouting that ICE was in the area and urging residents to lock their doors.

“Even though we’re afraid, you know we’re still showing up,” said Myra Vasquez, a Boyle Heights resident who rushed to White Memorial after hearing reports of ICE in the area. “We’re not going to allow them to just come into our communities and terrorize us because they’re the real terrorists causing harm.”

The confrontation peaked around 11:30 p.m. Video shared with Boyle Heights Beat shows agents pushing back protesters who had moved toward them, and the two sides begin shoving. Agents appear to pepper-spray people on the sidewalk. One agent then tackles a man and pins him to the ground, while a second person is pulled from the crowd. Both were detained.

The standoff continued past midnight. Zavala said agents got out of their vehicles and formed a line in front of the parking lot where paramedics enter, blocking an emergency exit. “They literally became White Memorial’s private security detail,” he said. Zavala said he and another person were sprayed with Mace.

The Dept. of Homeland Security declined to comment about the incident in Boyle Heights and, in a statement, the agency said they would “not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations.”

The spokesperson instead said that obstructing law enforcement is a federal crime.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” the statement said, despite the large turnout of protesters who encountered the masked agents at the hospital.

Father Brendan Busse, who pastors nearby Dolores Mission Church in Boyle Heights, rushed to White Memorial after seeing reports from the Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network of ICE at the hospital.

Busse, a Jesuit priest, said he witnessed people caring for each other and tending to those suffering from pepper spray. People there advocated for them to find treatment at White Memorial, Busse said. Community members, he said, “were obviously doing their best, not just to communicate their feelings, but to push, to instigate the dispersal of this ICE presence.”

As clergy, Busse said their presence can help combat a narrative of those advocating for immigrants as “somehow dangerous, or violent, or vulgar.”

“Just to be there is a sign that that’s not the only version of what this looks like,” he said.

Initially, Busse showed up wearing a hoodie, but he decided to change into his green stole he had in his car as things appeared to get tense. “Just try to do what I could to bring a presence of maybe a little moral authority,” he said.

“It’s bad enough that people have to lift up their voices to say something so obvious, that their lives matter, that our communities are sacred, that families belong together,” Busse said. “It’s bad enough that they have to be out at 3 a.m. in the morning to tell anybody that.”

“It’s even worse if they would have to suffer the consequences of retribution and violence that comes from speaking out in that way,” Busse added.

text:
Colombian authorities executed one of the most visible immigration operations of the year in the early hours of November 6, airlifting more than 80 Venezuelan nationals from a military base in Bogotá to the border city of Cúcuta, where they were formally expelled into Venezuela. The group — 74 men and six women — had been held in custody by security forces and were accused of involvement in criminal activities ranging from homicide to extortion across Bogotá, Medellín, and other Colombian cities.

A Pre-Dawn Roundup Across 15 Neighborhoods

The operation began the afternoon of Thursday, November 5, when Migración Colombia, the National Police, the Army, and Special Forces coordinated sweeps across 15 localities of the capital. Detainees were concentrated at the facilities of the Dijín — the criminal investigation directorate of the Bogotá Metropolitan Police — where migration officials reviewed each person's file and completed the administrative paperwork needed to formalize the expulsion measure. By early Friday morning, the group was transferred to the Comando Aéreo de Transporte Militar (CATAM), Bogotá's military air transport base on the city's western edge, and flown by military plane to Cúcuta. AFP journalists on the ground observed buses transporting the detainees — some with their hands bound — from the Cúcuta airstrip to the Tienditas international bridge, where Colombian authorities transferred custody to Venezuelan migration and security officials.

The Policy Behind the Operation

President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in early August as a U.S.-backed right-wing leader, issued a directive on August 23 instructing Migración Colombia and the National Police to launch nationwide operations targeting irregular migrants with criminal backgrounds. "Those who come to Colombia to commit crimes cannot find refuge in our territory," he said publicly, also instructing Migration Director José Luis Castañeda to proceed with the immediate expulsion of Venezuelans in irregular status who have judicial records. Between his inauguration on August 7 and October 29, Colombian authorities carried out 812 deportations and expulsions of foreign nationals.

Medellín Set the Pace Ten Days Earlier

The November 6 airlift was not an isolated event. On October 27, Migración Colombia expelled 98 Venezuelans from Medellín following verification procedures that identified individuals with repeated criminal conduct and security risks. That operation was led by Director Castañeda in coordination with the National Police, the Medellín Mayor's office, and the city's Personería. According to official figures, 80 percent of those expelled from Medellín had been in irregular migration status.

The Scale of the Challenge

Colombia hosts more Venezuelans than any other country in the world. According to Migración Colombia data updated through June 2026, there are 2.8 million Venezuelan nationals in the country, of whom approximately 847,000 were in an irregular migration status as of mid-year. The situation inside Venezuela shows little sign of improvement: the country was struck by a catastrophic double earthquake on June 24, 2026 — with consecutive tremors registering magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 — that left hundreds dead and tens of thousands displaced, complicating any scenario for large-scale voluntary or forced returns. Colombian authorities have stated that prior arrest records and administrative corrections do not automatically trigger a migration measure, an acknowledgment aimed at preventing the blanket stigmatization of the broader Venezuelan community in the country.

Rights Groups Raise Alarms

The Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA) has warned that Colombia's migration offensive places Venezuelan rights at serious risk, particularly given that expellees are being returned to a nation still struggling with the aftermath of natural disaster and deteriorating security conditions for many of those facing deportation. The tension between domestic pressure to maintain public order and Colombia's international human rights obligations is set to remain a defining flashpoint in migration policy debates in the months ahead. Under current Colombian regulations, an "expulsion" — the status applied to those with criminal records — carries no avenue for legal appeal, making it a permanent and irreversible sanction.

text:
Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman wasted little time signaling where she stands on immigration enforcement, joining anti-ICE protesters Saturday and leading chants demanding federal agents leave the city.

Raman appeared outside Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights following a tense overnight confrontation between federal agents and demonstrators at the hospital.

“I am an immigrant myself,” Raman told the crowd. “I have felt the fear that so many across this city, across this country have felt since these raids began.”

Speaking in Spanish, Raman led chants of “ICE out of Boyle Heights” and “ICE out of LA” before declaring the previous night’s incident an affront to Americans.

Outgoing Mayor Karen Bass also piled on, calling on the Trump administration to halt immigration enforcement around medical facilities.

“I condemn ICE’s action and call on the Trump Administration to stop all immigration enforcement in and around health care facilities.”

The backlash followed Friday night’s confrontation, when ICE agents brought a person in their custody to White Memorial’s emergency department for undisclosed medical reasons.

Hospital officials said agents blocked the emergency entrance for roughly two hours.

“When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize,” a hospital spokesperson told NBC 4, explaining the decision to reroute ambulances.

Hospital president Daniel Fontoura added: “White Memorial is a place of healing and safety for everyone, regardless of immigration status.”

Protesters alleged agents pepper-sprayed demonstrators and arrested several US citizens alongside the people they had come to detain.

At least one person was reportedly taken from doctors’ care to a detention center.

The LAPD responded to the protests but said officers did not participate in immigration enforcement.

The confrontation comes as LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell faces an uncertain future under Raman, who has pledged to replace him after defeating Bass in Thursday’s mayoral election.

The 45-year-old mayor-elect has criticized McDonnell for what she views as an insufficient response to ICE operations targeting illegal migrants in Los Angeles.

Her 100-day public safety plan also calls for hiring more 911 operators, expanding unarmed crisis response teams and auditing police compliance with the city’s sanctuary city law, which restricts the sharing of immigration information with federal authorities.

text:
Democrats are still celebrating major gains in this year’s midterm elections, in which the party’s switch from the minority to control of Congress is being seen as a sharp rebuke to President Donald Trump and his policies over the last two years.

Republicans at the highest levels are reckoning with steep losses and voter disapproval of the president’s actions on signature issues, including his unprecedented crackdown on immigration. Friday, Trump named Stephen Miller, architect of some of his most controversial immigration policies, White House chief of staff.

Earlier in the week, on a phone call with Fox News late Election Day, Trump suggested there was room to work with Democrats on his deportation agenda while also emphasizing his power to veto legislation passed by Congress.

“I can work with them on a lot of things,” Trump said. “We can work with them on immigration, I think.”

Vice President JD Vance wrote in a post on X the next day that he was “open” to changing immigration enforcement “by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance” but dismissed the idea of amnesty for immigrants.

Just two years earlier, voters brought Trump back into office in part on his promise to carry out a historic deportation campaign targeting the “the worst of the worst.”

What voters got was an aggressive surge of federal agents across the U.S. who at times violently detained immigrants, stormed communities wearing weapons and battle fatigues and killed two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis who protested their actions. Most of those who have been arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement under Trump have no criminal record.

Democrats, heeding broad pushback from voters on Trump’s immigration crackdown, are looking to dial it down and hold oversight hearings into the administration’s top officials.

As a new reality sinks in around Washington D.C., San Diego congressional members, policy experts and immigration advocates are already planning and hoping for big changes to come in January.

Here’s what they want to happen in the next couple years.

Congressional investigations

Some Democrats are already making a list of former and current Homeland Security officials they plan to bring forward to Congress for testimony and investigations.

Among those names: Miller, Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Border Czar Tom Homan and former U.S. Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino.

U.S. Rep. Scott Peters, D-San Diego, who represents California’s 50th Congressional District, was easily reelected to an eighth two-year term Tuesday. He said he wants to ask officials about their plans for immigration enforcement, their expenditure of agency funds, which reached historic levels in Trump’s second term, and “people getting killed in the streets.”

Three U.S. citizens have been shot and killed by federal agents conducting immigration enforcement during the second Trump administration — Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis and Ruben Ray Martinez in Texas. Dozens of immigrants have died in detention centers and some in communities during interactions with federal law enforcement in that time.

Hollie Webb, an attorney with the binational San Diego-based immigrant rights legal group Al Otro Lado, said third-country deportations should be investigated as well.

Early in Trump’s second term, his administration deported more than 250 men, most from Venezuela, to a high-security prison in El Salvador, where they were reportedly tortured. The administration has also sent immigrants to far-flung countries where they have little or no connections, including Uzbekistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Paraguay.

Others said Congress should be judicious with its investigations.

U.S. Rep. Juan Vargas, D-San Diego, who represents California’s 52nd Congressional District and won an eighth term Tuesday, said he supports oversight, but not “vengeance.” He said the next Congress should make legislation a priority.

“We do have to have oversight, absolutely, but we have to fix this,” Vargas said. “That’s what I think the American people want to see. They want to see us fix this, not retribution.”

‘Commonsense’ legislation

Immigration advocates like Lilian Serrano, who leads the Southern Border Communities Coalition, are ready to have Congress do more than just investigate.

“What we want to see is them actually doing what Congress is meant to do and change the laws or create laws that will actually protect people in our communities,” Serrano said.

She said that includes prohibiting immigration enforcement in places of worship and schools, which was previously limited under a policy during the Biden administration that also included medical settings, shelters and other sensitive locations.

Over the last two years, immigration arrests of parents near schools have shocked communities and sent fear into classrooms nationwide, including in San Diego.

Serrano also said Congress should look to rein in federal agents’ use of force and ensure that they face consequences when they violate the rights of U.S. citizens or other community members.

U.S. Rep. Mike Levin, D-San Juan Capistrano, was just reelected to a fifth term in California’s 49th Congressional District. Levin said commonsense reforms on immigration could also include banning federal agents from wearing face masks and requiring them to wear clear identification and obtain judicial warrants to enter private spaces and “avoiding the sensitive locations like schools and churches and hospitals.”

Levin and others are also eyeing comprehensive immigration reform, which Congress hasn’t passed in three decades, and looking to work with Republicans to get it done.

Vargas said he favors “an orderly border” but that “we need the people that are being deported.” He mentioned making reforms for immigrants working as farm laborers, construction workers, home care workers and those who were brought to the U.S. as children known as “Dreamers.”

Vargas said the U.S. should be “that place where you can still come, work hard and make something of your life and help your family.”

But Democrats hoping to seize on new majorities in Congress to pass immigration legislation will face a significant challenge in the White House: With Trump in the presidency, any bill passed with a simple majority runs the risk of being vetoed. Veto overrides require 67 votes in the Senate.

As it stands, Democrats will have 54 to 56 seats in the 100-person Senate and more than 250 in the 435-member House of Representatives, majorities not won since the 2008 election.

Tom Wong, an associate professor of political science who directs the U.S. Immigration Policy Center at University of California San Diego, said there could still be strategic options for Democrats.

One possibility is that Trump keeps pushing an unpopular aggressive immigration crackdown in line with what voters have seen and Republicans have supported over the past two years.

Another is that Democrats could pass bills through Congress that “publicly embarrass the Republican Party” if Trump decides to use his veto power to kill the bills, Wong said.

Power of the purse

Immigration enforcement agencies are enjoying historic funding with billions of extra dollars from a law passed during Trump’s first year back in office. That law covers federal spending through 2029.

But Democrats say Congress has a power of the purse that can be used as a check on the president.

Peters said some of the unspent funds provided by the so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” could be redirected.

Levin said Congress could force additional government funding to “come with some serious reforms,” such as limiting immigration arrests to those with serious criminal records.

But Wong said the congressional ability to limit funding for immigration enforcement under this administration is limited.

“The reality is that it is already funded at historical levels and it has the money it needs.”

Still, he said, Tuesday’s election showed that Democrats need to deliver real change and Republicans need to heed voters’ concerns on immigration and other issues — or face the consequences.

“If Republicans do not read the room correctly and do not compromise on major aspects of our immigration policies, they may be sinking themselves in 2028 without even knowing it,” Wong said.

text:
On Friday, President Donald Trump announced mid-afternoon that Stephen Miller, the white nationalist id behind Trump’s anti-immigrant policies, was going to be his new chief of staff — generating headlines and the first news cycle since Tuesday that was not a version of “Trump and GOP obliterated.”

Lashing out is going to be a regular occurrence now, in the wake of Tuesday’s midterm blue tsunami elections.

And yet, shortly before 5 p.m. on the Wast Coast, reality — and not showmanship — was on display, as the Justice Department dismissed its election lawsuit against California. It was a whining, two-page document — decrying how the courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court, wouldn’t let the administration engage in a plan that everyone found was likely illegal.

On Saturday, Judge Ana Reyes reminded Trump officials of another accountability path that can come from the other branches, as she announced her intention to name former D.C. U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu as the special master to investigate whether Justice Department and/or Interior Department lawyers committed any ethical violations in connection with their work in the the East Potomac Golf Course case. Then, there’s Congress. As Michigan Sen. Elisa Slotkin said at a University of Chicago event before the election, “We do have to have accountability” — not just for Trump but for those who have enabled him throughout the administration.

With Democrats already at over 250 seats in the House with several races still outstanding and near-clarity that they will have a 56-seat majority in the Senate once Alaska and Mississippi are called, Slotkin’s call for accountability — one in which she is, of course, not alone — is not only possible but imperative.

This is so not only because of what Trump and his administration have done. While understanding what a split government in our system of separation of powers is (he posted that he is “MR. VETO” on Friday night), Trump is unwilling even to acknowledge what that means when it comes to accountability.

On Saturday, Trump posted a rant that largely amounted to a declaration that he views any oversight from Congress of the executive branch as “extortion” and “Weaponization and Lawfare” and, yes, a “criminal act.” He specifically went after Slotkin for her mid-October remarks, saying that she “is saying that she is going to go after all young people that believe in Republican Values“ — even though she said no such thing and nothing even arguably like it.

Even before the election, on October 20, Greg Sargent reported at The New Republic that Republicans had picked up the Slotkin speech as some horrifying attack.

Since Greg already did the work, here’s a very accurate summary of the relevant part:

You can watch the key Slotkin monologue starting right here. Slotkin says “accountability” for the Trump administration requires Congress to pick high-profile examples of its “corruption.” She adds that such oversight should “not just focus on the president, but on the people who enabled him,” that is, on officials “who are doing his bidding.” Slotkin says she hopes real oversight might dissuade young people from joining the administration if they conclude association with a corrupt administration will buy them “a ton of problems.”

Here is where the part where she talks about young people, because it was a follow-on remark that was not part of her initial response. Specifically, she reiterated that she wants to focus not just on Trump but also “the people who enabled him,” and then added:

I want young people coming out of school to say, “Should I go work for the Trump administration? That sounds fun. I might get an opportunity.” I want them to be like, “Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that.” I want that deterrence message sent.

This is, simply put, right.

A young person should not want to join the Trump administration at this point. Trump has made his willingness to break U.S. laws, violate the Constitution, and violate international law clear; he has just promoted the architect of many of his most lawless acts to chief of staff; and his attorney general has made keeping Trump happy and serving as Trump and Miller’s lawyer his aim.

Even if you were a true believer, you would be an idiot if you thought joining the Trump administration was a smart career move right now.

Trump and the executive branch — in part, thanks to Chief Justice John Roberts and the Supreme Court — certainly have a lot of power. They will do things — and be able to do things — so long as they are in power that will cause great harm. That should not be forgotten, and is part of why all of the accountability measures are so important.

That said, Trump and those remaining can lash out and complain, but there is a new landscape coming and, in some ways, already here. As for Congress, this is not going to be the Mike Johnson-John Thune “do what you want” show any more, and Trump is intrinsically incapable of hearing “no.” From anyone.

But, “no” is coming.

Preservation letters are just the start.

There will be requests for information, hearings, subpoenas, legislation, actual pushback against impoundment, litigation, the possibility of impeachments, and more.

If you look at it like that, in an overwhelmingly Democratic House and strongly Democratic Senate, it makes sense why Trump would be lashing out on a Saturday afternoon.

It does not, however, change reality.
