title: Texas Cities Pull Back Cooperation With ICE After Midterm Elections - Newsweek
description:
Two cities in Texas are taking steps to restrict how local law enforcement interacts with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) following the midterm elections, led by an executive order in Houston and planned administrative updates in Austin.
Federal Enforcement Encounters Fuel Local Debate The actions follow a series of fatal encounters involving federal immigration officers that happened this year.
In January, U.S. citizens Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti were fatally shot by federal immigration officers in Minneapolis.
Cities With Rules Limiting Cooperation With ICE A number of municipalities outside Texas adopted or strengthened restrictions on local involvement in civil immigration enforcement this year.
The rules vary significantly and generally do not prevent federal authorities from independently enforcing federal immigration law.
text:
Two cities in Texas are taking steps to restrict how local law enforcement interacts with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) following the midterm elections, led by an executive order in Houston and planned administrative updates in Austin.

On Tuesday, Democrats swept every statewide race in Texas, Republicans' most populous stronghold, ending a three-decade losing streak in the Lone Star State.

Democratic state Representative James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state's scandal-plagued attorney general, to win a U.S. Senate seat, while state Representative Gina Hinojosa toppled three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the state's first Latina governor.

Read More on News

Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a Democrat, signed an executive order this week directing the Houston Police Department to notify ICE only when a person with an administrative immigration warrant is arrested for a jailable offense. Under the new policy, officers will no longer contact federal authorities solely because an administrative warrant appears during an encounter that results only in a warning or citation.

"I do this to begin a healing process, reduce fear and anxiety across our community," Whitmire said on Friday during a news conference. "I also do this knowing that elections matter."

Whitmire added that he views the executive order as "the right thing to do at the right time" and expressed hope that Houston's actions could serve as a template for municipal governments across the state.

In Austin, Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, announced Friday that he directed Police Chief Lisa Davis to draft revisions to the Austin Police Department’s general orders regarding federal immigration authorities.

Newsweek reached out to ICE by email Saturday for comment.

Federal Enforcement Encounters Fuel Local Debate

The actions follow a series of fatal encounters involving federal immigration officers that happened this year.

In January, U.S. citizens Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti were fatally shot by federal immigration officers in Minneapolis. On July 7, an ICE officer fatally shot Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during an attempted arrest in Houston.

Federal officials stated that Salgado Araujo attempted to use his vehicle against an officer, prompting the agent to fire in self-defense. Family members and civil rights organizations have demanded an independent investigation into the incident. Senator-elect Talarico later posted on X that he placed his "I voted" sticker at a memorial for Salgado Araujo.

The policy shifts reflect broader efforts by local governments nationwide to limit the use of local police, employees, facilities, and tax funds for federal civil immigration enforcement.

The pushback comes during an intensified federal immigration campaign under President Donald Trump, whose administration established a target of 1 million deportations annually. The Migration Policy Institute estimates that ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) executed roughly 980,000 formal removals and returns during the first 18 months of Trump’s second term.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis criticized the municipal moves in an email statement to Newsweek on Saturday.

“This will make Texans less safe," Bis said. "Seven out of 10 of the safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. Once again, Democrat politicians are putting criminal illegal aliens above the safety of American citizens.”

State Preemption and Legal Constraints

Texas law limits how far local jurisdictions can go in curtailing cooperation with federal authorities.

Senate Bill 4, the state’s 2017 anti-"sanctuary cities" law, restricts cities and police departments from banning or materially limiting officers from assisting federal immigration agents. Additionally, Texas Government Code §752.053 prohibits local entities from establishing policies that restrict officers from cooperating with federal authorities when deemed reasonable or necessary.

Houston’s new policy does not sever ties with ICE, nor does it hinder federal agents from conducting independent enforcement operations within the city. Officers remain required to contact ICE when an individual with an administrative warrant is booked on a jailable charge.

In Austin, any proposed changes to police general orders must undergo review by the city attorney to ensure compliance with state statutes.

Austin previously altered its enforcement guidelines earlier this year. In March, Austin police adopted a policy allowing, but not requiring, officers to contact ICE regarding administrative warrants when no arrestable charge existed. The department subsequently adjusted its guidance in April to state that officers "should" contact ICE when operationally feasible, following state threats to withhold approximately $2.5 million in grant funding.

Local leaders have signaled support for further restrictions. Austin City Council member Mike Siegel called on the city to "immediately limit police cooperation with ICE to the minimum required by federal law," while Council member Vanessa Fuentes advocated for "limiting local police contact with ICE."

Cities With Rules Limiting Cooperation With ICE

A number of municipalities outside Texas adopted or strengthened restrictions on local involvement in civil immigration enforcement this year. The rules vary significantly and generally do not prevent federal authorities from independently enforcing federal immigration law.

Biddeford, Maine—Approved October 20, 2026: The Biddeford City Council unanimously approved restrictions on municipal employees and resources being used to assist federal immigration enforcement, subject to legal and judicial-warrant exceptions. The ordinance is scheduled to take effect November 19. It comes after the death of Joan Sebastian Guerrero at the hands of ICE agents.

Upper Darby, Pennsylvania—September 16, 2026: The township restricted the use of local personnel, money, equipment, facilities and databases for civil immigration enforcement and barred detention solely on an administrative immigration warrant or civil detainer. The ordinance contains exceptions for criminal investigations, authorized task forces, emergencies, judicially authorized transfers and legally required cooperation.

Philadelphia—April 23 and May 7, 2026: The Philadelphia City Council passed its seven-bill "ICE Out" package on April 23. Mayor Cherelle Parker signed six measures on May 7 and allowed a seventh concerning masks and identification to become law without her signature. The measures restrict areas including municipal assistance with civil immigration enforcement, immigration-status information, staging on city property and warrantless access to nonpublic city facilities.

Portland, Maine—Approved May 4, 2026: Portland strengthened restrictions on city employees assisting federal civil immigration enforcement, including limits on access to nonpublic municipal property and sharing sensitive information. The ordinance preserves cooperation required by law or supported by a judicial warrant.

Davis, California—April 7, 2026: Davis expanded its sanctuary-city rules to restrict city staff and resources from assisting civil immigration enforcement. The ordinance also limits immigration-status information sharing and the use of city property for immigration-enforcement staging or operations, subject to federal and state legal requirements.

Lewiston, Maine—March 17, 2026: Lewiston voted 5-2 to make permanent restrictions first imposed through an emergency ordinance in February. The rules restrict city employees and resources from being used to assist federal immigration-enforcement operations except when required by law or judicial order.

Buffalo, New York—January 26, 2026: Buffalo issued an executive order restricting the use of city property, equipment, money and employees for federal civil immigration enforcement. The order preserves cooperation involving criminal investigations, judicial warrants and circumstances in which cooperation is legally required.

Cities including Boston; Seattle; New York City; Newark, New Jersey; Jersey City, New Jersey; Providence, Rhode Island, and San Diego have also adopted measures restricting specific aspects of federal immigration enforcement, including staging on city property, access to nonpublic facilities or sharing locally held information.

A new law banning police and sheriff's departments in New York from working with ICE took effect in August.

Whether other Texas cities follow Houston's example will determine whether the post-midterm developments grow into a broader statewide trend.

text:
Sen. Maria Elena Durazo said that it appears the hospital is earning a reputation for being an “ICE-friendly hospital.”

“What happened last night was unacceptable,” Durazo told the hospital’s administrators in the same parking lot where the blockade was held. “It’s unacceptable that ICE would go into our healthcare facilities. But we also believe that White Memorial can and should do more.”

Several hours earlier, patients arriving at the hospital were met by a large presence of masked agents who stood outside the hospital starting Friday evening and into the early hours of Saturday. Ambulances were diverted to nearby hospitals for about two hours while the activity took place.

Local residents and rapid response groups were kept away from the hospital and in multiple videos shared on social media, masked agents pushed away protesters and sprayed them with what appeared to be pepper spray.

The backstory ad what the hospital says

The series of events began after eyewitnesses said they saw federal agents detain a person and take them into the hospital before a crowd of protesters came to rally against the ICE agents, according to Raquel Roman, executive director of Proyecto Pastoral and member of the Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network.

Saturday’s rally, organized by the local rapid response group, started at Mariachi Plaza and coincided with a Dia de los Muertos celebration. People marched with signs that read “Protect the Sacred” and “Melt ICE” while others wore La Catrina face paint.

Community members, Durazo, Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, Assemblymember Mark Gonzalez and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman gathered outside the hospital around 2:30 p.m. with members of Proyecto Pastoral and Centro CSO to denounce the ICE activity that had taken place outside the emergency room.

Daniel Fontoura, president at Adventist Health White Memorial, said the hospital staff does not work with federal immigration agents.

“I don’t know what I can do to assure you there’s no special relationship, no special contract. When they show up, they show up,” Fontoura said, referring to the federal agents.

He added that the hospital would like to work with community organizations and elected officials to understand what they should do in these types of situations.

The LA Local was provided a copy of the letter handed to the hospital administrators. Durazo asks White Memorial leadership to provide a detailed account of what happened and determine why agents were allowed to block the ambulance entrance.

The letter also asks that the hospital “implement and enforce clear procedures” to block ICE agents from obstructing entrances and accessing patient rooms and to issue a public statement in English and Spanish “reaffirming the hospital’s unwavering commitment to caring for all patients, regardless of immigration status.”

The letter requests a written response from hospital leadership by Nov. 21.

“If these concerns remain unresolved, we will seek a review by the California Attorney General of White Memorial’s compliance with state law,” Durazo wrote in the letter.

The letter was signed by multiple community leaders and elected officials present at the rally.

Fontoura appeared flustered as he spoke to Durazo and the other officials. He told the crowd that hospital staff called 911 to try and stop the blockade. He was drowned out by people shouting, “Shame.”

About the rally

Derek Mejia, 30, a police accountability co-chair at Centro CSO, joined the rally Saturday afternoon.

He was part of a group who gathered outside the hospital early Saturday morning after federal immigration agents detained two people. By that time, Los Angeles Police Department officers arrived at the scene and an LAPD helicopter circled the area, Mejia said.

“It’s a shame,” Mejia said of the incident.

Mejia said he was at the rally because, “One, we want to show ICE that we’re not afraid and two, we want to let White Memorial know that their collaboration with ICE is not only detrimental to the community but that it needs to stop.”

Verita Topete of Centro CSO, addressed the crowd at the rally. “White Memorial is endangering the same community they claim to serve,” she said.

“ICE out of L.A. ICE out of Boyle Heights. ICE out of California,” Topete chanted, and the crowd followed suit.

The group then marched back to Mariachi Plaza before dispersing around 3 p.m.

They were also joined by Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, who represents Boyle Heights, along with CHIRLA’s Executive Director Angelica Salas, union organizer David Huerta of SEIU and Father Brendan Busse with Dolores Mission Church.

Mayor Karen Bass did not atend the rally, but denounced the ICE activity and in a statement called “on the Trump Administration to stop all immigration enforcement in and around health care facilities. Hospital leadership also had a duty to step in right away to protect patients and neighbors, and by all appearances, that did not happen.”

Raman, who was elected L.A.’s next mayor, did attend the rally and thanked community members who showed up to protests ICE’s presence several hours earlier at the hospital. She said that as an immigrant herself, she has “felt the fear that so many across the city and across this country have felt … since these raids began.”

“What happened last night at this hospital was an affront to the wishes of the American people and to the people of Los Angeles,” Raman said.

As she left the rally, community members shouted at Raman to “fire the police chief.”

Throughout her mayoral campaign, Raman said she will attempt to replace LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell after criticizing the department’s handling of ICE enforcement, protests and sharing data with federal authorities, which Raman says is a violation of L.A.’s Sanctuary City policies.

title: Supreme Court case could end lawsuits against federal agents like ICE - USA Today

Depending on the outcome of a case the court will hear Nov. 9, such suits could be blocked entirely.
“If Bivens is eliminated, then there’ll be literally no way to sue in federal court when a federal agent like ICE violates the Constitution,” he said.
The 1971 decision, however, is criticized by conservatives who think the then-liberal Supreme Court used it to grant rights that aren't spelled out in the Constitution.

text:
WASHINGTON – The widely shared images of immigration enforcement agents using violence to carry out the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown put the spotlight on how difficult it is to take federal officers to court.

Decades of Supreme Court decisions have limited the ability to seek damages from a federal employee accused of violating someone’s constitutional rights.

Depending on the outcome of a case the court will hear Nov. 9, such suits could be blocked entirely.

The plaintiff in the $3 million suit against a federal prison nurse is Kekai Watanabe, who says he should have been hospitalized or seen a specialist after being attacked during a gang-related fight at a prison in Honolulu in 2021. Instead, he was given over-the-counter pain medication and told to “stop being a cry baby,” Watanabe alleges.

An X-ray taken months later showed that he had a fractured coccyx and that bone chips had migrated to surrounding soft-tissue areas. He did not receive further treatment before being released in 2024 and remains in tremendous pain today, according to his lawyers.

The lawsuit gives the 6-3 conservative court an opportunity to overturn what’s left of a controversial 1971 decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents, that allowed people to sue federal officers for monetary damages.

Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the law school and a professor of law at the University of California, Berkeley, said the case has taken on special significance amid calls to hold immigration agents and others accountable for actions like the fatal shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis earlier this year.

“If Bivens is eliminated, then there’ll be literally no way to sue in federal court when a federal agent like ICE violates the Constitution,” he said.

The 1971 decision, however, is criticized by conservatives who think the then-liberal Supreme Court used it to grant rights that aren't spelled out in the Constitution.

In recent years, the court has sought to limit the ability to sue federal employees, including barring lawsuits in cases that are “different in a meaningful way” from the details spelled out in Bivens or in the only two other cases in which the Supreme Court has allowed similar constitutional claims.

An appeals court said Watanabe’s claim passes that test, ruling it is identical to a 1980 Supreme Court decision in which the high court said federal prison staff violated the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment when they failed to respond appropriately to a prisoner’s fatal asthmatic attack.

The Justice Department, however, argues that the 1980 decision is now “obsolete” because of more recent Supreme Court rulings limiting its reach.

“This Court should say as much,” the Justice Department wrote in a filing.

Attorneys for the prison nurse argue that the justices should go further and also get rid of the 1971 Bivens decision that underpinned the 1980 ruling.

“Those cases are relics of the bygone days when federal courts thought it appropriate to create causes of action Congress had not authorized,” the nurse’s attorneys said in written arguments. “The Court has since rejected every stitch of Bivens’s reasoning.”

Lawyers for Watanabe counter that Congress effectively authorized such lawsuits when it passed legislation in 1996 that limited – but did not end – those claims.

But recent rulings suggest that many justices believe Congress must pass a bill explicitly creating a right to sue.

Rory Little, who teaches constitutional and criminal law at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, predicted that the court will either “overrule an old civil rights precedent” or “once again” say it doesn’t apply to the latest case.

The result, Little wrote, “seems pretty much preordained.”

text:
A Sri Lankan immigrant who launched a multi-million-pound lawsuit against the Home Office for injuries allegedly sustained while in immigration detention has been caught working out at a gym and go-karting.

Vengadeswara Raw Gopalakrishnan claimed he had been left entirely incapable of working, studying, or even leaving his house unaccompanied due to "serious and long-term psychiatric injury".

However, following a High Court hearing, a judge has ruled the claim fundamentally dishonest and branded the deliberate exaggeration as a “scandalous" waste of court time and public resources.

The fraudulent £7 million claim was exposed after agents hired by the Home Office filmed the claimant leading a highly active lifestyle, The Independent reports.

Surveillance footage captured Mr Gopalakrishnan driving a car, eating out at restaurants, taking his children to school, and spending an hour exercising at a local gym.

Mr Gopalakrishnan arrived in the UK on a student visa in 2010 but overstayed after it expired in 2012. Following an unsuccessful asylum application, he was placed in immigration detention from September 2013 to February 2014.

He was eventually released on health grounds and granted indefinite leave to remain in 2023, at which point he launched legal action against the government department.

He falsely maintained that his detention had caused severe depressive illness with psychotic symptoms and ongoing post-traumatic stress disorder. His partner of ten years, Reena Mathew, acted as his "litigation friend"—a role designed to manage court cases for individuals who lack the mental capacity to do so themselves.

Ruling on the case, Mr Justice Mansfield found that the pair had deliberately fabricated and calculated the symptoms for financial gain.

Ordering Mr Gopalakrishnan to pay all of the Home Office's legal costs, the judge said: "It is clear to me that the claimant’s exaggeration of his symptoms has been deliberate, calculated and for the purposes of gain from these proceedings.

"By the standards of ordinary decent people, the claimant’s conduct in bringing and pursuing a claim for damages based on fabricated or exaggerated symptoms was dishonest."

As recently as April, Ms Mathew told the court that he required round-the-clock support and was completely unable to manage his finances, cook meals, or leave the house alone.

The deception began to unravel when Home Office records additionally revealed that Mr Gopalakrishnan had been working as a delivery driver. Furthermore, investigators discovered online records showing he had actively participated in a competitive go-karting tournament.

title: With 'wartime consigliere' Stephen Miller, Trump signals more confrontation, not moderation
description:

He also offered the White House press secretary position to combat sports promoter Dana White.
“If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now.
“Those on Capitol Hill looking to break away from the Trump administration will know that Stephen Miller is not going to sit idly by and watch that happen,” Republican strategist Ron Bonjean said.

text:
President Donald Trump’s decision to put longtime loyalist Stephen Miller in charge of the White House signals that the administration plans to respond to its bruising midterm defeat not with moderation, but with a more confrontational approach during Trump’s final two years in office, according to administration officials, Republicans and strategists who spoke to Reuters.

Voters delivered Republicans a historic rebuke in Tuesday’s midterm elections, handing Democrats control of Congress. But officials expect Miller, one of the most influential architects of Trump’s immigration agenda, to push the administration toward continued crackdowns, sharper cultural battles and greater reliance on presidential authority rather than compromise with lawmakers. “This signals the administration is going to have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years,” Trump donor and energy executive Dan Eberhart said.

Trump has publicly said he can work with Democrats, but his conduct since the election has suggested little appetite for retreat. On Saturday, he ordered the Justice Department to “look into” Democrats whom he accused of sending “threatening letters” to Republican donors and other allies. He also offered the White House press secretary position to combat sports promoter Dana White.

MAKE ynetGlobal MY TRUSTED SOURCE

Miller, 41, represents a markedly different style from outgoing chief of staff Susie Wiles. Wiles, a former lobbyist who managed Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, was widely viewed as a pragmatic operator able to balance competing factions around the president. Miller is regarded by supporters and critics alike as an ideological fighter with detailed knowledge of how executive power can be used and an unusually close political bond with Trump.

“If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now. This man saved America,” Miller said Friday at an event at Trump’s Florida estate. He joined Trump’s first presidential campaign in 2016 and went on to serve throughout his two terms, becoming best known for shaping the administration’s aggressive immigration policies.

Those policies have also become a political liability. An October Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 37% of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of immigration, down from 50% when he took office. Four U.S. immigration officials told Reuters they had seen no indication that enforcement would ease under Miller. “Nothing is changing, same quotas,” one official said on condition of anonymity.

Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, an occasional Trump critic who is retiring from Congress, said Miller dismissed warnings before the election that immigration and tariff policies were driving voters away. “We said, ‘You’re going to give us a bad midterm election,’ and he rejected it,” Bacon said. The White House said Miller would continue to deliver “historic successes,” but Bacon described the appointment as “doubling down on a failed strategy,” adding that it was “going over like a lead balloon in most of Congress.”

Miller’s influence is expected to extend well beyond immigration. He has overseen Trump’s executive orders, giving him a detailed understanding of the administrative tools available to the president. Several people interviewed by Reuters said they expect the White House to rely more heavily on executive action rather than bargaining with the new Democratic-controlled Congress, while Republican lawmakers who distance themselves from Trump could face increased pressure from the administration.

“Those on Capitol Hill looking to break away from the Trump administration will know that Stephen Miller is not going to sit idly by and watch that happen,” Republican strategist Ron Bonjean said.

A bigger role on Iran and Israel

The promotion will also give Miller greater influence over foreign policy, an area that has not traditionally been his main focus. Three sources familiar with his thinking told Reuters that Miller opposes prolonging the war with Iran, while remaining strongly supportive of Israel.

That position could create tension inside an administration in which Trump has threatened renewed strikes against Iran while also announcing plans to end U.S. aid to Israel. Miller’s views on the conflict could therefore become more consequential as he moves from a powerful policy adviser to the official responsible for managing the White House.

His rise has also unsettled some corporate lobbyists, who fear they will have less access than they did under Wiles. “This will be a big change,” a senior lobbyist at a Trump-aligned firm said. “Miller is there to focus on political priorities, like immigration and tariffs, stuff Trump cares about, and won’t have the same approach as Susie, who understood policies have unintended consequences.”

For Trump’s closest allies, however, that combative instinct is precisely the point. Senior administration figures and political supporters have praised Miller as the kind of loyal enforcer the president needs as he faces Democratic investigations, internal Republican dissent and the political consequences of the midterm defeat.

Asked if the midterms would usher in a pullback in immigration enforcement, one of the officials responded, "I would count on the opposite" with Miller as chief of staff.

The sources also said the administration believes the stunning electoral losses last week were largely driven by concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran — not its immigration crackdown.

"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorize our communities. There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News.

Bis cited the Trump administration's efforts to bolster security at the U.S.-Mexico border, where illegal crossings have plunged to historically low levels after soaring to record highs under former President Joe Biden's tenure.

Miller has been seen as a loyal foot soldier in President Trump's inner circle for a decade, since his successful 2016 presidential campaign, when he promised to shut down Muslim immigration to the U.S. and dramatically expand deportations of those in the U.S. illegally.

During that time, Miller has solidified himself as the chief architect of Mr. Trump's hardline immigration policies. Miller was one of Mr. Trump's top aides during his first administration, when officials banned immigration and travel from Muslim-majority countries and separated thousands of migrant children from their parents as part of a "zero tolerance" crackdown that was abandoned after massive public uproar.

But Miller has greatly expanded his power — and his influence over federal immigration policymaking — since Mr. Trump's return to the White House.

In less than two years, with Miller as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, the second Trump administration has effectively closed the U.S. asylum system; shut down refugee admissions, with a notable exemption for White South Africans; tightened access to different legal immigration benefits like green cards; and undertaken highly visible ICE and Border Patrol arrest operations across the country.

Those immigration enforcement operations have often triggered widespread community backlash, including in January, when federal immigration officials killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during a crackdown in Minneapolis that the administration scaled back following bipartisan outcry.

Miller has publicly floated the idea of suspending habeas corpus — the conditional right for people to challenge unlawful detention — for ICE detainees. Habeas cases have skyrocketed over the past two years, as the Trump administration has greatly narrowed other avenues for those fighting deportation to be released from ICE detention.

In addition to his immigration portfolio, Miller has also played an influential role in the Trump administration's crackdown on universities and legal groups, and its campaign to investigate allegations of fraud in Democratic-led states like Minnesota.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said the Trump administration's deportation efforts are likely to face some obstacles next year. She expects congressional Democrats to use their new powers to try to rein in ICE, including by issuing a flurry of subpoenas, holding oversight hearings and passing measures to limit immigration enforcement funds.

Cardinal Brown also predicts that some communities and states with newly elected Democratic leaders, like Texas, may scrap or limit policies that allowed or required local law enforcement officials to work with ICE. Last week, Houston's mayor said he would direct local police to limit their cooperation with ICE, following the election results.

But Cardinal Brown stressed Mr. Trump will likely veto any Democratic attempts to restrict ICE enforcement and noted the agency received $75 billion in funds through 2029 due to the "One Big Beautiful Bill" that the president signed into law last year.

"They're going to continue apace," Cardinal Brown said. "They have the money. They have the resources."

In the United States, Democrats won elections for attorney general in five states that lean toward the Republican Party: Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Kansas. The newly elected officials may reconsider the states’ cooperation with federal immigration agencies, strengthen protections for access to abortion and join interstate lawsuits against the policies of President Donald Trump’s administration, The Hindu reports.

A shift in legal strategy

State attorneys general set law-enforcement priorities, issue legal opinions and can challenge federal decisions in court. Republican attorneys general have actively opposed federal regulations over the past decade, promoted restrictions on gender-affirming medical care, rolled back diversity initiatives and supported expanded access to firearms.

Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson said he plans to review initiatives launched by his predecessor, Ken Paxton. These include legal action against out-of-state abortion service providers, claims linking over-the-counter medications to autism, and lawsuits concerning vaccine effectiveness. He also intends to assess the advisability of the state’s continued cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Plans of the newly elected officials

Johnson said he is prepared to join multistate lawsuits over what he called abuse of federal power. He also plans to focus the office’s work on antitrust cases and consumer protection.

In Iowa, Attorney General-elect Nate Willems pledged to pursue corporate polluters and restore the consumer protection division. In Ohio, John Kulewicz campaigned on a promise to counter corporate price gouging. In Kansas, Chris Mann said he seeks to make the office’s work less partisan and to review his predecessor’s lawsuits, including a case concerning access to the drug mifepristone for medication abortion.

text:
Republicans lost state attorney general races to Democrats in key states in the 3 November midterm elections, with potential consequences for lawsuits related to abortion, transgender rights and other issues that the outgoing Republicans championed.

Democrats will take over state attorney general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas.

Here are some of the pending lawsuits that could be affected by the election:

Abortion and transgender ​rights

Texas is among the states suing the US Food and Drug Administration over its approval of the abortion drug mifepristone, arguing that the agency failed to thoroughly evaluate the ‌drug's safety and effectiveness. Florida, where Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won a new term on Tuesday, would be the remaining plaintiff if Texas withdraws from the case.

The Democratic Attorney General-elect in Kansas, Chris Mann, could withdraw the state from a separate challenge to regulations that expanded access to mifepristone, which would leave Missouri and Idaho as plaintiffs.

Texas has also filed numerous lawsuits against out-of-state providers for remotely prescribing mifepristone to Texas residents. Nathan Johnson, the Democrat elected Texas attorney general this week, told Reuters ​he will assess pending lawsuits that Paxton's office brought to determine whether or not he will support them. "Everything will be examined," Johnson said.

Johnson also could decline to defend the state's near-total ​abortion ban in a lawsuit by the family of Tierra Walker, a Texas woman who died from a pregnancy-related condition after doctors refused to perform an abortion.

The ⁠state also could back away from at least three pending cases seeking to enforce a 2023 law banning gender-affirming treatments such as puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors.

In Georgia, Democrat Tanya Miller's election could ​impact the state's defense of HB 481, the 2019 law banning abortion after six weeks. Litigation over the ban is ongoing after the Georgia Supreme Court revived the law in 2024.

Pharmaceuticals

Another lawsuit that could draw scrutiny from ​Johnson, the Texas attorney general-elect, is his state's case against Kenvue, which alleges the Tylenol maker concealed purported links between acetaminophen use during pregnancy and autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children. Kenvue has denied any wrongdoing.

Doctors and medical groups consider acetaminophen, the active ingredient in Tylenol, as the preferred treatment for pain and fever during pregnancy, and there is no firm scientific evidence of a link between its use and autism or ADHD.

Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, ​in 2023 in another lawsuit accused drugmaker Pfizer of misrepresenting the efficacy of its widely used COVID-19 vaccine. Pfizer in a prior statement said its representations about its vaccine have been "accurate and science-based," and that ​Paxton's lawsuit had no merit.

Republican Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, who narrowly lost a reelection bid to Mann, also has sued Pfizer over similar claims.

Environment

Texas and 12 other Republican-led states are suing top asset managers including BlackRock, accusing them of violating antitrust law ‌through climate ⁠activism that reduced coal production and boosted energy prices.

The lawsuit in federal court is one of the most prominent legal challenges to environmental, social and governance (ESG) initiatives. Kansas is among the plaintiffs in the lawsuit. BlackRock has denied any wrongdoing. Vanguard Group in February settled claims against it in the lawsuit for $29.5 million.

Immigration

The new attorney general in Texas could also drop the state's defense of SB4, a Republican-backed Texas law that allows state authorities to arrest and prosecute people suspected of illegally crossing the US-Mexico border. The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals in April allowed the law to take effect as a challenge proceeds.

In another matter, the US Supreme ​Court is weighing whether to take up Iowa's appeal of ​a ruling blocking a law that would allow ⁠state officials to arrest and prosecute people who are in the US illegally. The state's attorney general-elect, Democrat Nate Willems, could decline to defend the law if the Supreme Court takes the case.

Voting rights and elections

Paxton's office is appealing a Boston federal judge's order that stopped the Republican attorney general from continuing to pursue ​a lawsuit against Democratic fundraising platform ActBlue over its donation practices.

In June, US District Judge Richard Stearns granted ActBlue's request for a preliminary injunction after ​the platform argued that Paxton's ⁠lawsuit violated its free speech rights.

In Georgia, a federal judge is weighing a fight over the state's congressional maps, which challengers said harmed Black voters. A federal appeals court in August vacated a 2023 ruling by the lower court that said the state's Republican-backed plan illegally diluted Black votes in violation of the Voting Rights Act.

In a ruling on Thursday, US District Judge Steven Jones in Atlanta paused further action in the litigation, citing "impending changes" in ⁠the leadership of ​the state attorney general's office.

Religious liberties

At the US Supreme Court, the new Texas attorney general could revisit the state's defense of ​a Texas law mandating the display of the Ten Commandments in public schools. Several Texas families, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, have asked the justices to invalidate the 2025 state law.

A divided US appeals court in April ruled that Texas can require public ​schools to display the Ten Commandments in every classroom. The Supreme Court has not decided whether to take up the case.

description:

text:
US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Stephen Miller, 41, would replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, following the Republican defeat in the midterm elections and the loss of both chambers of Congress.

Trump announced Miller's appointment on Friday after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, elevating the hardline immigration architect to one of Washington's most powerful positions.

The appointment, which takes effect on Monday, signals a political choice: Rather than moderate his policies after the electoral setback, Trump is promoting one of his most uncompromising architects.

In 2002, a 16-year-old high school student took the stage at his school in Santa Monica, California, and stood before his classmates. "I'm the only one here willing to say and do things that no one else would dare," he declared.

He then asked why students were required to pick up their own trash when the school employed janitors who were paid to do precisely that. His remarks sparked an uproar, and they removed him from the stage shortly afterward.

Nearly a quarter of a century later, that teenager, Stephen Miller, is poised to become one of the most powerful figures in the United States.

Miller is not simply another adviser seeking to please Trump. Over the past decade, he has become one of the few people who can translate the president's political instincts into executive orders, operational directives, and government policy.

Now, he will also be the man deciding who gets access to the Oval Office, which issues reach the president's desk, and how the White House operates.

From a liberal California high school to the top of a Republican administration

Miller's story begins in a place few would have expected to produce one of the leading symbols of the American Right.

He was born and raised in Santa Monica, a liberal city on the Pacific coast, in a Jewish family with Democratic roots. Yet, even as a teenager, he developed distinctly conservative views and clashed with teachers and fellow students over immigration, multiculturalism, and political correctness.

He began appearing on conservative radio programs, criticized the use of Spanish at school, and argued that the education system was imposing a liberal worldview on its students. Following the September 11 terrorist attacks, his opposition to what he described as anti-Americanism in educational institutions intensified.

He later became close to conservative activist David Horowitz, who had himself moved from the radical Left to the Right.

Miller continued to stir controversy at Duke University, where he studied. He gained national attention when he defended members of the university's lacrosse team who were accused of rape in a case that rocked the campus in 2006.

The charges were subsequently dropped, and Miller, who appeared on television to defend the players, began establishing a reputation as a fighter against the liberal establishment.

After graduating, he moved to Washington, working for Republican members of Congress and later for Alabama senator Jeff Sessions, who was considered one of the most prominent opponents of illegal immigration.

It was there that Miller's worldview took shape, with immigration seen not merely as a matter of law enforcement but as a question concerning the national and cultural identity of the United States.

When Trump launched his presidential campaign in 2015, Miller found a candidate who openly expressed ideas he had long believed in. He joined the campaign, became one of Trump's leading speechwriters, and helped shape his anti-immigration messaging and "America First" ideology.

Architect of immigration policy becomes one of Trump's closest allies

During Trump's first term, Miller was involved in shaping some of the administration's most controversial measures: restrictions on entry from Muslim-majority countries, reductions in refugee admissions programs, and the policy that led to children being separated from their parents at the Mexican border.

The measures drew fierce criticism and legal challenges but strengthened Miller's standing among supporters of strict immigration enforcement.

Unlike many advisers who parted ways with Trump following his defeat in the 2020 election, Miller remained by his side.

During Joe Biden's presidency, he co-founded the legal organization America First Legal, which pursued legal challenges against policies introduced by the Democratic administration, while maintaining close ties with the former president.

When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, Miller was appointed deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser. This time, he was not content merely to formulate ideas. He was directly involved in implementing them.

In May 2025, Axios reported that Miller and then-homeland security secretary Kristi Noem had demanded that senior Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials meet a target of at least 3,000 arrests a day, roughly three times the rate at the beginning of Trump's second term.

The policy led to widespread raids in American cities and confrontations between armed immigration agents and residents and protesters.

Miller was also involved in efforts to restrict legal immigration pathways, impose limitations on asylum, and change the constitutional interpretation that grants American citizenship to people born on US soil.

But his influence has long since extended beyond immigration.

He has also played a central role in the administration's battles with universities, efforts to eliminate diversity and inclusion programs, and the promotion of a vision that grants broader powers to the executive branch.

When the courts blocked administration measures, Miller did not hesitate to confront them as well.

After judges struck down some of Trump's import tariffs, he described the ruling as a "judicial coup." On other occasions, he attacked judges as Marxists and communists.

In an interview with Bloomberg in January 2026, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich described Miller's standing as nearly equivalent to that of a cabinet secretary.

According to Gingrich, Trump views him as someone capable of performing "six or seven different jobs."

Beyond immigration: Influence extending into foreign policy

Indeed, Miller has begun expanding his involvement in foreign policy and national security.

He participated in discussions concerning the American operation in Venezuela and the fight against drug cartels in Latin America.

When Trump raised the possibility of taking control of Greenland, Miller articulated a worldview in which international relations are ultimately determined by force.

"We live in a world where you can talk all you want about international niceties," he said in an interview with CNN's Jake Tapper.

"But in the real world, Jake, force, power, and the use of force are what govern. Those are the iron laws of the world and have been since the beginning of time."

Against the backdrop of that worldview, a New York Times report is particularly noteworthy.

According to the report, one of the arguments Miller made in favor of his appointment as chief of staff was the need to bring the war in Iran to an end.

According to people who heard his remarks, Miller explained that some of Trump's core supporters viewed the campaign as a betrayal of his promises to avoid prolonged wars in the Middle East.

The report does not necessarily indicate a change in Miller's fundamental position on the use of military force. It does, however, illustrate how closely he monitors the sentiments of the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement and the political dangers facing Trump.

His Jewish family and criticism from within

Miller's Jewish identity occupies a distinctive place in his story.

He is married to Katie Miller, who is also Jewish and has held positions in the Trump administration.

The couple married in 2020 in a ceremony officiated by Rabbi Aryeh Lightstone, who later helped advance the Abraham Accords and is now a member of the Board of Peace.

They have three children.

Yet, some of the harshest disagreements over Miller's policies have emerged within his own family and the Jewish community.

His maternal uncle, David Glosser, published an article in Politico in 2018 accusing his nephew of hypocrisy on immigration.

He recalled that the family's ancestors had fled persecution in Europe and that one of them, Wolf-Leib Glosser, arrived in the United States in 1903 with just eight dollars in his pocket.

According to his uncle, had Miller's preferred immigration policies been in place at the time, his family might never have reached America and escaped persecution.

Rabbi Neil Comess-Daniels, who taught Miller as a child at a synagogue in Santa Monica, also sharply criticized him, arguing that his policies contradicted the humanitarian Jewish values he had tried to instill in him.

In 2019, rabbinical organizations affiliated with the Reform, Conservative, and Reconstructionist movements called for Miller's dismissal following the publication of his correspondence, which prompted accusations that he had promoted white supremacist ideas.

Miller rejected the criticism and has previously argued that some of the attacks against him stemmed from antisemitism directed at a Jewish administration official.

By contrast, the Republican Jewish Coalition considers him one of Trump's most important allies.

Following his appointment as chief of staff, the organization's executive director, Matt Brooks, congratulated him and described him as one of the most influential and effective architects of the MAGA movement.

"He has never wavered in his determined and passionate defense of American sovereignty, freedom, and prosperity," Brooks said, adding that Miller was the right person to lead the president's team during the remaining two years of his term.

Among Democrats, however, the reactions were entirely different.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called Miller a "dangerous xenophobe," while Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer argued that the appointment proved Trump had learned nothing from the electoral defeat.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, warned that Democrats would continue investigating Miller's involvement in deportation policies and advised him to "get a lawyer."

'I pledge you my absolute loyalty'

"He saved our military from collapse, our economy from destruction, and our border from ruin."

He then addressed Trump directly.

"It is the greatest honor of my life to be your chief of staff. I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my complete dedication to your success and the success of this country."

Miller will now face a very different test from those he has encountered throughout his career.

For years, he was the man pushing Trump to fulfill his promises, sometimes through confrontation with other branches of government.

As chief of staff, he will also have to manage the White House, mediate between cabinet members and senior officials, contend with a Democratic-controlled Congress, and maintain the priorities of a president who is not known for organizational discipline.

The major question in Washington is whether a man who has made ideological struggle his life's work can also become an effective manager, or whether his appointment will turn Trump's final two years in the White House into a prolonged, head-on confrontation with his political opponents.

Either way, the Jewish boy who stood before students at a liberal California school nearly a quarter of a century ago and promised to say things no one else dared to say now occupies a position in which his words can influence the policies of the world's most powerful nation.

Dearborn police said its department was not given advance notice before a federal immigration enforcement operation resulted in the arrest of three people on Saturday, Nov. 7.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) operation took place near Warren Avenue and Mead Street in East Dearborn around 8 a.m., according to a news release from the Dearborn Police Department.

"Federal authorities contacted the Dearborn Police Department after the arrests had taken place," according to police. "There was no advance notification or coordination with the City of Dearborn or the Police Department."

As of Saturday afternoon, federal authorities have not provided the department with the names of those arrested or the reasons for their arrests, police said.

“Communication between federal agencies and local law enforcement helps support public safety and ensures we can respond accurately to residents’ questions and concerns,” Dearborn Police Chief Issa Shahin said in the news release. “We encourage federal authorities to communicate with our department when conducting operations in our community.”

The Dearborn Police Department said it is still seeking more information from federal authorities.

The incident comes shortly after Canton police and Plymouth-Canton Community Schools said they had no advance notice of immigration enforcement activity near Hulsing Elementary School on Oct. 20, prompting officials to shelter students and staff in place for more than an hour.

The ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Detroit Field Office and the Department of Homeland Security did not provide comment to the Free Press on the Dearborn operation as of Saturday afternoon. text:
Protesters gathered outside of a Boyle Heights hospital after federal immigration agents brought a person in their custody to the emergency room for treatment and blocked the entrance for hours on Friday.

Adventist Health White Memorial Hospital officials confirmed that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents brought the unidentified person to the hospital Friday evening, but they did not specify the nature of the patient's medical requirements.

As the agents stood outside the emergency room entrance, a large crowd of protesters began to converge at the hospital, some banging pots and recording the interaction on their phones.

Abraham Zavala, a community activist and rapid responder, said that the ICE agents maced him and others in the crowd.

"They were occupying four spaces. We heard this morning they were diverting traffic to other hospitals," Zavala said. Because they had a parking lot full of ICE agents."

Los Angeles Police Department officers were also called to the scene after learning of the gathering and a reported disturbance, but department officials said they did not take part in any immigration enforcement.

On Saturday, another group marched from Mariachi Plaza to the hospital on Cesar E. Chavez Avenue to express their outrage.

"They are not listening. They are not hearing what people are saying, which is that ICE enforcement has to abide by human rights, by constitutional rights," said Angelica Salas of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, or CHIRLA.

They were joined by Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who also condemned the agents' actions.

"Especially today, after elections showed that the brutality of the Trump administration is unwelcome, not just in LA, but all over this country," Raman said while speaking to the crowd. "What happened last night at this hospital wasn't a front to the wishes of the American people."

When protesters arrived at the hospital to hand over a letter demanding answers from officials, they found Adventist Health White Memorial Hospital President Daniel Fontoura waiting for them.

"I can tell you that ICE was not at our invitation," Fontoura said while speaking to media members. "When they block access to our patients ... they do us a disservice, and they have dishonored our commitment."

People in the community said they want more action and fewer words.

"This is our neighborhood. We will defend to the occasion like we always have," Zavala said. "We have a history of resistance and taking down anyone who tries to harm our community and our families."

LA Mayor Karen Bass also condemned what happened at the hospital, calling on the Trump administration to stop immigration enforcement at healthcare facilities.

"A hospital should be the one place where people feel safe. No one should have to think twice about receiving care or fear that a loved one's treatment could be interrupted because of their immigration status," Bass' statement said. "Hospital leadership also had a duty to step in right away to protect patients and neighbors, and by all appearances, that did not happen."

Following Bass' statement, hospital officials shared another statement from Fontoura, saying their "first and last call" is to care for patients "regardless of immigration status."

"I want to be clear: White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement, does not facilitate immigration operations, and will not allow immigration activities to compromise our commitment to patient care and safety," a hospital spokesperson said. "I know many of you are afraid. Every family in Boyle Heights should know they can come to us for care without fear. For more than 100 years, White Memorial has been your hospital, and that will not change."

When asked for comment, an ICE spokesperson said they would not disclose or discuss their law enforcement operations.

"ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches. This is just another false narrative to try to demonize our brave ICE law enforcement," the statement said, in part.

It's unclear if anyone was arrested or if federal agents detained anyone at the hospital.

text:
GEO Group has reached a settlement in a lawsuit filed more than 10 years ago alleging that its Aurora, Colorado, detention facility violated forced labor statutes.

The lawsuit alleged that the facility violated the state's minimum wage and forced labor laws by paying detainees $1 a day to work at the facility, sometimes under threat of solitary confinement. It was filed in 2014 on behalf of former detainees Alejandro Menocal, Marcos Brambila, Grisel Xahuentitla, Hugo Hernandez, Lourdes Argueta, Jesus Gaytan, Olga Alexaklina, Dagoberto Vizguerra, and Demetrio Valegra. The detainees said they were used to do janitorial work.

When the lawsuit was filed, Menocal told CBS Colorado, "It's their job to run the facility, and instead they used and abused us to run the facility, and that's why we're suing."

Hans Meyer, an attorney who represented the plaintiffs, said the class action lawsuit claimed the GEO Group was threatening detainees with solitary confinement to force them to do jobs that it would otherwise have had to fill from out in the community at higher rates of pay.

A judge dismissed the claim that the facility violated Colorado's minimum wage law by paying detainees $1 a day, stating they did not qualify as employees under state law. However, he did allow the lawsuit to proceed on allegations that GEO unjustly profited from the detainees and violated the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act, which prohibits forced labor.

Brandt Milstein, one of the plaintiff's attorneys, said there was a key difference between inmates working below minimum wage in state and privately run prisons and civil immigration detainees because they "are not being held for any criminal violation."

In 2018, a United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit ruling allowed a district court's decision to permit the nine plaintiffs to file the suit on behalf of approximately 60,000 people.

Following that 2018 decision, GEO Group told CBS Colorado, "We intend to continue to vigorously defend our company against these claims. The terms of the voluntary work program at all federal immigration facilities are directed by the Federal government and governed by federal law. All ICE facilities operated by GEO, including the Aurora ICE Processing Center, are highly rated and provide high-quality services in safe, secure, and humane residential environments that meet the needs of individuals in the care and custody of federal immigration authorities pursuant to the Federal government's performance-based national detention standards."

The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025. The GEO Group argued that, as a federal government contractor, it cannot be held liable for actions performed within the scope of federal authority and in compliance with government directions, also known as the Yearsley defense. The lower court ruled that the case should go to trial, and GEO immediately tried to appeal before the trial began.

The Supreme Court justices unanimously ruled 9-0 that the Yearsley defense does not provide immunity from suit and denied GEO Group the right to an immediate appeal.

According to court documents, GEO and the plaintiffs reached a settlement on Monday. The notice says that, after filing the motion for preliminary approval, they will work to get the court's final approval and notify and distribute funds to those included in the settlement. It did not state the settlement terms.

The details of the agreement have not yet been made public. Meyer said he could not share the terms of the agreement yet due to a court-issued gag order, but he welcomed the deal in a statement:

"I think on behalf of the plaintiffs that we represent, we're happy about the resolution. I mean, obviously, I think things could have turned out different, and we were definitely ready for trial, and were ready to hold you accountable," said Meyer. "But at least in terms of the focus here, really, is that this is a day in which our clients, people in the community, had their voices heard, finally. After 12 years of litigating, a trip to the Supreme Court and four trips to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals, we finally reached a resolution in this case that, at the very least, recognizes the claims that our clients brought, which had to do with being forced to work under threat of solitary confinement and being coerced and manipulated into working for $1 a day so that GEO could maximize its profits for corporate shareholders."

CBS Colorado has reached out to the GEO Group for a response, but has not yet heard back.

text:
WILLISTON, Vt. —

Almost 300 People gathered to march from Industrial Avenue to Harvest Lane, protesting actions taken by ICE. They carried tombstones and coffins with the names of those who died in ICE custody.

Protestors gathered in South Burlington at the White Cap Industrial Park where the National Criminal Analysis Targeting Center is housed, drawing chalk outlines of some of the people who have died in federal immigration custody.

"We want ice out of Vermont, but that begins with more people knowing that ICE is here and knowing what they do here," said protestor Drew Hudson. "First and foremost, we want people to know what these two buildings do, how they're connected to the broader things they may have seen video from Minneapolis, a video from Chicago, but not know that those tips are starting here in Vermont and that we have a role to play in this."

The crowd then marched to the Harvest Lane Facility for a moment of silence and prayer.

"I think the ICE enforcement issue and the level of surveillance going on and the brutality of the whole thing really needs to end," said Ned, a protester.

Lawyer David Kelley said he came ready to help out if the planned sit-in turned to arrests.

"We may be able to get back on track. I hope we can, but I feel like the rule of law and our Constitution have been badly injured and need to heal," he said. "I think maybe we will begin that process."

The sit-in stayed peaceful, with some receiving a paper saying they are subject to an investigation by the Department of Justice for obstructing access to federal property.

"It feels like what I have to face is so much less than what my immigrant friends and neighbors have to face that I'm glad to be doing this," said Steve Crofter, one of the people to get a paper.

In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said: "While the First Amendment protects free speech and peaceful assembly, it doesn’t protect obstruction of entrances to federal facilities like the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, which provides intelligence-driven leads for ICE and partner law enforcement agencies to locate and arrest criminal and other priority aliens who pose a threat to our nation’s communities."

Video posted on social media appears to show one person being detained outside the hospital. In the video, at least three officers in tactical vests are seen detaining someone at the intersection of Boyle and Pennsylvania Avenues around 11:30 p.m.

A group of about six more officers in tactical vests and masks can be seen walking around the area as another, whose vest says “Police ICE,” yells at the person recording to “back up” and “do not impede with the arrest.”

“You’re arresting U.S. citizens,” the person recording says. “18 USC 111, they’re interfering,” the officer replies, referring to Title 18, Section 111 of the U.S. Code: Assaulting, resisting, or impeding certain officers or employees.

In the video, a bystander who says the person being arrested is his brother can be seen speaking to the officer.

“Your brother assaulted a federal agent. He’s being arrested for assaulting a federal agent; he’s coming with us,” the officer tells them.

Boyle Heights Beat reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for more information about the incident but has not yet received a response.

LAPD response

The Los Angeles Police Department was first called to the scene at 11:59 p.m. to respond to a “large group causing a disturbance,” according to LAPD Officer Norma Eisenman. LAPD responded again at 2:24 a.m. as crowds continued to gather outside of the hospital.

“Officers responded to maintain public safety and keep the peace. At no point did LAPD officers assist federal immigration authorities with enforcement activities or detain any individuals in connection with immigration enforcement,” Eisenman said.

Video posted on social media by Izzy Ramirez shows a line of agents blocking the emergency loading dock around 2:30 a.m. as a crowd continues to shout at the agents and make noise.

“It was horrible for the local community. The ICE presence was a lot more than I’ve seen it visibly before,” said Roman.

What the hospital said

Japhet De Oliveira, corporate communications executive at Adventist Health, shared the following statement:

“Federal agents brought a person in their custody to our emergency department, and we cared for that patient with dignity and privacy, as we do for every patient. When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely care. White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement. We know last night frightened our neighbors. No matter what happens outside our doors, everyone who comes inside is our patient, and our focus will only be on that patient, and it will not change.”

Doctors at Adventist White Memorial last year reported that ICE agents were violating the privacy rights of detained patients and prohibiting contact with patients’ family members. While the hospital released guidelines to protect patients and support staff, doctors and advocates have said they fall short.

The Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network said it plans to lead a protest against ICE outside White Memorial at 2 p.m. Saturday.

text:
BOYLE HEIGHTS, LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- Community members and advocates gathered outside Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights on Saturday afternoon to protest the presence of ICE agents at the hospital.

Federal agents were at the medical center seeking medical treatment for a person in their custody around midnight, according to the Los Angeles Police Department.

Video from the scene showed a teenage girl being assisted by neighbors after she was pepper-sprayed during the demonstration.

"Don't tilt your head back, don't tilt your head back," one person is heard telling the teen.

"Don't touch it, don't touch it," another person says.

Video also showed tense confrontations outside the hospital between community members and federal agents. As ICE agents left the area, Los Angeles Police Department officers followed closely behind.

Community member Derek Mejia criticized the police response.

"LAPD wasn't concerned with the people that were arrested- brutalized by ICE or the two minors who were maced by ICE but they were concerned with keeping their buddies in ICE safe," Mejia said.

The protest drew community advocates and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who condemned the federal presence at the hospital.

"What happened last night at this hospital was an affront to the wishes of the American people and to the people of Los Angeles," Raman said.

During the demonstration, protesters entered hospital grounds and gathered around Adventist Health White Memorial President Daniel Fontoura, urging him to address the crowd.

"Give him the Mic! Give him the Mic," demonstrators shouted.

Fontoura said federal agents entered the hospital with a person in need of medical care. He also said hospital officials pushed back when agents sought access during a physician-patient consultation.

"There was a time when ICE actually wanted to break protocol and be in with the physician in that sacred physician patient encounter and we said no," Fontoura said.

Fontoura also explained why the hospital contacted the LAPD during the protest.

"When they lined up to prevent access to EMS trucks and ambulances to our facility that was not done with our approval," he said.

"So when those things happen we called LAPD and said help us with this predicament."

text:
A federal judge has ruled that the Mamdani administration has to give immigration officials the names and birthdays of certain people living in a large, city-run homeless shelter in the Bronx.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement claims they need the information as part of an investigation into residents that may be subject to deportation. But City Hall, which has barred city agencies from cooperating with ICE, has fought the subpoena in court and advocates are urging Mamdani to keep up the fight.

The mayor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment Saturday.

“The City has not shown that producing this list would be unduly burdensome,” the ruling by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan reads. “Under the applicable case law, the Court therefore has no choice but to compel the subpoena’s enforcement.”

The ruling requires the city to turn over a list of certain male residents that live in a shelter on Bruckner Boulevard along with their birthdays and any additional records that would help ICE identify the people who live there.

ICE had asked for the names of all the residents, but under Friday's ruling, the agency has appointed a special master to identify only residents with “serious criminal histories,” according to the ruling.

The shelter is a converted warehouse in the South Bronx that sleeps more than 2,000 and is the city’s last emergency migrant housing facility. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in February he plans to phase out the shelter by the end of the year.

Friday’s ruling comes after several failed attempts by the federal government to file similar subpoenas. Beginning in August 2025, ICE submitted four separate subpoena requests for personal information about residents of New York City shelters and the city fought them.

The city called a previous request a “fishing expedition lacking any legitimate investigative purpose,” according to the ruling.

The New York Immigration Coalition, which represents more than 200 immigrant and refugee rights groups throughout New York, is calling for the latest order to be appealed.

What “ICE has been trying to do for some time now is continuously launch these horrible campaigns of mass deportation against our community members,” said Murad Awawdeh, the president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition.

“ We believe that the city must appeal and that City Hall and Albany must act also on the simple principle of making sure they are also protecting everyone that's in their care.”

Awawdeh said that the city should not have to comply with the order because of the city’s sanctuary law policies, which limit cooperation between local government and ICE.

“Providing data on civil immigration enforcement…that's illegal as per our local law,” Awawdeh said.

Christopher also told ABC News they believe the release was partly due to an intervention by Congressman Derrick Van Orden, who contacted the Secretary of Homeland Security directly.

A Trooper since July 13, 2025, Van Der Merwe came to the United States from South Africa legally as a child and has waited seven years for an asylum interview, Christopher told WISN.

Christopher told WISN the family “followed the legal process and have waited seven years for an asylum interview.”

“He is included on his father’s pending asylum application and holds federal work authorization bearing an expiration date in 2030,” Christopher said told the news station.

description:
The Democratic mayor of America’s fourth-largest city is reversing course on cooperation with federal immigration authorities despite an executive order from defeated Texas Republican Gov.
The Lone Star State swung blue for the first time since its new senator-elect, James Talarico, was born, and Houston Mayor John Whitmire wasted no time Friday announcing new restrictions on cooperation with ICE.
In a statement put out Friday afternoon, Whitmire said, “I have signed an executive order directing HPD to no longer contact ICE for nonviolent offenses, helping reduce fear in our communities.
No contact with [ICE] over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses,” Whitmire told the AP.
The revised policy restored greater discretion for officers to contact ICE and wait for federal agents during encounters involving civil immigration warrants.
text:
The Democratic mayor of America’s fourth-largest city is reversing course on cooperation with federal immigration authorities despite an executive order from defeated Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott that threatened the loss of millions in state funding for noncompliance.

The Lone Star State swung blue for the first time since its new senator-elect, James Talarico, was born, and Houston Mayor John Whitmire wasted no time Friday announcing new restrictions on cooperation with ICE.

Whitmire told the New York Times that city police are not permitted to notify ICE if they encounter an illegal immigrant in “nonviolent contacts” like traffic stops or minor offenses.

“If they’re charged with a new crime, we’ll let ICE know as we get them to the jailhouse,” he told the paper Friday.

Abbott lost his bid for a fourth term Tuesday, and Talarico flipped one of the state’s Senate seats blue for the first time since Clinton Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen won his final re-election bid in 1988 — seven months before the current senator-elect was born.

Texas’ most recent Democratic governor, Ann Richards, the mother of former longtime Planned Parenthood president Cecile Richards, was elected shortly thereafter in 1990.

Whitmire did not respond to a request for comment but signaled to the Times that he made the decision at least in part because Abbott’s order requiring DHS contact caused “anxiety” among Houstonians.

In a statement put out Friday afternoon, Whitmire said, “I have signed an executive order directing HPD to no longer contact ICE for nonviolent offenses, helping reduce fear in our communities. Thank you to Chief Diaz, our state and local leaders for their collaboration. A step toward building a stronger Houston. Let’s Go to Work.”

He also acknowledged Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa won’t take office until January but characterized his decision as “responsible” and “more effective policy.”

A DHS spokesperson responded to Whitmire’s move in comments to Fox News Digital.

“We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities,” the spokesperson said.

“Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE.

“When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities.”

The spokesperson pointed to some recent criminal illegal aliens captured by ICE in Houston — including Alexander Montano of Cuba, convicted of willful homicide, burglary and forced entry into a residence.

Vietnamese national Ding Nguyen, also convicted of homicide, along with Guatemalan national Julio Camey, convicted of sex offense against a child, were also mentioned by the spokesperson.

“You write a citation or you warn them, and they go about their way. No contact with [ICE] over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses,” Whitmire told the AP.

A previous policy enacted in March by Whitmire and Police Chief Noe Diaz stipulated that if a background check revealed an immigration-related warrant, a sergeant would be called to oversee ICE involvement, according to Houston’s FOX affiliate.

The policy also said that if ICE could not make it to the stop within half an hour, the subject would be released.

The Houston City Council subsequently approved an ordinance in April limiting how long officers could detain individuals while awaiting ICE agents, but Whitmire backed revisions after Abbott threatened to withhold more than $100 million in state funding and then-Attorney General Ken Paxton launched an investigation into the city’s immigration policies.

The revised policy restored greater discretion for officers to contact ICE and wait for federal agents during encounters involving civil immigration warrants.

Whitmire’s latest announcement would instead limit such notifications to encounters involving jailable offenses, marking a return to the restrictions city lawmakers initially sought.
