text:
Houston's mayor on Nov. 6 directed his police force to cooperate less with ICE, a decision made within days of Democrats reclaiming a majority in Congress and sweeping statewide races in Texas.

The executive order directs Houston police to contact ICE only when the federal agency has a warrant for a person charged on a jailable offense. The guidance clarifies that suspected immigration enforcement by itself is no longer a basis to contact ICE or hold any person in custody.

“For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day,” Houston Police Chief Noe Diaz said. “HPD will no longer contact ICE if they have an administrative warrant and they are not arrested.”

The move is a turnaround from the federal government's aggressive immigration agenda nationwide and in Houston, where federal immigration officers fatally shot a Mexican homebuilder this summer. Texas is historically a Republican stronghold.

The directive is not the first time Houston city officials attempted to limit police cooperation with ICE. In April, the City Council passed an ordinance prohibiting officers from holding someone or extending a stop longer to wait for ICE.

Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican who has aligned himself with Trump’s immigration policies, threatened to withdraw about $110 million in public safety grants to Houston if it did not repeal the ordinance. The policy also faced legal scrutiny from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton for “materially limit(ing)” immigration enforcement.

This week, Democrat James Talarico decisively beat Paxton for the Texas Senate seat and Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Abbott in the race for Texas Governor.

“As I've said many times, elections matter,” Houston’s Mayor John Whitmire said. “I've been in contact with the new state leadership and bipartisan members of the Legislature. Quite frankly, this should be a nonpartisan issue.”

Whitmire, a Democrat, said in a press briefing today that the policy change is about “reducing fear and anxiety, not just within certain communities, but across all of Houston.”

Advocates at FIEL Houston, a nonprofit immigrant advocacy group, called the Mayor’s order a victory, adding that their community can now “breathe easier.”

USA TODAY has reached out to ICE for comment.

text:
Amid a historic turnout among Latino voters during the midterm election, Latinos in Colorado played a notable role in helping elect Democrats to state and federal seats. Exit polling shows new and long-time voters were driven not by party loyalty, but by economic pressures and concerns about immigration overreach .

Key findings from Colorado Latino Agenda’s biannual exit poll found that the majority of Latino voters — who represent the second-largest and second-fastest-growing ethnic voting bloc in the state — provided strong support for Democrats on Nov. 3.

The exit poll, commissioned by the Colorado Latino Agenda, surveyed 500 registered voters who identify as Latino between Oct. 19 and Nov. 3, with oversamples in Congressional Districts 1 and 8. The Colorado Latino Agenda is an initiative of Glenwood Springs-based Voces Unidas and the Colorado Organization for Latina Opportunity and Reproductive Rights.

Latino voters represent 17% of the overall electorate in Colorado. Roughly 67% of Latino voters in the state said they supported Democratic congressional candidates during the midterm, a 4% increase from 2024. Roughly 65% of respondents voted for Attorney General Phil Weiser in the gubernatorial race and 67% voted for Sen. John Hickenlooper in the U.S. Senate race, both of whom won their seats.

Latino support also contributed to wins for key congressional battles in Colorado — including the state’s 1st and 8th Congressional Districts — where Latino voters backed Democratic candidates by more than a 2-1 margin over Republicans. In Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, an 11-percentage-point increase in Democratic support from Latino voters between 2024 and 2026 helped flip the district to blue , electing Democrat Manny Rutinel over Republican incumbent Gabe Evans.

“The scale of what happened on Tuesday is already clear,” said Alex Sanchez, president and CEO of Voces Unidas. “We saw an El Niño-level blue tsunami swept from Texas to Arizona, and right here in Colorado.”

The support for Democrats in the midterms comes after findings from the 2026 Colorado Latino Policy Agenda survey revealed that — for the first time in six years — more Latinos said they believed the state was moving in the wrong direction than the right direction. Of the 66% who indicated they felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, 75% blamed Trump — up by almost 10 percentage points from 2025.

The shift in Latino voters supporting Democrats — and the increase in those who participated in the election — is a clear signal that Latinos are more loyal to the concerns of their community than they are to a particular party, said Gabe Sanchez, vice president of research at BSP Research. He added that the newly elected Democrats could just as easily lose that support if they fail to deliver on their campaign promises.

“Latinos are not party voters; they’re policy voters,” said Gabe Sanchez. “And as a consequence of that, I think there’s an opportunity for Democrats who did well in this election cycle with Latinos, but that opportunity obviously can be wasted if these expectations among Latino voters are not met.”

Latino voters cite the economy, immigration overreach as top issues

Rather than voting to support a particular party or candidate, the largest percentage of poll respondents — 36% — said their ballot was reflective of the issues most impacting their communities.

Latino voters overwhelmingly listed the economy as their top priority going into the midterms. Forty-four percent of respondents cited inflation and the cost of living as the top concerns for the federal government to address, with a greater 51% listing them as their top issues for the state to pursue.

Nearly half of respondents in the poll stated that groceries and food costs were creating financial pressure on their household, with 40% listing rent or mortgage costs and 38% listing gas prices as significant economic stressors. Other priorities closely aligning with inflation for Latino voters were improving wages, lowering healthcare costs and creating affordable housing, according to polling results.

When asked which party voters believed would do the best job at addressing their top concerns, 56% of respondents sided with Democrats. The other 44% either weren’t sure (3%), or were split between trusting Republicans (23%), both (12%) or neither (7%).

“Our hope as an organization is that the new governor in Colorado, the new legislature and the new leadership in Congress hopefully turn (their promises) into results, because we cannot mistake our support for unconditional loyalty and risk the same fate as those who have failed our communities before,” said Alex Sanchez.

Immigration policy also took center stage during the midterms. Approximately 73% of Latino voters also said that immigration played a significant role in how they voted during the midterms, including 52% of Republican voters.

Of the voters who said their decision was influenced by immigration enforcement in the United States, 59% said they were worried about keeping families together. Forty-seven percent also said they cared about preventing racial profiling and civil rights violations.

“Not only was (protecting immigrant rights) rounding out the top level of priorities, but it more than doubled in priorities since 2024,” said Gabe Sanchez. “We clearly think that was part of the energy and enthusiasm that drove a lot of Latinos to the ballot box across the state of Colorado in this cycle.”

Despite the impact of Latino votes in the midterm election, three out of every five Colorado respondents said they were not contacted by a candidate, political party, campaign or other group to discuss issues or encourage them to vote. Spanish speakers, those with less education, lower incomes and independent voters were among the least likely to be contacted.

Alex Sanchez said that the lack of information being provided to Latino voters likely contributed to confusion over certain ballot measures.

Many Latino voters, 39%, who participated in the exit poll expressed confusion over the way Colorado’s ballot measures were written. While voters largely agreed with the underlying values of various measures, support for the measures varied widely due to the large proportion who reported either not understanding or not voting on the measures, according to the exit poll.

Midterms see historic voter turnout among Latinos

Nationally, the midterms saw historic turnout among Latino voters. According to a 2026 voter poll released by UnidosUS and the Latino Community Foundation, roughly 17% of Latino voters cast ballots in their first federal election, while 41% returned to voting for the first time since 2022, the majority of whom were under 30 years old.

“While the numbers are still coming in, what we know so far indicates that this will undoubtedly be the largest turnout of Latino voters ever in a midterm election,” said Janet Murguía, president of UnidosUS. “It’s estimated that as many as 14.5 million Hispanics went to the polls. And I can’t help but reflect on the fact that President Trump asked voters across the country to pretend like he was on the ballot, and our observation is that Latino voters did just that by resoundingly rejecting his extreme policies and actions, and anyone who rubber stamped them.”

Similar to Colorado, Latino voters across the country listed economic concerns and the cost of groceries as leading issues, and displayed what Murguía called a “wholesale rejection of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.”

“Half of the Latino population have nothing left over after they pay their bills, or might even be struggling to make their bills each month, and more than 4 in 10 expect that the continuation of Trump’s economic policies would make them worse off in the next year,” said Gary Segura, president of BSP research.

For several Latino voters, the midterms represented their first time participating in an election as economic issues triggered broader activism. A significant portion of new Latino voters were also those aging into the electorate, according to UnidosUS data.

title: Our Voice: Election is Over, Fight to Defend Democracy and Human Rights is Not
description:
The Democrats have pulled off what is being called the biggest upset in the history of modern American elections.
They could be forgiven for taking a victory lap — but need to make it a short lap.
From the mountains to the plains, from the factories to the nameless office-workers — We need help to address urgent affordability realities.
Actually governing works to restore our faith in the efficacy of our government so that we can hope again.
But Trump is still president and he is already plotting what he can do without Congressional approval.
text:
This week, ‘We the People’ came roaring back, reasserting our role in this democratic republic to choose our leaders, loudly affirming our conviction in the checks and balances of a divided government, and our faith in the Rule of Law.

As recapped in this news piece earlier this week, the results of the 2026 midterm elections, described as a broad, and deep blue tsunami, have changed the political tenor of America. The Democrats have pulled off what is being called the biggest upset in the history of modern American elections.

More than 90 of the some 250 Democrats coming into Congress are millennials — this is a changing of the guard — a passing of the torch to a new generation of leadership. This could rightly be called a generational mandate.

They could be forgiven for taking a victory lap — but need to make it a short lap. America is in economic turmoil and the pain is deep and real. From the mountains to the plains, from the factories to the nameless office-workers — We need help to address urgent affordability realities.

At long last, we need an Ag Bill, we need SNAP benefits reinstated. We need the ACA health care subsidies back. We need sanity returned to the administration of Medicaid.

We need reinstatement of federal funding that has been withheld from blue states, including Colorado.

We need congressional oversight — quickly — to limit the administration’s attacks on our public lands and national parks.

While this new wave of congressional and state leaders gets their act together, President Donald Trump is proceeding to line up more shiny objects: the cruel architect of Trump immigration detentions and mass deportations Stephen Miller as Chief of staff. Just this morning he offered the job of White House Press Secretary to UFC president/fighter [Great Dane] Dana White (complete with a request to include his assistants, some of whom aren’t even from this country).

Honestly.

It’s been a rough last ten years — for the U.S. and the world. This county came close to anointing an authoritarian wanna-be effort. But it turns out that an overwhelming number of us believe in real democracy.

If this election shows us anything, it is that winning is one thing. What we desperately need now is for our elected leaders to govern.

Governing is different from winning — it is actually coming together to solve problems that will improve the lives and situations of the American people.Fail to govern on behalf of the people, and we will vote you out.

Actually governing works to restore our faith in the efficacy of our government so that we can hope again. Believe again.

Ethical governing might allow all of us to once again be proud, not just to be Americans, but of what this 250-year-old democracy means to the world. Hopefully the generations of Americans coming up behind us will recognize this as the repudiation of authoritarianism, corruption, and cruelty that has characterized Trump-ism.

But Trump is still president and he is already plotting what he can do without Congressional approval. This could be a rough couple of years. Buckle up!

text:
Houston Mayor John Whitmire announced Friday that police will no longer notify federal immigration authorities about administrative immigration warrants during routine encounters unless a person is arrested for a crime punishable by jail time.

The shift, announced days after Democrats swept key statewide races in Texas, marks a significant change in how Houston police cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Whitmire, a Democrat, signed an executive order changing the Houston Police Department’s procedures for contacting ICE, saying the move would ease fears in immigrant communities while maintaining public safety.

“I have directed the chief and HPD through an executive order that we will change our policy in regarding contact with ICE,” Whitmire said at a news conference Friday. “I do this to begin a healing process, reduce fear and anxiety across our community.”

Under the order, officers will no longer notify ICE about administrative immigration warrants during routine stops that do not result in an arrest. Police will still contact ICE if someone arrested for a new crime punishable by jail time also has such a warrant.

Houston Police Chief Noe Diaz said officers have already received updated instructions.

“If our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives the citation and goes about their day,” Diaz said. “HPD will no longer contact ICE if they have an administrative warrant and they are not arrested.”

The announcement follows Democratic victories in Texas, including Gina Hinojosa’s defeat of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, James Talarico’s U.S. Senate win and state Sen. Nathan Johnson’s election as attorney general. Democrats also captured the lieutenant governor’s office with Vikki Goodwin and the comptroller’s office with Sarah Eckhardt.

“Elections matter,” Whitmire said. “New leadership, new policies, and that’s what we’re responding to.”

Whitmire said he consulted incoming state officials, whom he expects will take a different approach to Senate Bill 4, the Texas immigration enforcement law that shaped Houston’s previous policy.

Whitmire, a former state senator who voted against the law, said his administration had previously complied with state directives because of concerns about losing funding.

More articles

“We were given direction that our funding would be withdrawn if we didn’t follow their direction of contacting ICE,” Whitmire said.

In April, Abbott’s office threatened to withhold roughly $110 million in public safety grants after Houston restricted detentions based solely on administrative immigration warrants. The city subsequently revised its policy to require officers to contact ICE when administrative immigration warrants appeared during background checks.

Whitmire acknowledged that the decision could prompt possible backlash from state or federal officials but said he was prepared to be held accountable.

“I accept that responsibility. I’m doing what’s in Houston’s best interest,” he said, adding that he hopes other Texas cities follow suit.

Diaz said officers’ interactions would continue to be monitored through department records and body camera footage reviews. He emphasized that Houston does not participate in the federal 287(g) Program, which authorizes certain local agencies to carry out immigration enforcement duties.

Whitmire said the change would allow residents to work, attend school and carry out daily activities without fearing that routine police encounters could trigger immigration enforcement.

“Unless you commit a new crime, a jailable offense, you have nothing to worry about,” he said.

text:
Federal immigration officers were seen outside a Boyle Heights-area hospital overnight, prompting some community members to protest outside the medical facility.

Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center confirmed the presence of federal agents on its property early Saturday, saying they transported an individual under their custody to the facility. A spokesperson for the hospital said the individual was taken to the medical center’s emergency room department for undisclosed reasons and that the agents blocked the entrance to the ER for two hours.

"When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely, respectful, and culturally sensitive care," the spokesperson said.

The hospital’s president, Daniel Fontoura, issued the following statement on the matter:

"Caring for patients is our first and last call. White Memorial is a place of healing and safety for everyone, regardless of immigration status.

"I want to be clear: White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement, does not facilitate immigration operations, and will not allow immigration enforcement activities to compromise our commitment to patient care and safety. Our role is care. Every patient brought to our hospital receives timely, respectful, and culturally sensitive care, and we protect their medical information, including immigration status.

"I know many of you are afraid. Every family in Boyle Heights should know they can come to us for care without fear. For more than 100 years, White Memorial has been your hospital, and that will not change.

"As we have in the past, we will continue to meet with community leaders, our longtime partners, to work together and ensure that every family in Boyle Heights knows White Memorial is here for them.”

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass condemned the agents' actions in blocking the entrance to the emergency department.

“Overnight, federal immigration agents gathered in force outside of the ambulance bay at Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights, effectively sealing off a critical entrance. For patients and families in medical crises, that presence was frightening at the worst possible moment.

“A hospital should be the one place where people feel safe. No one should have to think twice about receiving care or fear that a loved one's treatment could be interrupted because of their immigration status.

“I condemn ICE's action and call on the Trump Administration to stop all immigration enforcement in and around health care facilities. Hospital leadership also had a duty to step in right away to protect patients and neighbors, and by all appearances, that did not happen.

“All of Los Angeles stands with Boyle Heights, and we will use every lawful tool available to protect the community. Because in Los Angeles, we stand together, and we fight.”

In response to the federal agents’ presence at the hospital, Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, who oversees Boyle Heights, said she was “deeply troubled by reports of ICE activity” outside the facility.

As part of her statement, Jurado said, “The families I represent deserve to seek emergency care without fearing an encounter with immigration enforcement.” She also said she’s calling on the hospital to disclose and end any agreements it may have with United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement. See below for the Councilmember’s full statement.

The Los Angeles Police Department said officers were called to the area of the hospital for a disturbance involving a large group. A department spokesperson said officers responded to “maintain public safety and keep the peace.” They added that police officers did not help federal agents with any enforcement activities.

It’s unclear if any arrests occurred in connection with the disturbance call or if the federal agents detained anyone at the hospital.

NBCLA has reached out to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment.

Read below for Councilmember Jurado's full statement:

No one should be afraid to go to the hospital. As the Councilmember representing Boyle Heights, I am deeply troubled by reports of ICE activity and detentions outside White Memorial Hospital overnight. The families I represent deserve to seek emergency care without fearing an encounter with immigration enforcement.

I am calling on Adventist Health White Memorial to publicly disclose its agreements with ICE and end any voluntary medical-services contract with the agency. Every patient, including anyone in federal custody, must continue to receive appropriate, uninterrupted medical care. Hospital leadership must take immediate, concrete steps to protect patient privacy, support healthcare workers who advocate for their patients, and ensure that medical decisions remain with patients and their care teams.

ICE continues to wreak havoc in our neighborhoods, separating families, disrupting livelihoods, and creating fear around the most basic parts of daily life. When that fear reaches the emergency room, it puts the health of our entire community at risk. A parent bringing in a sick child or a person experiencing a medical emergency should be focused on getting help.

Earlier this year, I introduced a resolution, since adopted by the City Council, supporting stronger protections for patients and healthcare providers from immigration enforcement in medical settings. I will continue pressing for safeguards that protect access to care and hold institutions accountable to the communities they serve.

White Memorial serves the Boyle Heights community. Its leadership owes our residents clear answers about what happened overnight and concrete steps to protect patients, families, and staff. Our residents deserve a hospital they can trust with their lives.

These comments reflect the information currently available. As details continue to emerge, I will press for a full and accurate account of what occurred.

text:
A Biden-appointed federal judge ordered ICE's Denver field office director to appear in court Monday amid concerns that immigration authorities violated judicial release orders by immediately re-arresting detainees, including at least one instance outside a detention facility.

Nathan Rasper has been summoned as part of an inquiry involving 14 people who were re-arrested after being released from immigration detention. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) maintains that ICE complied with lawful court orders and that a judicial release order does not permanently shield individuals from immigration enforcement.

"When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time," DHS said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "ICE may seek to re-arrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage."

The Nov. 5 order issued by U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney followed an earlier ruling requiring the government to identify every case in Colorado since Oct. 27 in which ICE re-detained someone within 12 hours of a court-ordered release. Federal officials subsequently identified 14 petitioners who had been re-arrested after being released, but the filing did not provide the precise timing of when the re-arrests occurred. She directed officials to provide the exact dates and times of those releases and re-arrests and identify any additional individuals immediately detained following court-ordered releases.

OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP’S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’

The additional reporting requirements followed a Nov. 4 hearing in which Sweeney questioned whether ICE was circumventing judicial orders by briefly releasing detainees before immediately taking them back into custody. At that hearing, she ordered Rasper to appear at a follow-up hearing Monday to address the agency's practices.

The inquiry stems in part from the case of Ramon Quintero Alvarez, who was released from immigration detention on Oct. 27 before ICE immediately took him back into custody, according to a government court filing.

In a Nov. 3 court filing, federal government attorneys said they would not submit a legal brief defending the lawfulness of Alvarez's continued detention.

The filing prompted Sweeney to convene the Nov. 4 hearing at which Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew Soler and Kevin Traskos appeared alongside ICE Assistant Field Office Director Nichole Black, who testified under oath about the circumstances surrounding Alvarez's re-arrest.

APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS

At a Nov. 4 hearing, Sweeney ordered Alvarez be released and barred immigration authorities from detaining him again unless the government demonstrated, by clear and convincing evidence at a bond hearing, that he posed a flight risk or danger to the community.

The government must submit the additional information requested by Sweeney by 8 a.m. Monday, ahead of Rasper's scheduled court appearance later that morning. The proceedings could shed light on ICE's compliance with judicial release orders, but Sweeney has not indicated whether she intends to pursue contempt proceedings.

The dispute comes as ICE faces similar legal challenges across Colorado, where other Biden-appointed federal judges, including U.S. District Judges Nina Wang and S. Kato Crews, have presided over cases involving disputes over immigration detention and court-ordered releases.

title: Court rules against Home Office in asylum seeker kidnapping case - The Guardian
description:
The court of appeal has rejected claims by the Home Office that being kidnapped for ransom is not exploitation of trafficking victims.
They may be eligible for the support and recovery package trafficking victims are entitled to.
Being kidnapped for ransom is a common hazard for asylum seekers passing through Libya on their journey to Europe.

He and the other captives had to phone their families to beg them to pay their kidnappers the ransom money.
text:
The court of appeal has rejected claims by the Home Office that being kidnapped for ransom is not exploitation of trafficking victims.

The ruling means that many people who have been kidnapped for ransom, whom officials have previously excluded from being victims of exploitation under trafficking rules, will now have to have these claims considered. They may be eligible for the support and recovery package trafficking victims are entitled to.

Being kidnapped for ransom is a common hazard for asylum seekers passing through Libya on their journey to Europe. Many are fleeing conflict in countries such as Sudan and Eritrea as well as some Middle Eastern countries.

The legal challenge was brought by a Syrian asylum seeker who cannot be identified. The 25-year-old fled forced military conscription in July 2021, knowing he was likely to be imprisoned and tortured in Syria for refusing to fight.

He arrived in Libya, ultimately hoping to reach the UK. He and other Syrians were abducted by armed men and held in captivity for a month between August and September 2021. His money and phone were seized and they were driven through the desert for 24 hours, hearing gunshots, with no food and little water.

They were told they would not be released until their families agreed to pay a ransom of several thousand dollars. He was tied up and often beaten on his hands and feet by his kidnappers. He and the other captives had to phone their families to beg them to pay their kidnappers the ransom money. While they were on the phone, the kidnappers beat them so their families could hear screams. He was terrified that even if his family paid his captors, he might not be released and that his organs might be harvested.

The man was released after his family paid his kidnappers, and he made his way to Europe, crossing the Mediterranean from Libya to Italy by boat. He crossed the Channel from France to the UK on 16 May 2022 and claimed asylum.

The Home Office rejected his trafficking claim, arguing that because he had not been subjected to forced labour by his kidnappers, his experience did not meet the definition of exploitation in the trafficking rules. He challenged the decision in the high court, which ruled in his favour. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, appealed against the ruling.

While the government has pledged to support trafficking victims, the decision to exclude asylum seekers kidnapped for ransom in Libya has denied many the support the judges ruled they may be entitled to. Recent freedom of information data relating to asylum seekers who were confirmed to be genuine trafficking victims found that of the 1,778 confirmed victims between July 2024 and July 2025, 89% were forcibly removed from the UK, putting them at risk of being trafficked again.

While each trafficking claim must be considered on the facts of the individual case, the judgment found: “The secretary of state erred in not considering the question of whether kidnapping amounted to exploitation.”

The ruling could help thousands of potential trafficking victims, not only those who arrive in Britain in the future but also those previously rejected as being trafficking victims who were kidnapped and held to ransom in Libya. They can now get a fresh referral into the national referral mechanism for a new decision on whether there are reasonable grounds for them to be considered a victim of trafficking.

Jeremy Bloom, a consultant solicitor at Duncan Lewis, who represented the Syrian man, welcomed the ruling. “This judgment is a vindication of my client’s claim to be a victim of trafficking. The Home Office sought to restrict the definition of exploitation,” he said.

“We hope that it will also assist other victims of trafficking who have experienced similarly horrendous treatment to gain access to the leave and support that they need to recover from those experiences. Those individuals may include people who have had their claims to be a victim of trafficking refused, and who might now be able to ask for a new decision based on the law as set out in this judgment.”

Home Office sources said it would not be appropriate to comment on legal proceedings. A Home Office spokesperson said:“We are simplifying and strengthening protection and immigration routes, ensuring they are clear, targeted and focused on their intended purpose, while maintaining fairness and public confidence.”

Republicans suffered historic losses that saw both the House and Senate fall into Democrats’ hands in the new Congress. Democrats are on pace to win more than 250 seats in the House and at least 54 in the Senate.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING, BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS

text:
HOUSTON -- Houston's mayor on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, signing an order that he called a result of Democrats reclaiming power in Texas for the first time in decades.

The shift in the nation's fourth-largest city is one of the first actions to restrict U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in response to Democrats' rout in Tuesday's midterm elections. It is also a sign the results are already having an impact in Texas, where Republican leaders have enthusiastically embraced President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda.

The stunning victories included Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousting Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, which will make her Texas' first Latina governor and the first member of her party to hold the office in more than 30 years. Abbott, a Trump ally, has threatened Texas cities over attempts to curtail immigration enforcement.

"I've said many times, elections matter," Mayor John Whitmire said.

Whitmire, a Democrat, said the city would go after immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education." In the case of a traffic incident, "you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way," he said.

Under the mayor's directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if the person it stops is arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing or if ICE issues an administrative warrant, meaning that the person is wanted by immigration officials.

Houston has been a recurring scene of protests to Trump's immigration crackdown in the wake of one ICE officer fatally shooting a Mexican homebuilder and another striking a man with a car. Last week, a grand jury in Houston indicted the ICE officer who was inside the vehicle on charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

ICE has denied that the officer intentionally struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken, and criticized Whitmire over making the policy change.

"We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities," the agency said in a statement.

Despite a one-time $75 billion infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements -- many in Texas -- to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests.

Abbott has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. In April, he had threatened to take away nearly $200 million in public safety grants from Austin, Dallas and Houston after city officials in Houston tried to limit police officers' cooperation with ICE.

At the time, Hinojosa called Abbott's threat to withhold funds from cities "shameful." She and Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico took a moderate approach to immigration during their breakout campaigns, standing for robust border security but frequently criticizing Trump's crackdown, particularly over ICE officer shootings in Texas.

Spokespersons for Hinojosa and Talarico did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.

Information for this article was contributed by Elliot Spagat, Jesse Bedayn and Linley Sanders of The Associated Press.

title: Democrats to RFK Jr.: Resign Now or Be Prepared to Testify Before Congress | Truthout
authors: Anton Woronczuk, Mike Ludwig, Daniel Hunter, Chris Walker, Sharon Zhang, Julie Zenderoudi, Matt Simon, Marianne Lavelle, Dan Gearino, Shireen Akram-Boshar
description:
Voters elected multiple doctors and medical professionals who ran both as Democrats and opponents of the Trump-Kennedy approach to public health.
In North Carolina, pediatrician Annie Andrews won an upset over Republican scion Darline Graham while campaigning on expanding access to health care, including reproductive care.
All three have regularly publicly condemned Kennedy’s leadership of U.S. public health infrastructure.
At least a dozen Democrats called on Kennedy to resign when he appeared before the Senate Finance Committee in September 2025.
Bruce Mirken, the executive director of Defend Public Health, said the controversy surrounding Kennedy likely played a role in the GOP losing control of Congress.
text:
During the 2024 election, when backlash to pandemic-era safety protocols was still percolating on right-wing and alternative health blogs, the notorious anti-vaccine celebrity Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement were critical to President Donald Trump’s winning coalition.

Now, speculation is swirling about Kennedy’s future as Trump’s health secretary as Democrats prepare to take control of the next Congress and the president and GOP search for scapegoats following heavy losses in this week’s midterm contests. Voters elected multiple doctors and medical professionals who ran both as Democrats and opponents of the Trump-Kennedy approach to public health.

Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive who won a Senate seat in Michigan, is an epidemiologist and served as public health director in both Detroit and Wayne County before running for office on a campaign promoting Medicare for All. In North Carolina, pediatrician Annie Andrews won an upset over Republican scion Darline Graham while campaigning on expanding access to health care, including reproductive care.

In Ohio, Amy Acton infamously overcame a vicious attack ad produced by her opponent’s campaign to become the next governor of Ohio. But before that, the state’s residents got to know Acton from her regular briefings while leading Ohio’s Covid-19 pandemic response. All three have regularly publicly condemned Kennedy’s leadership of U.S. public health infrastructure.

Meanwhile, MAHA is increasingly fractured, and Trump’s alliance with Kennedy is reportedly on the rocks after both men angered the movement’s fans by failing to deliver on key issues such as the regulation of toxic pesticides. As health care costs soar and the public contends with outbreaks of easily preventable diseases including measles and food-borne cyclospora, Democrats are calling on Kennedy to resign from his post or face lawmakers in hearings next year as voters hand them control of Congress.

“The time is now. RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion,” said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland) in a social media post on Monday.

Along with Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), Alsobrooks has tracked Kennedy’s performance as secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as well as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The lawmakers released a report in February titled “Costs, Chaos, and Corruption: 365 Days of Secretary Kennedy’s Disastrous Leadership” that documented Secretary Kennedy’s actions at HHS in 2025, including making historic cuts to medical research, restricting access to vaccines, and amplifying bunk science and misinformation that undermine trust in the public health system.

As election results were tallied on the evening of November 3, Wyden posted a single word to social media: “Subpoenas.”

Kennedy “does not like to testify in front of Congress, and he will be dragged in there quite a bit, and that will not be enjoyable for him,” said Amanda Seitz, the Washington policy reporter for KFF News, during a post-election briefing on November 5.

At least a dozen Democrats called on Kennedy to resign when he appeared before the Senate Finance Committee in September 2025.

Seitz said Democrats now have a long list of Trump allies to investigate, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and the officials responsible for a deadly mass deportation campaign in which dozens of people have been killed by federal immigration agents or in custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The long list for accountability could provide Kennedy with some breathing room, but the health secretary remains one of the most controversial members of Trump’s cabinet and will eventually be forced to testify before committees controlled by Democrats, should he stay in office.

“For a while the White House was basically telling him to back off of his vaccine work, but they have let him focus on that again; it’s very important to him, he has studies he wants to complete,” Seitz said. “I think he wants to stay on and see that work be completed, but does [appearing before Congress] become so untenable for him that he doesn’t want to stay?”

In March, STAT reported that Kennedy had tapped anti-vaxxer David Geier to conduct a study on potential links between vaccines and autism in children, a conspiracy theory that animates the anti-vax movement but was debunked by researchers years ago. Geier does not have a medical degree and was disciplined by the State of Maryland’s Board of Physicians for practicing medicine without a license.

The unfounded claims about a link between vaccines and autism traces back to a study from the 1990s that was retracted in 2010, and a preservative that had come under scrutiny was removed as a precautionary measure from children’s vaccines in 2001. However, Kennedy regularly promotes flawed research to keep the theory alive.

Throughout Kennedy’s tenure, experts have warned that he is unethically unraveling a vaccine system painstakingly built over decades to stop disease and keep millions of children safe. Even the right-wing New York Post said Kennedy’s sharing of vaccine misinformation “isn’t just mind-bogglingly irresponsible, it’s downright cruel.”

A big question is whether or not Trump believes that Kennedy is still serving his political interests, Seitz said. Ahead of the midterms, Kennedy campaigned heavily for GOP candidates in Iowa, where Republicans hoped his message about eating healthy and recovering from addiction would resonate with voters in the agriculture-heavy state. However, the midterm results are in, and conservatives are complaining that Iowa voters swung further left than voters in any other state.

Upcoming confirmation hearings for key positions within HHS could provide a preview of the pressure Kennedy will face when Democrats are in the majority.

“If you are Heidi Overton, you are pretty nervous right now,” Seitz said, referring to Trump’s nominee to run the FDA.

Polls show that the economy and cost of living were top of mind for midterm voters, along with rising insurance premiums and health care costs exacerbated by deep spending cuts made by Trump and Republicans and administered by HHS. Bruce Mirken, the executive director of Defend Public Health, said the controversy surrounding Kennedy likely played a role in the GOP losing control of Congress.

“I think polls have generally shown that Kennedy’s policies are not popular, that trust in federal health agencies has declined since he has been in charge, and I think that had an effect,” Mirken told Truthout in an interview. “He also propelled a whole lot of doctors and nurses to run for office on the Democratic side, and a number of them won.”

At a time of declining trust in government, polls show that the public puts far more trust in individual doctors and nurses than agencies such as the FDA and CDC, which could provide El-Sayed, Andrews, and other Democrats in Congress with the credibility and leverage needed to push Kennedy out. At the same time, polls show that voters are frustrated with the Trump administration’s health care policies — including policies around vaccine access for children, an issue Kennedy exploited to become famous in the anti-vax movement.

“As long as Kennedy remains in office, it’s going to remain a problem, but Congress can damn well hold hearings and shine a spotlight on this,” Mirken said. “That can and should lead up to impeaching and removing Robert F. Kennedy Jr; that’s a heavy lift, but it’s time to try it.”

text:

ONALASKA, Wis. (WKBT) — A 21-year-old Wisconsin State Trooper who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was released from ICE custody Friday night, according to his attorney.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who lives in Onalaska and works out of the Tomah post, was detained by ICE agents at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison on Nov. 5 while waiting to board a domestic flight. His attorney Marc Christopher claims when Van Der Merwe showed agents his federal work permit and explained he had a pending asylum application, they told him they "did not care," before detaining and taking him to the Dodge County detention facility.

According to Van Der Merwe's attorney, he will be released shortly and will be placed on an order of supervision which requires Van Der Merwe to meet with ICE regularly and to be monitored by an electronic device. However, his attorney says 'our fight is not over.'

"His release does not erase what he and his family have been through," the office stated. "There is still no explanation why DHS detained him or why exactly he is now being released. Those are the answers we seek and Carel and his family, and work community deserves.  We continue to stress how DHS’s own agency, USCIS, authorized him to work. He used that authorization to serve and protect Wisconsin communities. Yet that same agency, detained him. We hope DHS will provide an explanation."

ICE's detainee locator previously showed a Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, born in South Africa, was in ICE custody at the Dodge Detention Facility in Wisconsin. Van Der Merwe no longer appears on this site.

In a statement to News 8 Now, ICE said it arrested Van Der Merwe on Nov. 5 during a targeted enforcement operation at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. ICE says Van Der Merwe entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019 but overstayed his admission. ICE added that Van Der Merwe will receive due process and remain in custody pending removal proceedings. ICE also noted that work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States.

The Wisconsin State Patrol confirmed Van Der Merwe's employment in a statement to News 8 Now, saying it is aware of the situation and that Van Der Merwe has been employed with the State Patrol since July 13, 2025.

Van Der Merwe came to the United States legally from South Africa as a child. His family claims they have followed the legal immigration process and waited seven years for an asylum interview. He is listed on his father's pending asylum application and holds a federal work authorization card through 2030, according to Christopher. Wisconsin State Patrol hiring rules allow noncitizens with valid work authorization to serve as troopers.

"Carel came here legally as a child. His family pursued asylum through the legal process. He holds federal work authorization and serves Wisconsin as a State Trooper," Christopher said. "Now the same government that authorized him to work has locked him up."

According to a statement, Van Orden, who represents Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, contacted DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin directly after learning of Van Der Merwe's detention.

"As soon as Congressman Van Orden became aware of the situation, he contacted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to discuss the trooper's case. The trooper will be released immediately and will be responsible for working with the appropriate authorities to resolve his outstanding immigration paperwork and address his legal status. Congressman Van Orden appreciates Secretary Mullin's attention to this matter."

Congresswoman-elect Rebecca Cooke (D-WI), who will represent Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District in January, released a statement on the detention prior to Van Orden's announcement.

"I am disturbed at reports that a valued member of our Wisconsin community, Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, was unjustly detained by ICE. If these reports are true, ICE's behavior is unacceptable. This is a public servant who puts his life in danger to keep Wisconsinites safe. And it comes after ICE has repeatedly put our communities in danger by violating fundamental rights. I will investigate this incident and demand an explanation from ICE officials about why a member of Wisconsin law enforcement is being treated this way - and I will stand up for him until he is released."

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

text:
An Indiana Republican wanted Stephen Miller fired after the midterms. Two days later, Donald Trump gave Miller the job of running his White House. Congressman Marlin Stutzman called the promotion a “horrible decision”. Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors”. Miller takes over from Susie Wiles on Monday, November 9.

Miller, 41, helped design Trump’s immigration crackdown as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser. His promotion puts him in charge of the staff who turn presidential decisions into action, just as Democrats are about to take over the House and Senate. Some of the policies they want to investigate are his.

ADVERTISEMENT

Sign up for Open Magazine's ad-free experience

Enjoy uninterrupted access to premium content and insights.

Why did Trump pick Miller after losing Congress?

Trust was Trump’s public explanation. Miller joined his 2016 campaign, wrote speeches in his first term and returned as a senior aide in 2025. Reuters reported that Trump had told people he wanted a more aggressive White House after the vote. That helps explain why he chose an aide who knows how to push an agenda through agencies when Congress is unlikely to pass it. Trump has also said he is willing to work with Democrats. The White House credited Miller with helping secure the border and reduce violent crime.

Open Magazine Latest Edition is Out Now!

The Era of Forever Wars

29 Oct 2026 - Vol 05 | Issue 44

Coping with an explosive Middle East

What can Miller do from the new office?

He can decide who briefs Trump, which proposals are ready for a decision and how White House staff follow through. An immigration proposal might need Homeland Security to run it, Justice Department lawyers to defend it and budget officials to find the money. Miller can bring those people together and press for a timetable. Trump still makes the presidential decisions, and agencies have to act within the authority the law gives them.

Why have Republicans split over the choice?

Stutzman sees Miller’s immigration crackdown as part of what cost Republicans votes. Republican senator Mike Lee praised Miller’s record on law enforcement. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called him a “dangerous xenophobe” and demanded his removal. AP’s survey of midterm voters gives that argument some context. About six in 10 said the administration had gone too far in enforcing immigration laws.

ADVERTISEMENT

Where did his immigration politics come from?

Before Trump, Miller was a Republican congressional aide and an early advocate of tighter immigration limits. Emails published by the Southern Poverty Law Center in 2019 show him encouraging a Breitbart editor to cover The Camp of the Saints, a novel popular with white nationalists that depicts migration to Europe as an invasion. Trump’s then press secretary attacked the centre’s credibility.

How did family separation work?

In 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced that prosecutors would pursue criminal charges against people referred for crossing the border illegally. When authorities sent parents into criminal custody, children were taken into a separate system. Miller defended the administration’s approach. A Justice Department watchdog found that officials understood prosecutions would split families and failed to plan adequately for reunification. A 2023 settlement put limits on future separations and offered support to affected families.

ADVERTISEMENT

What did 3,000 arrests a day mean?

It was a target Miller set for immigration arrests, according to Reuters. An arrest is the start of a case or detention. A deportation is a removal from the country. As enforcement broadened, agents went after people living in the US without legal status, including people without criminal records. Reuters reported that Miller urged agents to target Home Depot locations where day labourers gather. That shows how a number set in Washington can change where agents look for people.

How far did Miller push presidential power?

In May 2025 he said the administration was looking at suspending habeas corpus, the right to ask a judge whether the government can legally hold you. As of November 7, there was no public move to put that idea into effect. Separately, Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act, a 1798 law, to speed removals of alleged members of Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua gang. The Supreme Court required advance notice and a chance to challenge removal under that law.

What did a wrongful deportation reveal?

In a separate case, the government sent Kilmar Abrego Garcia to El Salvador despite an immigration judge’s order protecting him from removal there. The administration acknowledged an administrative error. In April 2025, the Supreme Court required the government to help secure his release from Salvadoran custody. The case showed how hard it can be to undo a removal once someone is in another country’s prison.

ADVERTISEMENT

Why did the Alex Pretti shooting become part of Miller’s record?

After federal agents fatally shot Pretti in Minneapolis in January 2026, Miller called him a “domestic terrorist” and a “would-be assassin”. Reuters verified footage showing Pretti holding a phone during the encounter. Miller later said agents might have departed from protocol. The episode matters for a chief of staff because the White House’s account can reach the public hours before investigators have established what happened.

ADVERTISEMENT

Does Miller’s reach extend beyond immigration?

Yes. Reuters reported that he helped drive federal workforce cuts and administration fights over diversity programmes and universities. He also backed US military strikes on suspected drug boats. In January he told CNN that Greenland should be part of the United States and sidestepped questions about ruling out force. Reuters also reported that he pushed to expand a Puerto Rico voting-machine inquiry after it found no evidence of hacking.

ADVERTISEMENT

Can Trump still restrict birthright citizenship?

In June, the US Supreme Court ruled that children born in the US to parents who are there temporarily or without legal status are citizens at birth. That includes families on temporary work visas. The administration has since issued a separate order targeting travel for the purpose of giving birth.

Where does that leave H-1B workers?

The H-1B lets US employers hire foreign workers for specialised jobs. In September, Trump extended a $100,000 payment requirement for certain applications. Federal judges in two cases blocked the policy, and the administration appealed. Indian-born beneficiaries accounted for 71% of approved H-1B petitions in FY2024, so the outcome matters to Indian workers and employers. The next change would come through a new policy or a court ruling.

ADVERTISEMENT

Can Democrats stop the crackdown from Congress?

They can hold hearings, subpoena records and pursue new funding limits. House oversight Democrat Robert Garcia has already signalled an investigation. Trump can veto legislation, and Congress has previously funded enforcement into 2029. That means the most immediate change may be who has to answer for the raids, detention conditions and spending in public. Miller takes over the White House in November. The committees that want those answers gain their new majorities in January.

text:
Three days after the devastating defeat of the Republican Party in the US midterm elections, President Donald Trump doubled down on anti-immigrant bigotry by removing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and replacing her with Stephen Miller, who has spearheaded the administration’s violent campaign against immigrant workers.

The appointment was a particular slap in the face to millions of Hispanic voters who turned sharply against the Trump administration, particularly in Texas, where Democrats swept every statewide office, electing a US senator for the first time since 1988 and ousting three-term governor Greg Abbott, a key Trump ally.

There were 50-point swings against the Republicans among young Hispanic men, particularly in the counties along the Rio Grande, and the election of the first Hispanic governors of Texas and California, the two most populous American states. Trump was urged by Republican congressional leaders to tone down his campaign targeting immigrants. Instead, he did the opposite.

Miller is Trump’s longest-serving policy aide, having the main responsibility for anti-immigrant efforts in the first Trump term, when he advocated for the family-separation policy that imprisoned immigrant children, thousands of whom permanently lost contact with their parents. In the second term, he has pushed for punitive measures like deporting immigrants to third countries where they don’t know the language or have any family, as well as advocating repressive measures directed against the American population more broadly, such as deploying ICE agents to airports and National Guard troops to Washington DC, Memphis and other cities.

His most notorious statement—out of many crude lies—came after the murder of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis by federal agents, last January. He smeared Pretti as an “assassin” because he was lawfully carrying a licensed weapon when federal agents threw him to the ground and executed him at point-blank range.

Miller has long been Trump’s main speechwriter, making him responsible for some of the most demented and reactionary diatribes in US political history. He drafted Trump’s “American carnage” speech, delivered at his first inauguration in 2017.

His personal arrogance and vitriolic insults also dovetail with those of his “commander in chief.” In an appearance on Fox News during the summer he called the Democrats a “party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” who “hate” Americans and are “unworthy of power.” He warned that if the Democrats won the midterm election, “everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”

But Miller is also a student of neo-Nazi politics, clearly influenced by his reading of Hitler and other fascists, despite his Jewish upbringing— his ancestors fled the czarist pogroms.. He has justified the immigration crackdown in terms taken from the fascist “Great Replacement Theory,” which posits a conspiracy financed by Jewish billionaires to replace the white population of the United States with immigrants from the “Third World.”

“If you bring those societies into our country and then give them unlimited free welfare, what do we think’s going to happen?” he said on Fox News last year. “We need a moratorium on immigration from third world countries until we can heal ourselves as a nation.”

He has also publicly embraced an unlimited American expansionism, particularly in the Western Hemisphere, that makes Hitler’s lebensraum seem only minimally ambitious, defending Trump’s threats to seize Greenland, incorporate Canada as the 51st state and overthrow the government of Venezuela—or any other country—and seize its resources.

The Democratic Party has won 256 seats in the House of Representatives, compared to only 161 for the Republicans, with 18 still undecided. It has captured at least seven Republican Senate seats, giving it a 54-44 margin, with narrow leads in both Alaska and Mississippi, which have grown as counting continues.

Under those conditions, the selection of Miller is a declaration by Trump of complete indifference to the wishes of the American people, expressed in the midterm vote, for an end to the war in Iran and the war against immigrants, and a reduction in the spiraling cost-of-living.

The Democrats, having benefited electorally from the mass hostility to the Trump administration, welcomed the opportunity to posture as opponents of Miller. Representative Hakeem Jeffries, likely the next Speaker of the House, issued a statement saying, “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands… His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.”

Senator Chuck Schumer, the future Majority Leader, said that Trump had “learned nothing” from the election. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration,” he said. “Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

The truth is that the congressional Democratic leadership regrets the selection of Miller because it cuts across their plans for bipartisan collaboration with the Trump administration, particularly if it can reach agreement with the White House on escalating US military intervention in the US-NATO war against Russia in Ukraine.

This is the main concern of the Democratic leadership, one that was kept under wraps throughout the election campaign, when they made demagogic appeals on affordability although neither they or the Republicans will lift a finger to halt the steady erosion of working class living standards while Wall Street billionaires amass ever greater wealth.

Lawyers for the farm argued that officials in the executive branch should not be allowed to assess damages against family-owned farms. Sun Valley Orchards went out of business following the assessed damages.
“There is no precedent or history supporting agency adjudication of such employment-related issues," lawyers for the farm wrote. "The government’s contrary argument would vastly expand the public rights exception for immigration-related claims to encompass myriad issues involving temporary workers."
Lawyers for the government disagreed with Sun Valley Orchards. The lawyers argued that Congress has given authority to administrative agencies like the Department of Labor to adjudicate worker issues.
"Administrative adjudications provide an efficient mechanism for ensuring that employers who participate in that vast program comply with those terms and conditions," the lawyers for the government wrote in a brief to the court.
Alex MacDonald, co-chair of the law firm Littler Mendelson’s Workplace Policy Institute, said the dispute represents a unique case where the Trump administration is defending a policy that argues for more government regulation, likely because it falls into the category of immigration policy.
Justices on the high court will decide whether the federal courts are equipped to step in with workplace disputes or if administrative bureaucracy has the say. MacDonald said the court’s opinion on administrative authority will have broad influence for migrant worker disputes moving forward.
“Depending on the way the court decides this case, yeah, it could have implications for those other [migrant worker] statutes,” MacDonald said.
The case balances a unique blend of public and private rights, MacDonald said. He said the right to equal housing and fair employment would often be settled in a courtroom under Article III of the Constitution. However, the government has leeway to handle any of these issues when immigration is involved because it poses a national security issue.
Thomas Berry, director of the Cato Institute’s Center for Constitutional Studies, said migrant worker programs are discretionary and provide for different legal processes.
“If you participate in a discretionary privilege program, you also do not get an article 3 court right,” Berry said.
MacDonald said legal precedent provides for a gray area in adjudication of migrant labor disputes. He predicted justices will deal with definitions of the word “impose” in federal laws that give executive agencies the power to handle migrant worker disputes.
“We're looking at one word in a statute that just says 'impose,'” MacDonald said about the high court’s potential thought process. “That's not obvious to us that that should be an administrative hearing with what we've said about cases that should go to article three courts.”
Berry raised the possibility that a high court ruling in favor of Sun Valley Orchards could allow for deportation proceedings to be handled differently, a critical issue for the Trump administration.
However, MacDonald said the statutes for deportation proceedings provide requirements for a specific hearing to take place, unlike when adjudicating migrant worker disputes.
“[A] removal proceeding is not about a dispute between an employer and a worker involving employment law,” he said. “So, there's not that same private rights element to it.”
However, lower courts could alter other work visa proceedings with similar statutory language at issue. This could mark a significant shift for the Trump administration while it attempts to restrict foreign workers in other visa programs.
“A lot of the statutes, at least the ones I'm familiar with, are similarly unclear about the department's authority or how it is supposed to go about enforcing the relevant statutes,” MacDonald said.
Justices on the high court will hear arguments in the case on Tuesday and are expected to issue a decision by June 2027.

text:
Days after voters rejected his second-term agenda in a resounding midterm blowout, President Donald Trump is turning to one of the chief architects of those policies to lead the White House, elevating Stephen Miller to chief of staff.

Miller is best known as an immigration hawk. He has been an ardent champion for the mass deportation campaign that has been a centerpiece of Trump’s second term, and the administration's push to end birthright citizenship. He also is a fierce and longtime Trump loyalist who has shown little inclination for working with Democrats, setting up a potentially contentious two years ahead.

Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have sparked intense backlash, putting a spotlight on the tactics employed by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. There were widespread demonstrations after federal agents shot and killed two people in Minneapolis earlier this year during immigration operations.

After the second shooting, Miller called the man who was killed, Alex Pretti, a "domestic terrorist" and portrayed him as a grave threat to law enforcement, but that narrative quickly unraveled. Miller later said federal agents may not have followed "protocol" as the administration adopted a more conciliatory tone amid the uproar.

The president told Fox News on election night after Republicans lost control of Congress that he hopes to work with Democrats, mentioning immigration as an area where both sides might be able to come together. But Miller's appointment could signal a more uncompromising stance on immigration, and other issues, even as Latino voters shifted dramatically towards Democrats in the midterm election.

During Trump’s first administration, Miller helped craft a travel ban targeting predominantly Muslim countries. It was struck down as illegal or unconstitutional by lower courts, but later upheld by the Supreme Court.

Miller’s influence during Trump's second term has extended far beyond immigration. As deputy chief of staff for policy, he has been deeply involved at all levels of policymaking.

'Unapologetically' using military

Miller, 41, also has been a driving force in Trump's muscular approach to foreign affairs and threats of intervention abroad, once declaring that "nobody’s going to fight the United States militarily over the future of Greenland." He championed the U.S. effort to remove Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, saying afterward that “The United States is using its military to secure our interests unapologetically in our hemisphere."

Trump’s selection of Miller to replace the outgoing Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, a longtime aide with a more low-key profile, comes after Democrats won both the House and Senate in a landslide. The midterm election centered around the president, whose approval rating is at record lows amid discontent over immigration policy, the economy, the war in Iran and other issues that Miller had a hand in.

Democrats have signaled they will launch an aggressive oversight campaign, with Trump administration officials facing a barrage of congressional hearings and potential subpoenas.

Miller is fiery speaker who often lashes out at Democrats. Two sources close to the administration noted that Miller is known for being combative, and said his new role indicates Trump is girding for a fight.

Before the polls closed on Election Day Nov. 3, Miller fired off a social media post urging voters to "Send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt leftwing politicians who want to steal your future and destroy the inheritance of your children. Get to the polls and protect the ones you love."

The president praised Miller as he departed the White House on Nov. 6, noting he has been with him from the beginning. Miller was a policy adviser and speechwriter for Trump’s 2016 campaign and in his first administration. His wife was a spokesperson for Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, when he ran the Department of Government Efficiency and now hosts a podcast featuring administration officials.

“He gets it. Very good politically,” Trump said of Miller. “He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

Trump’s critics said Miller’s appointment suggests the president is doubling down on an approach that voters rejected.

“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, said on social media. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

Contributing: Joey Garrison, Francesca Chambers, Reuters

text:
A 21-year-old South African-born Wisconsin State Patrol trooper who was detained Nov. 5 by federal immigration agents was released from custody Nov. 6, according to his attorney.

Attorney Marc Christopher confirmed to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who was traveling to visit family with a valid work permit, had been released from the Dodge County Jail and was awaiting a ride from his supervisor, the head trooper in Tomah.

Christopher said Van Der Merwe was released under an order of supervision, which requires him to periodically check in with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He will also likely be subject to electronic monitoring, potentially through an application on his cellphone rather than an ankle bracelet.

Christopher said he plans to speak with Van Der Merwe to discuss the next steps in his case. He expects Van Der Merwe will eventually share his experience publicly but wants to give him time to readjust following his release.

"I just told him I wanted him to get back, get reacclimated, just get settled, because I know he's gone through a very dramatic experience," Christopher said.

Van Der Merwe came to the U.S. from South Africa with his family on visas at age 14, Christopher said. His family has been waiting seven years for their asylum case to be heard.

Earlier, Christopher slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for detaining a Wisconsin law enforcement officer who has permission to work, saying he was "flabbergasted" by the agents' decision to use its resources to target Van Der Merwe.

"I almost can't even believe that they would be so brazen as to do this. But they are," Christopher said. "There's no reason for them to detain him other than to indiscriminately pick up as many people as they can."

Van Der Merwe, who lived in New Mexico with his family, wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but could not because he was not a permanent resident, Christopher said. He graduated with a degree in criminal justice in New Mexico, then researched states where he could do similar work with his status and found Wisconsin.

Van Der Merwe was living in Onalaska and working in Tomah for the Wisconsin State Patrol over the past year. His work authorization is valid until 2030.

Attorney disputes ICE's assertion about legal status

ICE's argument is that Van Der Merwe – as a teenager in the U.S. with his family – overstayed his visitor's visa.

"He entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019. In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement. "Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S."

Christopher pushed back on that assertion.

"That is just absurd and ridiculous," Christopher said. "They've been here lawfully. They have been waiting for their application to be adjudicated and to be decided by immigration."

The family, who are White South Africans, had applied for asylum on the grounds they were persecuted. A family member had been attacked, Christopher said.

Van Der Merwe did not decide to come to the U.S. himself, as he was brought by his parents, and he chose a career in law enforcement to serve his new country, Christopher said.

ICE agents detained him Nov. 5 at the Dane County Regional Airport just after he went through security, Christopher said. He was traveling to visit his family in New Mexico. Agents handcuffed him, shackled his legs and put him in a van and drove him to Dodge County Jail, which holds ICE detainees.

Christopher said it seems that the Transportation Security Administration tipped off ICE when he bought his ticket, and agents met Van Der Merwe at the airport. Christopher has heard of ICE making arrests at the Milwaukee and Appleton airports through similar tip-offs, he said.

Lawyer hopes Congress changes the way ICE can operate

Under the Trump administration, ICE has not been setting bond for detainees voluntarily unless a judge orders it. Trump administration policy changes have made many detainees ineligible to even seek bond and leave detention.

Christopher said he hopes Wisconsin's congressional delegation takes note of the case and institutes changes to the way ICE can operate. He was critical that ICE would use its resources to arrest Van Der Merwe, then hold him in custody.

"You're going to use your resources to go after this guy? You're going to use our tax dollars to detain this guy? It doesn't make any sense," Christopher said.

As part of its summer surge in street arrests in Milwaukee, ICE arrested a 20-year-old Milwaukee man, Giovanni Sosa, who had lived in the U.S. since age 4. In detaining him, ICE gave him paperwork that said – at age 4 – he had overstayed his visa. Sosa spent a month in detention at the Dodge County Jail as he waited for the chance to post bond.
