The post ICE detains two U.S. citizens protesting outside White Memorial Hospital, rapid response groups say appeared first on LA Local.
text:
Federal immigration agents detained at least two people late Friday outside Adventist White Memorial Hospital in Boyle Heights, where protesters had gathered after reports of immigration enforcement activity, according to rapid response groups. Protesters remained at the hospital into the early hours of Saturday, where immigration agents maintained a large presence.

It appears the incident began after people witnessed someone being detained and taken into the hospital, according to Raquel Roman, executive director of Proyecto Pastoral and member of the Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network. That spurred a crowd of protesters to rally against ICE agents, who then detained two protesters who are U.S. citizens, Roman said.

ICE activity was also reported near Mariachi Plaza at 5:50 a.m. Saturday, according to witnesses, and outside the East LA Sheriff’s Station, where agents have been seen detaining people in the L.A. County-designated ICE-Free zone.

Arrests captured on social video

Video posted on social media appears to show one person being detained outside the hospital. In the video, at least three officers in tactical vests are seen detaining someone at the intersection of Boyle and Pennsylvania Avenues around 11:30 p.m.

A group of about six more officers in tactical vests and masks can be seen walking around the area as another, whose vest says “Police ICE,” yells at the person recording to “back up” and “do not impede with the arrest.”

“You’re arresting U.S. citizens,” the person recording says. “18 USC 111, they’re interfering,” the officer replies, referring to Title 18, Section 111 of the U.S. Code: Assaulting, resisting, or impeding certain officers or employees.

In the video, a bystander who says the person being arrested is his brother can be seen speaking to the officer.

“Your brother assaulted a federal agent. He’s being arrested for assaulting a federal agent; he’s coming with us,” the officer tells them.

Boyle Heights Beat reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for more information about the incident but has not yet received a response.

LAPD response

The Los Angeles Police Department was first called to the scene at 11:59 p.m. to respond to a “large group causing a disturbance,” according to LAPD Officer Norma Eisenman. LAPD responded again at 2:24 a.m. as crowds continued to gather outside of the hospital.

“Officers responded to maintain public safety and keep the peace. At no point did LAPD officers assist federal immigration authorities with enforcement activities or detain any individuals in connection with immigration enforcement,” Eisenman said.

Video posted on social media by Izzy Ramirez shows a line of agents blocking the emergency loading dock around 2:30 a.m. as a crowd continues to shout at the agents and make noise.

“It was horrible for the local community. The ICE presence was a lot more than I’ve seen it visibly before,” said Roman.

What the hospital said

Japhet De Oliveira, corporate communications executive at Adventist Health, shared the following statement:

“Federal agents brought a person in their custody to our emergency department, and we cared for that patient with dignity and privacy, as we do for every patient. When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely care. White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement. We know last night frightened our neighbors. No matter what happens outside our doors, everyone who comes inside is our patient, and our focus will only be on that patient, and it will not change.”

Doctors at Adventist White Memorial last year reported that ICE agents were violating the privacy rights of detained patients and prohibiting contact with patients’ family members. While the hospital released guidelines to protect patients and support staff, doctors and advocates have said they fall short.

LAist watchdog reporting

In October 2025, LAist's Jill Replogle reported that doctors at White Memorial hospital in Boyle Heights told her that hospital administrator directives allow federal immigration agents to interfere in medical decisions and block doctors from properly treating detainees who need emergency care.

Read the investigation: At a Boyle Heights hospital, ICE agents call the shots, doctors say

What's next

Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, who represents Boyle Heights, said she was “deeply troubled” by the reports overnight and demanded answers from hospital leadership. She said:

“I am calling on Adventist Health White Memorial to publicly disclose its agreements with ICE and end any voluntary medical-services contract with the agency. Every patient, including anyone in federal custody, must continue to receive appropriate, uninterrupted medical care. Hospital leadership must take immediate, concrete steps to protect patient privacy, support healthcare workers who advocate for their patients, and ensure that medical decisions remain with patients and their care teams.”

The Boyle Heights Immigrant Rights Network said it plans to lead a protest against ICE outside White Memorial at 2 p.m. Saturday.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought — at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests.

Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes.

The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China.

Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands.

The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant’s role in ancient societies.

“It’s extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context,” said co-author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern.

“It’s only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that’s been dead for almost 3,000 years,” he said.

It’s not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said.

The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians — ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine.

The team, deployed “essentially out in the middle of nowhere,” lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe.

Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear and animal-style motifs. But the team “struck gold” as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said.

“It’s only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that’s been dead for almost 3,000 years,” he said.

Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and “they are not there by accident” but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said.

Results were published Thursday in the journal Science.

Not all independent experts were convinced.

The hair analysis “is scientifically weak” and there’s not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email.

“For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible,” Auwaerter said. “This matters because the hair data carry the abstract’s main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties).”

Today, scholars don’t consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses — seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth — their presence alone doesn’t confirm drug use.

Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn’t distinguish consumption from external exposure — in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange.

But Elisa Guerra Doce of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study.

In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that “cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite.”

Crichton, the author of “Jurassic Park” and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for “ER,” the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.

Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved the “The Pitt” is derivative of “ER.”

The court agreed with the plaintiff that “both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it.”

The opinion also said that both feature “very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy.”

Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that “WBTV continues to maintain that ‘The Pitt’ is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal’s decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds.”

The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have “generic similarities” that would exist in “any dramatic story” that features “overworked doctors and staff.”

The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle, John Wells, who created “The Pitt” and worked on “ER,” and R. Scott Gemmill, a “Pitt” executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.

Sherri Crichton’s lawsuit alleges “The Pitt” is a rebranded version of an unauthorized “ER” reboot that she had rejected.

Her husband had secured a coveted “frozen rights” provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs or other productions derived from “ER” without Crichton’s consent, or his estate’s consent after his death from cancer in 2008.

After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed “ER” reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

Micki Boden wanted a wedding cake that checked off a couple of big boxes — personalized and tasty. Instead of a traditional tiered cake, the San Fernando Valley native went with a favorite from her school days.

“My favorite cake of all time is the coffee cake that I ate through my entire K-12 education going to LAUSD public school,” Boden said.

Boden attended elementary school in Studio City and middle school in Sherman Oaks before graduating from a Reseda high school.

Boden and her husband, Matt Stollman, met in 2016 while working on the reality television show Big Brother and eventually started dating. The two got engaged in 2025.

With the groom’s family traveling from the East Coast for their wedding in October, the couple wanted to provide a uniquely L.A. experience.

“We wanted something that was gonna be fun, that was gonna be memorable for people,” Boden said.

They held their wedding at the Valley Relics Museum in Van Nuys, surrounded by San Fernando Valley memorabilia, and got a California favorite — an In-N-Out truck — to serve guests.

The search for a cake that fit

But when it came to the wedding cake, the couple struggled to find something suitable. Neither Boden nor Stollman liked frosting, and traditional wedding cakes didn’t excite them.

“We explored the more traditional tiered cake setup, and it just wasn’t meshing well,” Boden said.

Boden kept returning to the coffee cake she ate throughout her years in public school. Los Angeles Unified School District had published its official recipe online, but she wasn’t confident she could bake it herself. So she reached out to the district to ask for help.

How LAUSD made it happen

Thomas Cohen, a public relations representative at the district, and Manish Singh, the director of food services, arranged for a chef at Mulholland Middle School in Lake Balboa to prepare the wedding cake. The chef also shaped part of the cake into a heart just for the couple.

Singh said the district doesn’t take cake orders from the public — but made this exception.

“We were doing it just to make one of our Angelenos, an ex-LAUSD student, make her special day even more special,” Singh said.

For the bride, it was the icing on her big day.

“I think it’s all just part of being an L.A. student,” she said. “The fact that we have these amazing memories from childhood, I think it’s just so meaningful for a lot of people.”

The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.

The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans’ significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government’s request.

The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump’s administration’s effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.

The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with multiple immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump’s direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state’s Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably “commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones.”

“The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary,” the motion said.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state’s 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.

Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to “safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn’t have an effect on the upcoming election.”

“We want to stop the illegal voting. We don’t want to chase it later,” he said outside of court the week before the election.

California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It’s not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.

The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — San Diego city and school district leaders are demanding answers after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained an 8-year-old boy during an immigration check-in.

The third grader, a student at Fay Elementary in City Heights, was removed from his family on Wednesday. Advocates say his uncle had brought him to the check-in. The uncle had been caring for the child since the boy's father was deported in March 2025.

Sean Elo-Rivera learned of the child's situation when he got a call from San Diego Unified Superintendent Dr. Fabiola Bagula.

"She called very upset because one of her students, one of the district students, one of my constituents, a 3rd grader, had been removed from their family," Elo-Rivera said.

Wister Gaetan, the co-founder of the Haitian Bridge Alliance and an immigration advocate, has been in touch with the child's family. He said the father's deportation happened when he accidentally drove into Mexico, and said the family was here with Temporary Protected Status from Haiti. President Trump ended that protection this summer.

"Nobody should accept that this minor, who should be in school, is a threat to our society," Gaetan said.

Elo-Rivera, San Diego Unified leadership, and several teachers' unions have now sent a three-page letter straight to DHS and HHS. The letter demands the child be brought back into his community and asks the agencies to change placement policies so children taken into federal custody can stay close to their families and schools while continuing their education.

"My concern starts with what we're doing to kids that's just incredibly cruel," Elo-Rivera said.

"That's just incredibly cruel, and if you don't If it's not bad enough what they're doing to the adults, let's keep in mind what they're doing to the kids," Elo-Rivera said.

In a lengthy statement, ICE said the child was taken to the check-in by a man claiming to be his uncle. A spokesperson said the uncle couldn't establish legal guardianship in accordance with federal law, so the child was removed and placed in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement.

ICE added that the boy was initially brought to the U.S. by a man who claimed to be his father and was later deported to Mexico by Customs and Border Protection.

The exact whereabouts of the child are unclear. ABC 10News reached out to the Office of Refugee Resettlement to find out where he is and so far haven't heard back.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security appears to once again be moving forward with its decision to turn a warehouse on Route 46 in Roxbury into an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center.

In a federal court filing on Nov. 6, the state informed a judge that DHS entered into a $31.8 million contract with a private company to convert the warehouse into a detention facility.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said the agency does not comment on pending litigation. The New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness did not immediately return a request for comment Nov. 7.

Shortly after rumors began spreading late last year that ICE planned to purchase the 470,000-square-foot warehouse on a narrow stretch of Route 46 – the actual purchase was confirmed in February – the all-Republican Roxbury Council passed a resolution opposing the use of the warehouse for detaining immigrants.

The town joined the state in the lawsuit to stop the plan until the Department of Homeland Security addressed "serious state and local concerns about water, sewage, and public safety, accounting for the site’s sensitive environment, or considering if this warehouse is an appropriate place for detention."

In May, a court order barred DHS from "undertak[ing] any activities" at the site to turn it into the detention center, with limited exceptions until after an environmental assessment and a chance for the state to challenge the results of the assessment.

The DHS encountered opposition from residents and protest groups, as well as the lawsuit. On June 29, DHS announced that it would not move forward with its plans to convert the warehouse. However, just two weeks later, on July 11, DHS reversed its decision and informed both township officials and the court that it intended to proceed with its plans to retrofit the warehouse for detention use.

The state's status report indicated that after several submissions to the court, DHS remained uncertain about converting the warehouse into a detention facility.

"According to public reporting [on Nov. 6], DHS entered a $31.8 million contract with a private company [on Nov. 5] to convert the Roxbury warehouse site into an immigration detention facility," the report said. "Upon learning of this report, [the state's] counsel immediately contacted counsel for DHS, who advised plaintiffs for the first time that DHS has decided to proceed with pursuing a detention facility at the Roxbury site."

According to the court filing, New Jersey's attorneys contacted a DHS attorney, who could not confirm whether the contract report was correct, but said money had been allocated for "maintenance, design of ICE's preferred alternative and the [National Environmental Policy Act] analysis of that design."

New Jersey requested a copy of the contract to see if DHS's characterization is accurate and that if it entered into a contract to change the warehouse into a detention facility, there are "significant concerns" about DHS's compliance with the court order, which generally bars the federal agency from doing any work on the warehouse.

In September, there were reports that DHS was using the warehouse to house people arrested in ICE raids after Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner said a resident told her that her father, who was arrested in a raid, believed he had been held there.

At the Oct. 27 council meeting, Roxbury Township officials said the New Jersey Attorney General's Office has not found credible evidence that ICE agents processed detainees inside the warehouse.

Township Attorney Anthony Bucco confirmed that U.S. Department of Justice officials "admitted" to him that on two occasions, detainees were "processed in the parking lot" of the warehouse, but "they did not go in."

State and local officials say they are continuing to monitor the property for ICE activity. But Bucco, addressing inquiries from the public, said an Attorney General's Office investigation cannot "prove that there was anyone in the facility."

Roxbury officials continue to explore their options to stop ICE's use of the warehouse, which they say will strain the township's resources, including infrastructure, electrical and water supplies, sewer system and police security.

Bucco said the township is in a "holding pattern" after officials requested access to the site from the Department of Justice. According to Bucco, the DOJ said if they wanted access "through the legal process," they would have to ask for it.

Staff writer William Westhoven contributed to this story.

title: Stephen Miller Will Drag the GOP Further Into the Electoral Abyss | The New Republic
authors: Matt Ford, VILE Greg Sargent, Edith Olmsted, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling, Malcolm Ferguson
description:
“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” Trump said in a post on his personal social-media website.
“Stephen Miller is a wartime chief of staff,” Brent Scher, the editor-in-chief of The Daily Wire, said on Twitter on Friday.
Katie Zacharia, a woefully inept hire who falsely described her legal credentials, only lasted four days as White House press secretary last month.
A White House chief of staff’s power and responsibilities can vary.
For Democrats, Miller represents all of the Trump administration’s worst decisions—its authoritarianism, its bigotry, its arrogance, and its foolishness—in one person.
text:
As a high school student, Stephen Miller once told a booing crowd of his classmates that he was “sick and tired of being told to pick up my trash when we have plenty of janitors who are paid to do it for us.” Now he gets to reckon with a colossal political mess of his own making as the next White House chief of staff.

President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Miller, his deputy chief of staff and domestic-policy advisor, would take the top job in a post-midterms shakeup starting on Monday. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” Trump said in a post on his personal social-media website. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff—She has done a great job!”

Friday’s announcement came after Trump and Miller had effectively handed control of Congress to the Democrats. Two years of disastrous results on corruption, immigration, tariffs, and the Iran War alienated enough of the electorate that Texas went blue after 40 years of GOP control. Now Trump may have just handed Democrats the White House in 2028 as well by promoting his most extreme and destructive advisor to oversee the last two years of his presidency.

The shift was met with applause in the most far-right corners of American conservatism. “Stephen Miller is a wartime chief of staff,” Brent Scher, the editor-in-chief of The Daily Wire, said on Twitter on Friday. “This is going to be awesome.” Benny Johnson, a far-right YouTube personality, wrote on the social-media website that White House aides kept texting him “it’s Miller time” after the news broke. “It’s like the dogs have been let off the chain,” he added.

As Trump’s top domestic-policy advisor, Miller has functioned as a servile but ruthless shadow president for a chief executive who cares more about television footage than policy details. Like all authoritarians, Trump has attracted a mixture of thugs who revel in violence, weaklings who crave service to bullies, and opportunists who hope to advance their own fortunes. Miller has championed the deportation of as many immigrants as possible from the United States, taking an extreme approach even by GOP standards that evokes ethnic-cleansing campaigns and white nationalism.

Miller is also hostile to the American constitutional order and to international law. He argued unsuccessfully for Trump to suspend habeas corpus to round up immigrants last year and told CNN’s Jake Tapper in a January interview that the U.S. should acquire Greenland by force. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” he said, in remarks that would not sound out of place for a mid-20th-century German speaker.

His own leadership qualities are hardly stellar. Miller has a reputation throughout D.C. for openly berating junior staffers and senior officials alike for not effectively executing his draconian policies. A 2020 New Yorker profile recounted how he ended one such meeting with Department of Homeland Security officials by emotionally letting down his guard. “I didn’t mean to come across as harsh,” Miller reportedly confessed, describing his obsession with deportations. “It’s just that this is all I care about. I don’t have a family. I don’t have anything else. This is my life.” (He is now married with four children.)

During Trump’s second term, he escalated a series of immigration raids in Los Angeles in 2025 by reportedly telling federal immigration officials to arbitrarily gather people off the streets. “Miller came in there and eviscerated everyone. ‘You guys aren’t doing a good job. You’re horrible leaders.’ He just ripped into everybody. He had nothing positive to say about anybody, shot morale down,” an unnamed DHS official told The Washington Examiner last May, recounting a meeting that he had attended. “Stephen Miller wants everybody arrested. ‘Why aren’t you at Home Depot? Why aren’t you at 7-Eleven?’”

The snatch-and-grab tactics that DHS officials pioneered in Los Angeles and other major cities throughout 2025 came to a deadly conclusion this spring. Miller had championed the administration’s siege of Minneapolis, where thousands of federal agents poured into the city and began grabbing suspected immigrants off of the streets at will. Massive protests and community actions disrupted some of the raids as Minnesotans tried to protect their neighbors. One federal agent shot and killed Renee Good, a writer with three kids, as she tried to drive away from one clash in her neighborhood in January. Another agent gunned down Alex Pretti, a local nurse, who tried to render medical assistance to a woman that the agent had knocked to the ground.

Footage of the shootings and protests prompted an intense public backlash to Trump’s immigration policies. Millions of Americans were horrified at the sight of masked federal agents gunning down their fellow citizens in the street with no consequences. Miller was not among them. He described Good and Pretti as “domestic terrorists” and forcefully advocated for the administration’s tactics in Minneapolis throughout the campaign. After other Republicans begged him to change course, Trump wound down most of the operation shortly after Pretti’s killing and fired Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem a few months later. Miller stayed put.

Miller has often argued in recent years that Democrats are “not a legitimate political party,” but rather a “domestic extremist organization.” Nonetheless, his elevation is good news for Democrats in the short and long term. Trump had initially struck a rare conciliatory note in the wake of the GOP’s crushing losses this week. He accepted the election results after more than a decade of election denialism when things didn’t go his way. His administration’s half-hearted, half-baked efforts to challenge ballots and candidates in Alaska, California, and elsewhere faded away overnight.

“We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” Trump told two New York Times reporters in a phone call on Election Night, referring to Democratic leaders. “We’ll probably work something out.” Similar messaging from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer led to growing rumbles in Democratic circles about whether they should be elected House speaker and Senate majority leader, respectively, when the new Congress takes over in January.

A defter and more chastened Trump might have made life difficult for Democrats in Washington by trying to compromise with them, dividing a fractious political party that is normally united in opposition to him. Miller’s promotion has brought that potential honeymoon period to a close. “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries said in a post on Twitter on Friday. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Trump’s announcement is also the first major shake-up of his administration’s top ranks since Democrats recaptured Congress by overwhelming margins on Tuesday. The president said he wouldn’t dismiss Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Thursday despite calls by conservatives for him to step down or be fired. Democrats and Republicans alike blame him for the disastrous course of the Iran War. Outgoing Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, a frequent Trump critic, plans to bring an impeachment vote against Hegseth later this month. Congressional Democrats are reportedly eager to target him with oversight hearings next year as well.

Indeed, nearly all of Trump’s second-term departures have been women. Secretary of Labor Lori Chavez-DeRemer resigned over reports of the toxic, harassment-fueled workplace that she allegedly cultivated. Trump dismissed Attorney General Pam Bondi for failing to prosecute his enemies and botching the Epstein files scandal. Noem was shuffled out of her role after the failed siege and occupation of Minneapolis, as well as a variety of corruption and personal-misconduct scandals. Kimberley Guilfoyle, the president’s son’s ex-girlfriend, lost her job as ambassador to Greece for soliciting payouts in writing from foreign billionaires in September. Katie Zacharia, a woefully inept hire who falsely described her legal credentials, only lasted four days as White House press secretary last month.

Trump’s chiefs of staff also have a tendency to not stick around for long. Wiles was the fifth person to serve in the position so far. The role is a stressful and grueling one under any president. Only three of the twenty-five people to hold the post since 1981 have served for an entire four-year term, and none have done it in the last twenty years. Most do not even make it to a second year. Wiles’ tenure was the second longest one of Trump’s tenure, and was awarded to her in thanks for masterminding Trump’s re-election campaign in 2024.

A White House chief of staff’s power and responsibilities can vary. Generally speaking, they oversee the political staff at the White House. They coordinate policy decisions by the president and various other portions of the executive branch. They liaise with Congress and foreign officials. They go on cable news shows and talk to reporters behind the scenes. Some chiefs of staff, like Jim Baker under Reagan or Rahm Emanuel under Obama, can become nationally known figures in their own right, wielding more influence than even top Cabinet officials.

Like her fellow Trump-era predecessors, Wiles fell on the weaker end of the spectrum. Trump is notoriously capricious and mercurial. He is prone to trusting long-time sycophants like Miller over newer faces and more experienced voices. John Kelly, who served as Trump’s second chief of staff during his first term, later publicly warned Americans ahead of the 2024 election described the then-ex president for whom he had worked as a fascist and predicted that he would govern like a dictator if re-elected that fall.

Indeed, during the first half of his second term, Trump exulted in his lack of constraints—thanks to a MAGA-stocked executive branch and congressional Republicans’ supine posture—and simply did whatever he wanted. By most accounts, Wiles had comparatively little influence to other prominent Trump allies. She found herself overshadowed by Elon Musk, the South African-born billionaire who destroyed federal agencies and laid off civil servants in the first few months of 2025, and by Miller himself, who oversaw the Trump administration’s sprawling mass-deportation agenda.

Now, Miller gets to supervise the wreckage of his own mistakes. He enthusiastically championed Trump’s tariff policy, which drove up prices for Americans and wiped out entire markets for U.S. agriculture and manufacturing. After the Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs in January, he denounced the justices in the majority as “cowardly.” Even many devout MAGA enthusiasts regarded the Iran War as a betrayal of Trump’s promise to avoid wars in the Middle East and prioritize American interests. Miller has vocally defended Trump’s decisions even as the economic and political fallout doomed his fellow Republicans at the polls.

For Democrats, Miller represents all of the Trump administration’s worst decisions—its authoritarianism, its bigotry, its arrogance, and its foolishness—in one person. There is little doubt that Miller will continue to push the second Trump administration down its self-destructive path, and that he will drag the rest of the GOP down with him. Vice President JD Vance, the putative GOP frontrunner for 2028, gets to spend the next two years publicly defending every extreme decision that Miller makes even as the electorate demands a new course. Other Republicans on the campaign trail will have to decide between embracing Miller’s unpopular policies or distancing themselves from an angry, vengeful power center of far-right American conservatism.

Past presidents have spent the last two years of their administration trying to make things a little easier on their party and their successors. George W. Bush faded out of public view in 2007 and 2008 to avoid tarring the rest of the GOP with his deep unpopularity after the Iraq War and Hurricane Katrina. Bill Clinton, stung by the Lewinsky scandal and his then-historic impeachment, rarely appeared on the campaign trail in 2000 as Vice President Al Gore sought to turn the page. With Miller at the helm, there will be no quiet twilight for the Trump era. The two men will continue to inflict as much harm as they can on the country—and, by extension, on any remaining hope for the GOP to stay in the White House or reclaim power in two years’s time.

authors: Will Weissert, Associated Press, Moriah Balingit
description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is behind many of the administration's signature domestic policy initiatives — especially its sweeping crackdown on immigration.
Miller also warned that "a generation from now," people "will not know the country that they are living in.
Family separation: 'No one is exempt from immigration law' During Trump's first term, Miller championed a strict immigration deterrence policy that previous administrations had been hesitant to adopt: family separation.
WATCH: Stephen Miller says 'America's doors are closed fully to asylum seekers' after Supreme Court rulings "The message is that no one is exempt from immigration law," he added.
The tactic sparked widespread outcry, and the Trump administration did not revive it in its second term.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is behind many of the administration's signature domestic policy initiatives — especially its sweeping crackdown on immigration.

An outspoken defender of Trump's most far-reaching goals to remake government going back to his 2016 run for president, Miller is known for his harsh language and unapologetic bombast, attracting outsized attention from supporters and critics alike. His record is likely to be scrutinized by Democrats in his powerful new role as he leads Trump's White House through a difficult lame duck period after the Republican Party lost both houses of Congress.

Here are some memorable things Miller has said through the years:

On immigration: 'We are being conquered'

During a 2023 spike in illegal border crossings, Miller described migrants as invaders, even though many were escaping poverty and violence in their home countries.

"We are being conquered," he told Fox News Channel in December 2023, commenting on the sharp rise. "We have millions of people coming in from different cultures and different ways of living and different belief systems."

Miller also warned that "a generation from now," people "will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there's massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable."

He called a Minneapolis man killed by ICE a 'domestic terrorist'

After federal agents shot and killed Alex Pretti during protests against the Trump administration's hardline immigration policies in January, Miller posted on social media that the 37-year-old Minneapolis resident was a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin" who had "tried to murder federal agents."

Later, Miller said in a statement that the federal officers in Minneapolis "may not have been following" protocol.

America 'created' Venezuela's oil industry and Greenland 'obviously' should be part of the US

In January, after a daring U.S. military operation captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Miller used a lengthy post on X to decry "reverse colonization" in which he suggested that Western nations were sacrificing too much for the developing world and that such a practice "has been a long self-punishment of the places and peoples that built the modern world."

WATCH: What Trump picking Stephen Miller for chief of staff signals about his agenda

In another post, he defended the right of the U.S. to take over Venezuela's vast oil reserves, writing: "American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela. Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property. These pillaged assets were then used to fund terrorism and flood our streets with killers, mercenaries and drugs."

He defended Trump's assertion that the U.S. was now running Venezuela, by telling CNN's Jake Tapper: "You can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else. But we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world."

In the same interview, Miller also argued that the U.S. could seize Greenland by military force from NATO ally Denmark. "Obviously, Greenland should be part of the United States," he said.

"Nobody's going to fight the United States militarily over the future of Greenland," Miller said.

Speeding up deportations by suspending habeas corpus

In May of 2025, Miller suggested that the Trump administration was looking for ways to expand its power to deport migrants who are in the United States illegally. To achieve that, he said officials were "actively looking at" suspending habeas corpus — the constitutional right for people to legally challenge their detention by the government.

"The Constitution is clear — and that of course is the supreme law of the land — that the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus can be suspended in a time of invasion," Miller said.

"So, I would say that's an option we're actively looking at," Miller said. "Look, a lot of it depends on whether the courts do the right thing or not."

In the nearly 18 months since, the idea has not been publicly pursued by Trump and his administration.

Family separation: 'No one is exempt from immigration law'

During Trump's first term, Miller championed a strict immigration deterrence policy that previous administrations had been hesitant to adopt: family separation. It called for routinely having federal agents separate children from their parents if families were apprehended illegally crossing the border.

Miller defended the policy to The New York Times in 2018, saying it "was a simple decision by the administration to have a zero tolerance policy for illegal entry, period."

WATCH: Stephen Miller says 'America's doors are closed fully to asylum seekers' after Supreme Court rulings

"The message is that no one is exempt from immigration law," he added.

The tactic sparked widespread outcry, and the Trump administration did not revive it in its second term. Still, Miller has helped promote mass deportations of people already living illegally in the U.S. that has divided families according to legal status.

Arguing about the true meaning of the Statue of Liberty

During Trump's first term in 2017, Miller appeared in the White House briefing room to detail for reporters plans to cut back on the number of green cards issued, while prioritizing English speakers and skilled workers.

Asked if doing so might violate the spirit of the poem on the Statue of Liberty, that reads in part, "Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free," Miller responded, "I don't want to get off into a whole thing about history here." He then did just that.

"The poem that you're referring to, that was added later, is not actually a part of the original Statue of Liberty," Miller said.

Birthright citizenship is 'suicide'

When the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump's attempt to throw out birthright citizenship — which grants citizenship to any child born on U.S. soil — Miller said immigrants and their children pose an existential threat to the nation.

"This is absolutely a deep knife wound in the heart of the American republic," he told Fox News Channel in June. "If your ruling requires you to suicide your civilization, your reading of the Constitution is wrong."

On vaccines: 'Nobody has studied it'

Miller is one of many members of the administration who has expressed skepticism about childhood vaccines. In August, he praised the president for signing an executive order aimed at curtailing the vaccine schedule for children.

READ MORE: Stephen Miller's rise to prominence and influence on the Trump administration

"Millions and millions of parents feel they've been pressured when their children are just weeks out of the hospital to take five shots, six shots, seven shots all at once," said Miller, a father of four, including an infant born in June. "Nobody has studied it. Nobody's looked at it. Nobody's thought about it."

His comments contradict what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said, which is that research shows getting several vaccines simultaneously "does not cause any chronic health problems."

The Democratic Party 'does not care' about U.S. citizens

In August 2025, Miller appeared on Fox News Channel to respond to criticism from Democrats over Trump's deployment of the National Guard in Washington and other U.S. cities — brushing aside concerns that the presence of troops was frightening residents, while having only a questionable impact on crime.

Miller used the occasion to take aim at Democrats more broadly.

"The Democrat Party does not fight for, care about or represent American citizens," he said. "It is an entity devoted exclusively to the defense of hardened criminals, gang bangers and illegal alien killers and terrorists."

Miller added: "The Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization."

text:
A federal lawsuit seeking to block Montana’s Initiative 194 was filed on election night, before the Associated Press called the race.

Montana voters approved I-194 with about 65% support.

The Montana Free Press reported the lawsuit was filed at 11:15 p.m. Tuesday — about 18 minutes before AP called the measure.

The initiative would bar corporations, nonprofits and other organizations from spending money to support or oppose candidates, political parties or ballot measures.

Individuals acting on their own and political committees are exempt.

Unless a court blocks it, the law is scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

The case, Frontier Institute, et al. v. Knudsen, et al., was brought by the Frontier Institute, Montana Republican State Central Committee and other groups.

They are suing Attorney General Austin Knudsen and Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen.

The plaintiffs argue I-194 violates their First Amendment rights and that its wording could make it unclear what political speech organizations are allowed to engage in.

“The lawsuit says, under Supreme Court precedent, I-194 is unconstitutional because it interferes, it restricts the ability of corporations or entities to engage in election-based advocacy,” University of Montana law professor Constance Van Kley said.

Supporters of I-194 say the measure takes a different approach from the one rejected by the U.S. Supreme Court in Citizens United.

They argue Montana is defining the powers it grants to organizations, rather than directly restricting their speech.

The plaintiffs are seeking a preliminary injunction, which would pause enforcement of the law while the lawsuit moves through court.

Van Kley said both sides have an opportunity to make their case, and either side may appeal an adverse decision.

A preliminary injunction would not be a final ruling on whether I-194 is constitutional.

The plaintiffs are also asking the court to permanently block the law.

text:
DODGE COUNTY, Wis. (WBAY) - The law firm representing Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe says that he will be released from custody and placed on an order of supervision.

Van Der Merwe was taken into custody by ICE on Thursday, with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issuing a statement saying he overstayed his legal time limit allowed in the U.S. But the law firm representing the trooper says he was legally authorized to work in America.

Van Der Merwe is currently in removal proceedings following his release, which means he will need to defend his case before an immigration judge.

The Christopher & De Leon Law Office released a statement, saying: “Carel’s family is aware and deeply grateful to every reporter and news outlet that took the time to share his story and ask questions about his detention. But our fight is not over.

His release does not erase what he and his family have been through. There is still no explanation why DHS detained him or why exactly he is now being released. Those are the answers we seek and Carel and his family, and work community deserves. We continue to stress how DHS’s own agency, USCIS, authorized him to work. He used that authorization to serve and protect Wisconsin communities. Yet that same agency, detained him. We hope DHS will provide an explanation."

The press release says Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe is a Wisconsin State Trooper who has served for nearly a year. It says he is a 21-year-old who lives in Onalaska and works out of Tomah.

Per the press release, Van Der Merwe came to the United States legally from South Africa as a child. When ICE officers approached him while he waited to board a domestic flight, he said that he had a work permit and a pending asylum application.

According to Van Der Merwe, the officers said they did not care, placed him in handcuffs and shackles, and took him to immigration detention in Dodge County.

In a statement to Action 2 News, DHS stated ICE arrested Van Der Merwe on November 5 during a targeted enforcement operation at the Dane County Regional Airport in Madison.

DHS said Van Der Merwe entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019, but overstayed his admission.

“This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” said DHS. “To be clear: work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S.”

Christopher & De Leon said Van Der Merwe and his parents followed the legal process when they entered the U.S. and have waited seven years for an asylum interview. The law firm says he is included on his father’s pending asylum application and holds federal work authorization bearing an expiration date in 2030.

WisDOT and its Division of State Patrol said they are aware of the situation involving Trooper Carel Van Der Merwe. The trooper has been employed with State Patrol since July 13, 2025, according to the DOT.

text:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he believes he can work with Democrats after their sweeping midterm victories, including potentially on immigration, even as he praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the architect of some of his administration's most hard-line immigration policies, as an "MVP."

Speaking to reporters after attending the UP.Summit near Kennedy Space Center in Florida, Trump was asked what Democratic-led initiatives he could get behind.

"I think a lot," Trump said. "I mean, I said before, immigration is one, the tax cuts. There may be certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient and better. A lot of economic development that we can do."

Read More on Politics

"I think we could do a lot of things together, actually," he added. "A lot of them are about common sense also."

His comments came hours after Trump announced that Miller would replace outgoing Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, elevating one of the most influential and uncompromising figures in his administration following Republicans' bruising defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections.

The selection of Miller could complicate Trump's stated hopes of finding common ground. USA Today described Miller as an immigration hawk who has championed Trump's mass-deportation campaign and noted that he has shown little inclination to work with Democrats.

Democratic leaders immediately attacked the appointment. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats would "fight him every step of the way," while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker, called Miller a "reckless extremist" and said he should be fired rather than promoted.

Trump Calls Miller a 'Great Fighter'

Trump offered an emphatic endorsement of Miller when asked Friday about a characterization of his longtime aide as a "wartime consigliere."

"He's a great fighter," Trump said. "He's been with me right from the beginning, 2015, with me from before 2016."

Trump called Miller "very loyal" and "smart," adding: "He's been an MVP every year."

Miller, 41, has been a powerful force behind Trump's immigration agenda. During his second term, Miller has championed mass deportations and helped drive the administration's effort to end birthright citizenship. His influence has also extended into foreign policy and other areas of the administration.

That record makes Trump's reference to immigration as a potential area of cooperation particularly notable.

Democrats have reacted to Miller's promotion as a sign that Trump is doubling down rather than moderating after the election. Schumer said Trump had "learned nothing from his historic defeat," while Jeffries described Miller as a "dangerous xenophobe."

Miller's promotion follows Wiles' resignation after Republicans lost control of Congress. Trump said earlier Friday that the administration had to "make some moves" following the election.

Trump Offers Postmortem of Republican Losses

Trump also offered a fresh assessment Friday of what he feels went wrong for Republicans, directing some of his frustration toward the Senate and its failure to advance legislation.

"We had a bad election because of a few things," Trump said.

"One thing was not getting things approved in the Senate," he added, while also pointing to higher oil prices.

Trump was particularly frustrated about legislation stalling in the chamber.

"The Senate is getting nothing passed, and it's just killing our country," he said. "That means Democrats and Republicans are just not getting anything done."

Trump described the Senate as a "roadblock" and said voters had noticed the lack of legislative progress.

"Our voters saw that," he said. "And that's one of the problems we had, in my opinion."

He singled out the SAVE America Act, legislation backed by Republicans that would impose proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registration, arguing that its failure to pass hurt the party politically.

Trump stopped short of placing the blame personally on Senate Majority Leader John Thune, whom he described as "a good man," but said the Republican leader needed to "get things done."

The remarks expand on explanations Trump offered in the immediate aftermath of Tuesday's election. He previously cited oil prices and Republican candidates and emphasized that he himself had not appeared on the ballot.

Trump Blames Democratic Wins for Market Rout

Trump also pointed to the stock market as evidence, in his view, of a negative reaction to the Democratic victories.

"When they heard that the Democrats won that election, the market dropped $3 trillion, the highest amount in history," Trump said.

The claim refers to Thursday's steep market sell-off, but Trump's assertion that the Democratic victory triggered the losses is disputed by the broader market picture. The downturn was led heavily by technology and semiconductor shares amid concerns about artificial intelligence valuations and data-center investment.

Trump predicted the losses would be temporary.

"It'll level up and we'll do great things," he said.

His comments nevertheless highlighted the unusual political landscape facing the White House after Tuesday's vote: Trump is blaming Democrats and legislative gridlock for some of the problems confronting Republicans while simultaneously saying he is ready to work with the party that will control Capitol Hill.

With Miller now preparing to run the White House staff, Democrats appeared less optimistic about the prospects for cooperation.

Schumer said Miller's elevation showed Trump was "doubling down" following the election, while Jeffries said Democrats would oppose the administration's immigration agenda.

Trump, however, struck a different tone when asked Friday about working across the aisle.

"I'm very much open to it," he said.

Transcript AILSA CHANG, HOST: The former head of the Chicago FBI is suing top Trump officials, alleging that he was falsely blamed for a botched federal case.

text:
Transcript

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

The former head of the Chicago FBI is suing top Trump officials, alleging that he was falsely blamed for a botched federal case. That's the latest fallout from the Trump administration's failed attempt to prosecute a group of ICE protesters in Chicago.

Douglas DePodesta is alleging that he was forced to resign because the U.S. attorney blamed him falsely when the case against the protesters fell apart. Now a judge has ordered the U.S. attorney to testify in her courtroom. Reporter Jon Seidel with the Chicago Sun Times and Chicago Public Media has been following this case and joins us now. Welcome.

JON SEIDEL, BYLINE: Hi.

CHANG: Hi. OK, so take us back to the start of all this. What exactly happened in the case against the protesters?

SEIDEL: Yeah, sure. This is one of those cases that stem from the big deportation campaign that hit Chicago last year. It was known as Operation Midway Blitz. And basically, during a protest, a federal agent's SUV wound up being surrounded by a large crowd of people, some of whom were pushing the SUV and allegedly causing damage to it.

But from that crowd, only six people were charged. And most of them were involved in local Democratic politics, including a progressive candidate for Congress who'd caught the attention of the White House. And that scenario all raised questions about selective prosecution.

But the case fell apart last May for a completely different reason. Judge April Perry discovered alleged misconduct by federal prosecutors when they were trying to secure the indictment from a grand jury. For example, a prosecutor is accused of speaking to grand jurors outside the grand jury room.

CHANG: But isn't it unusual for a former top FBI official - in this case, DePodesta - to sue the Department of Justice? Like, has this ever happened before?

SEIDEL: I mean, I certainly can't recall a lawsuit like this in Chicago, and, you know, he's also suing the FBI director, Kash Patel, and the attorney general, Todd Blanche. And, you know, federal law enforcement agencies - they always tout the significance of strong partnerships when it comes to fighting crime. And the former FBI boss, Douglas DePodesta, had just such a partnership in Chicago with U.S. attorney Andrew Boutros here only four or five months ago. So it's really extraordinary to see them now becoming legal adversaries.

CHANG: Yeah.

SEIDEL: It's - also a note, there's this family tie at the center of the lawsuit, and this is where it kind of gets complicated. DePodesta's sister-in-law is a former federal prosecutor in Chicago. Today, she's actually a prominent defense attorney.

CHANG: Oh.

SEIDEL: And she represents one of the six protesters. And Boutros allegedly told his superiors that the pair had conspired to tank the case. But DePodesta insists he's never had improper discussions about a case with his sister-in-law. Also this lawsuit is also leading to new revelations about what went on behind the scenes in the protester case, and it's undermining claims that prosecutors have made to Judge Perry. And so more could come out if the lawsuit is allowed to move forward.

CHANG: Wait, is the lawsuit the reason why Judge Perry wants the U.S. attorney to testify?

SEIDEL: Not necessarily. Judge Perry has separately been trying to decide what to do about these allegations of misconduct against the prosecutors. And Monday, she made quite clear she doesn't believe everything they've told her in court.

She's also clearly bothered by the Justice Department's third highest ranking official, Stanley Woodward. He inserted himself into the case last week just before a deadline for the DOJ to turn over documents to the judge, and she, in turn, accused him of trying to cause a delay. She also pointed out that usually attorneys appreciate it when they're given a chance to prove they haven't lied in court.

CHANG: OK, so that's why the judge wants to see the U.S. attorney testify.

SEIDEL: Yeah. She's clearly skeptical of the claims made by Boutros and his team throughout these proceedings. She said her sole focus is on lack of candor and other misconduct that might have occurred in her courtroom.

CHANG: That is Jon Seidel from the Chicago Sun Times and Chicago Public Media. Thank you, Jon.

SEIDEL: You're welcome.

title: After their midterm win and Stephen Miller's promotion, Democrats… - National Newswatch
description:
What's more, Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement.
And the key architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, was elevated Friday to become Trump's chief of staff -- suggesting immigration enforcement may not slow down any time soon.
The administration ramped up immigration enforcement during the first two years of Trump's second term, launching major operations in multiple cities and sending arrests soaring.
DHS also came under criticism for alleged corruption and misuse of funds it was granted to carry out Trump's immigration agenda.
Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
text:
The lofty goals come after two years in which Democrats, while in the minority, were limited in how much they could counter Trump's supercharged and, at times, chaotic immigration enforcement. But there are clear limits to what they can achieve even after Democrats' epic win, with Trump -- who rode into power in part on a promise to curb immigration -- in office for another two years and wielding his veto power.

What's more, Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement. And the key architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, was elevated Friday to become Trump's chief of staff -- suggesting immigration enforcement may not slow down any time soon.

Here's a look at what might come next for immigration after Election Day:

Investigating alleged corruption and ICE policies

Democrats appear ready to use the power of congressional oversight to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. That strategy will likely resonate with voters angry aboutt how enforcement operations were carried out in places like Minneapolis or ICE arrests of longtime immigrants integrated into American society.

The administration ramped up immigration enforcement during the first two years of Trump's second term, launching major operations in multiple cities and sending arrests soaring. DHS also came under criticism for alleged corruption and misuse of funds it was granted to carry out Trump's immigration agenda.

Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. And about 6 in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to "help the country," while less than half, about 4 in 10, said they do more to "hurt the country."

Rep. Robert Garcia, a Los Angeles-area Democrat who will take over the House Oversight Committee and is a prominent critic of Trump's immigration agenda, warned the administration to "lawyer up," adding that investigating alleged abuses at DHS was one of his priorities.

The next Congress will "address the Trump administration's assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable," said Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee.

Those investigations could delve into issues like DHS purchases of massive warehouses to hold arrested immigrants; whether ICE cut corners when hiring thousands of new deportation officers; or deaths in ICE detention facilities.

Garcia and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut held shadow hearings featuring family members of people killed during immigration enforcement operations, a whistleblower exposing problems with ICE training, and American citizens caught up in immigration enforcement operations.

No Republicans attended and Democrats couldn't subpoena witnesses. Now they can, opening up a new level of scrutiny of the administration's actions.

Calls to put forward a Democratic vision for immigration

The last time Congress even came close to passing comprehensive immigration reform was in 2013. That proposal cleared the Senate but died in the House.

Border crossings that surged under the Biden administration further served to dampen any Democratic enthusiasm to talk about legalization for any immigrants.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy for Third Way, a Washington, D.C., think tank, said Democrats need to show voters their own vision for immigration and border security and not just focus on oversight hearings of what happened during the last two years.

"They should lean into oversight, but I think that they also need to couple that with a proactive vision for what immigration should look like in the United States," said Pierce.

At least one of the party's new senators is ready for the discussion. During an interview with Fox News after the election, Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas discussed the need to pass comprehensive immigration reform, including a pathway to citizenship for immigrants living and working illegally in the country for years.

In the House, Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico pointed to the Democratic gains made with Latino voters and the higher numbers of Latino lawmakers who will take office next year as reasons for Democrats to not shy away from talking about immigration issues.

He said Democrats should find ways to address immigration through a lens of affordability, a central issue for voters. For example, they could tackle staffing shortages by creating a new visa class for workers who provide care for children or the elderly.

"This cannot be a third-rail issue for Democrats," said Vasquez. "We can actually reform our immigration system to bring costs down for all Americans and at the same time give people who are either here undocumented or want to come to this country an opportunity to have legal status."

Democrats' power to curb Trump's immigration agenda is limited

Trump, shortly after the election, said he was prepared to work with Democrats on certain issues, highlighting immigration as one of them. But that collaborative tone may not bear out in practice.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed on social media, "Deportations will continue." A few days later, Trump promoted Miller to become his chief of staff.

Immigration and Latino activists lambasted Miller's promotion, calling it an act of defiance after voters spoke clearly at the polls and a sign the president would continue his immigration policies. California's Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla, who's been a key critic of Trump's immigration agenda, said Trump was choosing to double down by picking Miller and vowed, "So will we."

It's unclear if Democrats and the White House will find a middle ground to successfully pass immigration legislation. With Trump in office for another two years, he can veto any Democratic legislation, and Republicans have the money and the personnel to pursue Trump's immigration agenda regardless of Tuesday's results.

Republicans during the summer of 2025 supercharged immigration enforcement with $150 billion intended to expand immigration detention capacity, finish the border wall and hire thousands more deportation officers. Earlier this year they frontloaded routine funding for ICE and Border Patrol for the next three years.

"My fear is that enforcement will get worse. And the country will also see that Congress does not have many tools to stop the executive branch because the executive branch power on immigration has grown so vast," said Andrea Flores, who was a policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Conservatives want action from lame duck Congress

Many administration supporters want this current Congress -- in the little time it has left -- to pass laws solidifying the gains the Trump administration says it has made on border security and immigration. Without codifying changes to asylum law or tightening requirements on employers to verify workers' immigration status, they warn, a different administration could quickly reverse the new immigration landscape Trump has shaped.

NumbersUSA, an advocacy group that seeks to restrict immigration, has a timer on its website counting down the days until this Congress is over with a warning to "make border security permanent."

"If this Congress in the lame duck does not secure the border with lasting legislation," said the organization's co-president, Jeremy Beck, "then this Congress will have failed to meet the moment."

___

Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed to this report.
