AG Todd Blanche rebuffs Rep. Robert Garcia's plans to investigate Stephen Miller: 'I'm his lawyer'

Attorney General Todd Blanche responded sharply tonight to Rep. Robert Garcia's pledge to investigate incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

"This is so disgusting to see them not even wait till the week is out before actually laying their cards on the table," Blanche said in an interview with Fox News. "I mean, you have Garcia saying, minutes after Stephen Miller was promoted to be the chief of staff to the president of the United States of America, telling him to lawyer up."

He added: "Well, I'll tell you what, Stephen Miller has a lawyer. It's me. It's me and the entire Department of Justice."

White House staff members are typically represented by White House counsel, rather than the DOJ, when the investigation or charges have to do with the members' official duties.

Garcia, who is set to take over as chair of the House Oversight Committee, said in a statement today that "Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts."

"Stephen Miller should lawyer up," Garcia wrote, echoing his message to Republicans on Election Night when he wrote simply, "Lawyer up."

Garcia told reporters on Wednesday that he plans to pursue four main investigations in the new term, focusing on the "Trump Crime Family," abuses by ICE and DHS, corporate corruption and the Epstein files. Asked who should be worried by the investigation, Garcia named Miller as a target.

"Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down," Garcia wrote today. "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families."

Trump says there will be 'very little' departures from his Cabinet post-election

Trump told reporters tonight that he intends to have "very little" departures from his Cabinet following White House chief of staff Susie Wiles' exit today.

Asked whether he expects more exits in the coming months, Trump said, “Very little. We have a great — we have a great Cabinet.”

Trump said that he was not unhappy with his team because of the results of the midterm elections, but "it's just time" for change.

"Sometimes you change. The election wasn’t my election. I wasn’t on the ballot," he said.

The comments come shortly after a clip of his upcoming "60 Minutes" interview was aired on CBS News tonight, which included Trump saying he did expect to fire more Cabinet members. That interview was taped before Trump announced Wiles' departure.

Venezuelan man who said voices told him to kill Trump is arrested near White House, DHS says

A Venezuelan man who had guns in his vehicle and told officers that voices in his head urged him to kill President Donald Trump was arrested yesterday near the White House, the federal government said.

The Department of Homeland Security said today that Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos was approached by Secret Service officers who alleged he was acting suspiciously while parked on Constitution Avenue.

“When they confronted the suspect, he said that he heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C. and kill President Trump,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement.

Chrinos, who federal officials said was in the country illegally, was in a vehicle that had been reported stolen, officials said. He told officers there were weapons inside, and officers then found an AR-15 style rifle, a MAC-10 handgun, a Glock 43X pistol, and ammunition, DHS said.

Trump says he may fire Cabinet members, adds he has confidence in Pete Hegseth

Trump said that he may fire members of his Cabinet following the historic sweep by Democrats in the midterm elections, though didn't name any targets.

Asked by Ross Douthat whether he would make dismissals in an interview for CBS News' "60 Minutes" set to air Sunday, Trump said, "I do, a little bit."

“I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good, but I’ll be doing maybe a few changes. I don’t want to mention who,” Trump said.

The interview was filmed prior to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’ exit today, so it’s unclear whether any additional changes are coming.

Douthat asked about speculation that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may be on his way out, to which Trump said he has confidence in him.

"Look, we've won two wars. We've won Venezuela and taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already," he said. "And you could call it a territory. You could call it whatever you want. We won that war in less than one hour and nobody was killed."

Asked whether he credits Hegseth for that, Trump said, "No, but he was a part of it."

Trump's comments to CBS News that he was considering firing Cabinet members comes after he told Fox News on election night that the losses "had nothing to do with my Cabinet."

"No, I don't think so," Trump said when asked whether he'd be making changes. "It was just a point — honestly, look, I've been doing a lot of great things for a long time, and it's just a point in time."

Rep. Brendan Boyle wants Democrats to negotiate with Trump, not fear his veto power

Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., who is poised to become the next chair of the House Budget Committee, told NBC News today that Democrats will have to "negotiate" with the White House to achieve their legislative agenda.

"The thing we have to do is pass it in the House, then second, with our sizable Senate majority, pass it in the Senate. Put it on his desk," Boyle said, referring to sending bills to Trump. "Make it clear to the American people: we’re fighting to bring costs down. He’s the one who’s stopping us. "

Asked whether that's enough, since making Trump look bad doesn't actually deliver for the American people, Boyle said it could start a negotiation process.

"That can also lead to a negotiation, right? Because in the end of the day, Congress still has the power to the purse," Boyle said. "We do have to pass a budget in order to keep the government functioning. I’m interested in having a negotiation with this president."

Boyle said he hopes Democrats can work with Trump on healthcare and the Iran war, and noted that on tariffs, "maybe we won’t be able to get all that we want, but maybe we will be able to get at least half."

"I’m not in a position though where I would accept the idea that, well, we shouldn’t do anything because we’re afraid he’s going to veto it. I don’t accept that," Boyle said.

The newly re-elected congressman said that negotiation starts "with the White House and specifically the president himself."

"Because we know with this White House, at the end of the day, it’s Trump who’s calling the shots," he said.

On his upcoming role at the head of the Budget Committee, Boyle said, "it's a very important position, very powerful committee." He said that he does not have an interest in running for the Senate in 2028, saying, "I can have a much bigger impact on policy as the chairman of the Budget Committee than as a freshman member of the Senate."

Boyle said he would immediately highlight three things in his new role: combating Trump's "big, beautiful bill," passed last year, with new legislation to address healthcare cuts, eliminating Trump's tariff policies, and cutting off authority "for this reckless war in Iran" to address soaring gas prices.

Trump faults Republican candidates for historic midterm losses: 'I was not on the ballot'

Trump tonight blamed Republican candidates for their losses in the midterm elections, saying, "if we were on the ballot, we would have won."

"By the way, I was not on the ballot. Just in case you had any question," Trump told a crowd at the John F. Kennedy Space Center. "Because if we were on the ballot, we would have won, but we weren't."

Trump added, "But these guys were, and they won. That's why we're so proud of you," referring to the Florida politicians in the audience.

The president's quip comes after he told voters for months to "pretend" he was on the ballot. Trump used the phrase at all of his midterm rallies in the weeks leading up to Election Day, which he repeatedly touted as being successful events.

Trump tonight pointed to the massive drop in the stock market yesterday, which wiped out $2.8 trillion worth of wealth. The market has steadied today, though investors are weighing the impact of Democratic wins on AI development.

"You know our country lost 3 trillion, all because of an election," Trump said. "If we would have gained 3 trillion, I probably would have been more unhappy. But you know what that means? That means that they thought somebody else did well in election."

Hasan Piker draws new viewers as he jokingly ushers in ‘Woke 3.0’ on election night

At times Tuesday evening, Hasan Piker appeared shocked by what was happening on his livestream.

“I can’t even read the chat,” he said as messages and notifications whipped across the screen. “This is crazy.”

New followers were flooding his Twitch stream, where he was watching and reacting to election results. At various points, more than 200,000 people were tuned in, far outpacing his average viewership of 34,000. It became the most-watched independent media stream online — one that surpassed some mainstream outlets.

That night, Democrats recorded sweeping wins in the midterm elections, a result that many online called a “blue-nami.” The shift was the culmination of growing frustration with the Trump administration throughout his second term over issues of affordability, corruption, immigration and the Iran war.

Susie Wiles' departure marks the 7th prominent woman to leave the Trump administration this year

Susie Wiles' resignation as the White House chief of staff brings the number of prominent women who have left the Trump administration this year up to seven.

Wiles joins the ranks of former press secretaries Katie Zacharia and Karoline Leavitt, Attorney General Pam Bondi, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and former intelligence director Tulsi Gabbard.

All of those women have been replaced by men thus far, with the exception of Zacharia and Leavitt, as a new press secretary has not yet been named.

So far, Todd Blanche has replaced Bondi as attorney general, Markwayne Mullin took over for Noem as DHS secretary, Chavez-DeRemer was succeeded by Keith Sonderling as labor secretary, Jay Clayton was named DNI after Gabbard, and now Miller will take the reins from Wiles.

Wiles' departure is particularly notable, as she was the first woman to ever take the office of White House chief of staff and was Trump's longest serving chief of staff.

Stephen Miller says he is 'honored beyond words' to step into new role as Trump's chief of staff

Stephen Miller called Trump "the most transformative political leader in American History," in his first public comments following the president's announcement that the MAGA favorite would be replacing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

"It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff," Miller, who has been at the forefront of the delivering Trump's mass-deportation agenda, wrote in post on X.

Miller thanked the "incomparable Susie Wiles for her years of devoted service to the President and the Country, and for her friendship."

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," he wrote, adding that Trump "has single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it."

The transition from Wiles, the first ever female White House chief of staff, to Miller follows the stunning victory of Democrats in ruby-red areas on Tuesday.

Trump appealing dismissal of his $10 billion defamation suit against Wall Street Journal

Lawyers for the president have formally filed notice they're appealing the dismissal of his $10 billion defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal over a story about a birthday card he allegedly sent late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein two decades ago.

Trump's attorneys filed notice they would be appealing U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles' ruling tossing the case on Wednesday, and did so at the 11th U.S. District Court of Appeals yesterday.

Gayles had found Trump’s amended suit fell far short of the high legal bar to show the paper had published the story with “actual malice” — essentially knowledge the underlying claims are false or were made with a reckless disregard of whether it was false.

Trump sued the paper last July after it published a story about a birthday book Ghislaine Maxwell had assembled for Epstein’s 50th birthday in 2003. The book appeared to include a card from Trump, who had been friends around that time with Epstein, who would later be charged with sex trafficking.

The card featured a hand-drawn outline of a naked woman with what appeared to be Trump’s first name signed in the pubic area.

Trump denied having anything to do with the card. His suit accused the paper of making up the existence of the note and argued the article should not have run because of his denial, which was included in the story.

Epstein’s estate later released a copy of a card matching the Journal’s description. Trump and the White House maintained the document is a fake, and his suit said the signature on the card looks nothing like his, which the judge took issue with in his ruling.

Gayles wrote "it is unclear why President Trump argues the September 8 Article shows that his signature 'could not be more different' than the one in the Letter, when it contains several examples where President Trump’s actual signature and sketches are similar to those in the Letter."

Eliott Rodriguez files lawsuit to block 'biased' election official from participating in the Miami-Dade recount

Eliott Rodriguez, congressional candidate in Florida's 27th Congressional District, filed a lawsuit today to bar the Miami-Dade supervisor of elections from participating in the recount of his tight race against GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar.

Rodriguez alleges that Alina Garcia's participation in the recount process "presents a serious, objective risk of bias and would violate Rodriguez’s Fourteenth Amendment right to due process."

“An election official who has publicly announced a winner while her son-in-law and daughter represent that candidate has no business deciding contested ballots in the same race,” Fernand Amandi, general consultant for Rodriguez said. “Garcia’s refusal to step aside is indefensible. We are asking a federal court to protect the impartial process voters deserve.”

The 16-page complaint cites a statement published by the Miami Herald from Garcia on Tuesday night in which she said, “María Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.” It also claims that that Garcia's daughter and son-in-law represent Salazar in connection with the race's recount, creating an "objective bias."

With 99% of expected votes in, Salazar has 50.2% of the vote to Rodriguez's 49.8%, according to NBC News' Decision Desk.

Deputy Supervisor of Elections Juan Mendieta told NBC News' affiliate NBC6 that Garcia will not recuse herself from the process. Garcia also acknowledged that ballots for the race were still being counted, saying earlier this week that, "There are still ballots to be reviewed before the process is complete; specifically, 202 vote-by-mail ballots in congressional district 27 are undergoing the curing process."

Because the margin of the race is at 0.46%, it falls within Florida's threshold for an automatic recount. The canvassing board is scheduled to reconvene today to review the ballots.

The lawsuit filed today is an escalation following a demand by Rodriguez's legal team yesterday that Garcia recuse herself. The complaint asks for a declaration that participation by Garcia "as a voting or deciding board member in this contest violates due process," as well as a preliminary and permanent injunction barring her participation.

Salazar, who has already claimed victory in the race despite there being no official call, said in a post on Instagram yesterday, "My opponent is behaving like an election denier, attempting to turn this process into a political circus because he does not like the election outcome."

Former Trump health adviser accuses Susie Wiles of prioritizing special interests as chief of staff

About an hour before Susie Wiles announced her departure as White House chief of staff, former Trump administration health adviser Calley Means accused Wiles of blocking MAHA priorities and putting the lobbyists' interests over Americans’ health.

Means left his role last month as an adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a key White House advocate for the MAHA agenda. This afternoon, Means told podcaster Joe Rogan that he resigned because a group of people in the administration were acting contrary to voters’ interests in order to secure money for the midterms or enrich their families.

Means said Wiles in particular had a “stranglehold” over the administration’s policies, noting that he tried to launch an initiative to investigate the amount of sugar in children’s diets, but Wiles told him it couldn’t be done because “I need the sugar industry money.”

Means said Wiles’ team also pushed to make flavored e-cigarettes and vapes more widely available, an action that led to the departure of former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary. Before joining the White House, Wiles was a lobbyist whose clients included a tobacco company.

When reached for comment on Means' comments, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said that the administration had “secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

“After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement.

Means, however, claimed that Kennedy had been sidelined in the White House’s policy discussions about the weed killer glyphosate. Trump ultimately issued an executive order to boost the supply of the glyphosate in the U.S. and the administration backed Bayer, the manufacturer of a glyphosate product, in a Supreme Court case.

Means said the last straw for him was the federal government delaying the release of a federal definition of ultra-processed food, which had been one of Means’ biggest priorities. The administration teased a definition in August but has yet to release one.

In lieu of a statement, the Department of Health and Human Services pointed NBC News to Kennedy’s post this afternoon on X.

“Draining the swamp is a mandate, and we have an obligation to deliver,” Kennedy wrote. “President Trump and I intend to keep fighting until the American people—not corporate influence—drive our health policies.”

In separate posts, Kennedy said he was grateful to Wiles “for her calm and inspiring leadership and wisdom” and called her replacement, Stephen Miller, “the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration” aside from himself.

DNC Chair Ken Martin touts 2026 success with young men and minority groups

Ken Martin, chair of the Democratic National Committee, said this afternoon that Democrats won big on Tuesday because "we didn't take anyone for granted."

"We didn't leave anyone behind across key constituencies of the Democratic Party; we won back support that had swung away in 2024," Martin said on a "People's Victory Briefing" livestream hosted by the DNC.

Martin said that Democrats won back Latino voters by 28 percentage points this cycle, a key voting bloc that Trump had garnered support from in 2024. He also said that Democrats won back young voters by 33 points, noting that young men moved toward the party by 38 points.

Asian and Black voters also leaned back toward Democrats this election cycle, by 17 and 9 points, respectively, Martin said. These key groups helped fuel a "historic sweep" of overall voters who swung 15 points toward Democrats nationwide, he added.

"We listened to voters who sat out in 2024 after voting in 2020," Martin said, adding that Democrats also "made a bet" last year to start investing resources in states under Republican control.

"We knew that campaigns aren't won in the final weeks with expensive TV ads," Martin said. "Instead of hoarding our money until the end, we invested it early and often in the proven ways to build a movement."

Shelby Wiltz, the DNC's national political director, noted that Democrats made investments "all year long, really for two years, into red states and purple states," adding that "is why you see states like Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina in play."

Martin also previewed "critical" gubernatorial races in Kentucky, Louisiana, and Mississippi coming up in 2027.

"As we wait for Scott Colom's race to get called, we know that those states are now in play," he said, referring to the Mississippi Senate candidate who is holding a slight lead over GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries says Miller is 'a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist'

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries reacted to the news that longtime Trump aide Stephen Miller will be the new White House chief of staff, calling Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” in a post on X.

“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor,” Jeffries wrote. “Fire him today.”

Trump announced today that Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy and a homeland security adviser, will become his chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles.

Sen. Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was discharged from the Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Maryland, after suffering what his doctor called a “small hemorrhagic stroke” last weekend, his office announced Friday.

Murphy, 53, said in a written statement that he will be spending “several weeks at a rehabilitation center” after being discharged from the hospital.

Read the full story here.

Trump says he 'wanted to make a change' with the White House chief of staff

Trump addressed his decision today to name Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, telling reporters that he "wanted to make a change."

“Stephen’s been with me from beginning. He gets it — very good politically, and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job, great manager," he said outside the White House before traveling to Florida.

Trump said that outgoing chief of staff Susie Wiles has "done a very good job."

How Abdul El-Sayed swung young men from Trump by 55 points in Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed huddled with key advisers in August to game-plan what would become a huge moment in his Senate campaign: a primetime interview with Fox News’ Jesse Watters.

In thinking through how to start the conversation, one adviser asked El-Sayed where he thought he might find agreement with the conservative host. The team tossed around coming up with a populist-minded policy position to discuss, according to two people close to El-Sayed who were familiar with the conversation.

Read the full story here.

Trump names Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

President Donald Trump announced today that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles will step down this week, with Stephen Miller replacing her.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Read the full story here.

Israel reels as midterms and Trump’s $4 billion aid cut point to dramatic shift in U.S. relations

TEL AVIV — If this week’s midterm elections landed a knockout blow to Republicans, they also delivered a stinging slap in the face to Israel.

In addition to checking the power of a president whom Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly called “the greatest friend Israel has ever had,” the midterms herald the arrival of a handful of progressive Democrats in Congress who have made their avowed pro-Palestinian, anti-Israeli views central to their political identities.

Read the full story here.

Trump says he met with Putin envoy, sees Ukraine deal soon

Trump said he met privately with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy yesterday. The president would not disclose what he discussed with Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, but predicted a deal could emerge soon aimed at resolving the Russian war in Ukraine.

News of the encounter come after the Russian official appeared with representatives from Ukraine at a White House event organized by first lady Melania Trump.

A U.S. delegation is scheduled to mediate talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and Nov. 11 between representatives from Russia and Ukraine.

Read the full story here.

GOP House Oversight Chair James Comer says 'there's a lot of questions about Hegseth'

House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer, R-Ky., signaled today that Republicans are not happy with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the administration's handling of the U.S. war on Iran.

“I can tell you with a high level of confidence there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran," Comer said in an interview on NewsNation.

He added, "I think Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

Comer has rarely criticized Trump or the administration.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that Hegseth "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists."

Parnell added that Hegseth is "100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office."

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said he plans to introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth, which could come to the House floor as early as next week. In a video posted on social media yesterday, the defense secretary preemptively dismissed the move.

Trump said earlier this week that the war was partially to blame for the Republicans' losses in the midterms. Vice President JD Vance said on Wednesday that the conflict was the "real reason" for the GOP rout.

Trump has told some allies he is considering replacing Hegseth, asking them who they think should succeed him, two people familiar with discussions told NBC News this week.

Congressman-elect Richard Ojeda pays tribute to his father on social media

Army veteran and Congressman-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., said today that his father died of Parkinson's disease just days after seeing his son elected to Congress.

In a post on X, Ojeda wrote: “On Election Night, I got to tell him, ‘Pop, we won.’” A video included in the post shows the emotional moment between father and son.

On Tuesday, Ojeda defeated his GOP opponent, Rep. Richard Hudson, in the race for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District.

“A part of me believes he held on just long enough to see his son make it to Congress,” Ojeda wrote of his father. “He won’t be there when I’m sworn in. But I know he’ll be standing right beside me.”

Ojeda concluded the post by dedicating his future in Congress to his dad, who in recent years had lived with the degenerative brain disorder.

“These next two years are for you,” the post said.

Democrat Scott Wiener wins House race to succeed Pelosi, NBC News projects

Democrat Scott Wiener has been elected to represent California's 11th Congressional District, which covers San Francisco, NBC News projected this morning.

Wiener will fill the seat held by Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who's retiring from Congress at the end of the year after serving in the House for 40 years, including as speaker and minority leader.

Wiener has served in the California Senate since 2016 and previously was a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors.

Pelosi had endorsed progressive Connie Chan, a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, in the general election race.

In a statement Wednesday, Pelosi praised Chan's campaign and congratulated Wiener on his election.

"Representing San Francisco is an extraordinary honor and a profound responsibility," she said. "My office stands ready to assist in the transition, and I wish him success in service for the people of our City."

Colorado approves Proposition 135: Prohibit gender-affirming surgery for minors, NBC News projects

Colorado voters have approved Proposition 135: Prohibit gender-affirming surgery for minors, NBC News projects.

See the latest results here.

Van Hollen not eyeing Senate majority leader role, source says

As Senate Democrats digest the impact of a majority larger than they were ever expecting to have, there is talk about whether someone will challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in the race to be majority leader.

A number of the incoming Democratic freshman senators have said they want new leadership for Democrats, and one name that has been floated is Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

But a source familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking rejected that idea.

“As the senator has said publicly, he is not looking at the majority leader role and is actively ‘kicking the tires’ on the 2028 presidential election to shape the direction of the party and the country as we fight to end a rigged economy and overhaul a corrupt political system,” the source said.

“Prior to selecting a majority leader, Sen. Van Hollen believes the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people," the source added. "He’s made it clear that the new Democratic majorities need to use their power to push a proactive, economic agenda.”

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said in an interview with CNN this week of Van Hollen that, “I’ve been very clear: I think he’d be an amazing Senate majority leader,” adding, “Of course, that’s a choice he has to make about whether or not he wants to pursue that.”

U.S. attorney who led DOJ's 'grand conspiracy' investigation resigns

The U.S. attorney who led the Justice Department's “grand conspiracy” probe into those who conducted various investigations of Trump is stepping down, Attorney General Todd Blanche said on a post on X this morning.

Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, is resigning just days after the midterm elections swept Democrats back into power on Capitol Hill, with party leaders promising a vigorous investigative agenda as they prepare to take over Congress.

“We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro," Blanche said in his post.

Quiñones' resignation follows that of Joe diGenova, who worked under him. DiGenova resigned in September amid clashes with DOJ leadership over the speed of the investigation, NBC News previously reported.

“Everybody was in their lane, and then some lanes got crossed, and then I decided to leave,” diGenova told NBC News. “I want to underscore that we were following the principles of federal prosecution all along the way, and we did that. We were moving smartly, and I underscore we were moving smartly, and then things, you know, got where they got.”

The investigation focused initially on the 2016 Russia investigation and then on the FBI's search of Mar-a-Lago, which led to the federal indictment of Trump by then-special counsel Jack Smith's office in the classified documents case.

The U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, a bright spot for the economy

The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, a surprisingly strong number that includes what appear to be some AI-related construction and manufacturing jobs.

American workers have so far seen relatively few benefits from the AI boom that has driven the stock market higher and fueled trillions of dollars in spending by the world’s top tech giants.

Read the full story here.

Trump says he's '100% in favor of Super Intelligence'

As global tech stocks have plunged over fears about the midterm election's effect on AI development, Trump said this morning that he's "100% in favor" of the technology.

"As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them. They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!" he wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Before the election, he said he wanted to rename AI as "super intelligence."

There was a dramatic sell-off yesterday of U.S. tech stocks in the wake of the elections of candidates Tuesday who ran on reining in data centers and regulating AI — key issues for many voters. The fears spread today to markets in Asia and Europe.

Jay Rockefeller, heir to famed dynasty and healthcare advocate in Senate, dies at 89

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families who during three decades in the Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died today at his home in Washington, The Washington Post reported. He was 89.

His family did not ​provide a cause, the newspaper added.

Read the full story here.

Schumer dismisses concerns that he's not fit to lead Senate Democrats

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., last night dismissed concerns about whether he's a good fit to lead his caucus as majority leader in the new Congress.

In an interview on MS Now, he was asked for his response to people who feel like he's not the right person for that role.

"The bottom line is: first ... we’ve had a very, very strong finish here, and I have worked really hard to get the results we got. But second, the issue is not me, Lawrence. The issue is unity, fighting together. We still have a big job to do," he said.

Asked about Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, not supporting him for majority leader, Schumer said, "I said, your job is to win the seat. We need to take back the Senate. Our enemy is not each other. Our enemy is Donald Trump and the Republican senators who just go along" with all the "I’m not allowed to say it on your show — that he does. That’s the focus. The focus is unity."

Global market rout deepens after midterms intensify AI fears

An intensifying rout of tech stocks hit global markets today, with a surge of red tickers spreading from Wall Street to Asia and Europe after the blue wave of the U.S. midterm elections fueled fears over AI development.

The steep losses in Asia — Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020 — came after a dramatic plunge in U.S. tech stocks following the success of anti-AI candidates, which deepened concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom.

Read the full story here.

Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth yesterday dismissed a renewed effort in the House to bring articles of impeachment against him as early as next week.

In a video on social media, Hegseth said, “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

Hegseth was referring to Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment when the House is back in session. Lawmakers are scheduled to return to Washington on Monday.

Read the full story here.

'Blue arrows everywhere': How Trump's 2024 coalition shifted in 2026

NBC News’ Sahil Kapur joins "Meet the Press NOW" to break down how the 2026 midterm results show shifts in some of the key voting blocs that brought Trump back to the White House in 2024.

Judge blocks construction on Trump’s D.C.-area arch after commission’s approval

A federal judge late last night temporarily blocked construction on Trump’s “Triumphal Arch” shortly after a planning commission led by the president's appointees approved it.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted a temporary restraining order blocking the administration from “initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation” or other steps in the arch project for 14 days.

Chutkan’s order came within an hour of the National Capital Planning Commission’s approval of the massive and controversial arch project, which would sit in Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Read the full story here.

Trump to deliver remarks at NASA's Kennedy Space Center

Trump is scheduled to travel to NASA's Kennedy Space Center today in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

The president is set to deliver remarks around 6 p.m. ET, according to the White House.

His visit will take place during the Max Power event, which according to NASA is "a two-day aerospace festival celebrating the past, present, and future of flight and space exploration." The event will feature air shows, cutting-edge technology showcases, and immersive space exhibits to create an unforgettable experience."

Trump signed a proclamation about space Tuesday, which said that next summer, Artemis III would begin a test flight campaign as part of the effort to return astronauts to the moon.

"We will return to the Moon by 2028, lay the foundation for a permanent American lunar presence, and hasten the day when an American becomes the first human to set foot on the red dunes of Mars," the proclamation said.

The goal will be to "establish a permanent presence in space to extend the reach of American exploration, preserve our frontier spirit, and strengthen our national security for centuries to come," it said. "The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity — and that nation will be the United States of America."

text:
Happy Friday! A blue wave could be good news for litigation funders.

Funders have battled a series of Republican-introduced federal bills that would enact disclosure requirements or set parameters on outside investment in US litigation. Victoria Sahani, a Boston University School of Law professor, says those bills will be “dead on arrival when the Democrats take over.”

On the state level, efforts to regulate the industry have been more bipartisan and have had more success. Ed Gehres, managing partner at Invenio LLP, a law firm focused on litigation finance transactions, says funders have to remain vigilant.

“This is the time to build a moat,” he said. “The important thing is to build this political capital when you don’t need it as much.” Read More

Bloomberg Law subscribers can get this Litigation Finance newsletter in their inbox on Fridays. Sign up here.

Burford YPF Update

A Republican senator and attorneys generals from 14 states and one territory submitted amicus briefs asking the US Supreme Court to review the YPF ruling. The YPF case is famously backed by litigation funder Burford Capital.

After the court decision that ordered Argentina to pay $16.1 billion to investors was reversed earlier this year, the claimants had a few different options. One was to seek a US Supreme Court review.

Burford Capital published its unaudited financial results for the third quarter on Wednesday, and during the earnings call CEO Christopher Bogart said the briefs were “a pretty significant development in the process of that case.”

The funder reported it had total revenue of $135 million, achieved $100 million of de-leveraging, and closed the quarter with more than half a billion dollars of cash on hand.

What I’m Reading

Michael Di Gennaro, chief growth officer at the Law Practice Exchange, wrote for Bloomberg Law Perspectives about MSOs and how companies looking to invest in multiple legal practices will need to consider economies of scale and cross-marketing opportunities. He cites Charlesbank Capital Partners’ investment in an MSO supporting Wood Smith Henning & Berman as an example of private capital pursuing legal practice areas outside of personal injury.

Disputes between litigation funders and the law firms they finance are surfacing in federal courts across the country, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Texas-based Galindo Law Firm filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after rapidly scaling into a high-volume mass tort practice with the support of tens of millions from private lenders.

Litigation funder Loopa Finance announced the appointments of Raquel Assis and Roberto Gassmann as investment managers, reinforcing its commitment to expanding its presence across Latin America, Europe and the United Kingdom. Assis will focus on consolidating Loopa’s growth in Brazil and Gassmann will focus on further strengthening its presence in Europe and the UK.

Leading the News

House Democrats Plot Trump Probes to Prioritize in Majority

Democrats are leaving open the possibility of impeaching or subpoenaing President Donald Trump, saying nothing is off the table as they prepare for two years of investigations in the House majority.

Musk DOGE Probe Competes With Democrats’ Oversight Priorities

Resurgent Democrats are wrestling with how best to investigate Elon Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency against a long list of priority targets, including alleged conflicts of interest involving President Donald Trump’s family and the extent of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.

PR Nightmare Threatens Companies Called for Congressional Probes

Congressional investigations may evoke a courtroom feeling, but companies facing potential Democratic probes should address them as more of a public relations campaign.

Law Firm Deals to Face New Hill Scrutiny

Democrats pledging to put heat on law firms that made deals with President Donald Trump now have more tools at their disposal thanks to majorities in both chambers of Congress. The question is: How hard will lawmakers press for answers?

Nine large firms last year pledged $940 million in free legal services in the pacts with Trump. The deals came as the president lobbed executive orders against firms because of their ties to lawyers he sees as enemies.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, poised to lead the powerful House Judiciary Committee next Congress, is among the Democrats who have been asking firms for more information on the Trump deals. They say at least two firms — Kirkland & Ellis and Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom — are stonewalling those efforts.

Democrats will enter the new Congress with a long list of oversight targets, including Trump immigration enforcement, Justice Department misconduct allegations, and funding for the White House ballroom project. It remains to be seen where the Trump deal firms figure into the priorities, Ryan Tarinelli reports.

Commentary & Opinion

Weil Gotshal’s Closest Relationship Cost the Firm Everything

A law firm, even one with 1,200 lawyers, is simply a collection of relationships: partners deciding to work together. It thrives when those relationships are strong. And it can die if they wither.

At Weil Gotshal & Manges, there was no relationship more important than that between Mike Aiello, its highest paid partner and most prodigious business generator, and Barry Wolf, its longtime executive partner. Their story is the story of Weil’s final decade. Their relationship dictated the firm’s strategy and decisions. It decided who stayed at the firm and who left. And when it shattered, the firm did too.

NOAA Review Sends California Coastal Program Into Troubled Waters

Alston & Bird attorneys examine the review and renewal of California’s registration under the Coastal Zone Management Act. The results could have broader implications for coastal governance and environmental policy nationwide.

Weil Shows What Happens When Any Partner Could Leave at Any Time

The lesson from the sudden collapse of Weil is that the largest law firms are now businesses in every sense, and they can fail the way businesses fail, Major, Lindsey & Africa president John Cashman says.

Exercise Your Constitutional Rights to Protect the Rule of Law

Ten retired US judges ask what can citizens do when federal officials charged with protecting their legal rights disregard them? The very essence of citizenship is to exercise the constitutional rights of free speech and peaceful assembly in these circumstances, they say.

Partners Who Stay Through Firm Collapse Need Defined Protections

When a firm closes, what happens to the partner who stays? Fidelium Advisors’ James Dixon says firm leaders should confront those questions before the first serious wave of departures.

CHICAGO (WLS) -- Days after a midterm election that saw monumental gains for Democrats, President Donald Trump announced his longest-serving chief of staff, Susie Wiles, has resigned.

description:
This is a guest post by David Leopold, America’s Voice Legal Advisor and former president of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.
Voters handed Democrats the House and the Senate in an election where Trump’s war on immigrants was on the ballot.
So now that the country has spoken, will Trump’s assault on immigration finally end?
The American people deserve answers for millions of immigration status revocations and a collapse in citizenship approvals.
Congress’s job now is simple and urgent: end Trump’s lawlessness and restore accountability, order, and, above all, human decency; make sure the Constitution still means something for everyone within our borders, and that cruelty ends now.
text:
This is a guest post by David Leopold, America’s Voice Legal Advisor and former president of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

On Tuesday, Nov. 3, the American people spoke loud and clear with one voice: Enough. Enough violence. Enough cruelty. Enough chaos. Mass deportation must end.

Voters handed Democrats the House and the Senate in an election where Trump’s war on immigrants was on the ballot. For nearly two years, this administration promised to go after dangerous criminals. Instead, it turned its fury on the very immigrants who embody America’s core values: family, community, and hard work. Trump didn’t send ICE after “the worst of the worst.” He sent masked agents in military gear to seize parents and children at immigration court, disappear longtime neighbors into a maze of prisons, banish people to foreign gulags, and terrorize immigrants and U.S. citizens all over the country.

Americans saw the violence first-hand in their communities or beamed into their home night after night. They watched children torn from parents, neighbors dragged from their cars, U.S. citizens murdered in the streets, and a government at war with its own people. The rights under our Constitution were ripped apart. The American people did not need a lawyer to tell them this was wrong, lawless and unjust. Their intuition and conscience told them. And when they voted they answered with a thunderous “No!”

This election was a demand to restore due process, fairness, and humanity. And Americans reset the table. From deep-red Texas to blue-state Maine, Republicans lost their seats because voters refused to keep feeding a vicious, out-of-control machine. Voters saw the Trump administration’s bad governance. The message could not have been louder or clearer.

So now that the country has spoken, will Trump’s assault on immigration finally end?

Not by itself. Ballots alone do not unlock a single ICE prison cell. Families are still behind bars tonight. The voters have done their part; now the Democratic Congress must do its part. It must act boldly and without apology, knowing it carries a clear mandate to hold Trump accountable, not to enable his lawlessness.

On day one, it should take three steps.

First, wield the power of the purse. It is Congress’s strongest weapon. Republicans have already poured roughly $145 billion into ICE, much of it to cage human beings. But the annual spending bills that fund most of Homeland Security are now in Democratic hands. Not one more dollar should flow without basic guardrails the public already supports: visible identification of ICE agents, body cameras, and judicial warrants.

Second, use subpoena power to drag the truth into the light. Americans deserve to know where ICE is holding people; more than 16,000 have vanished from its online locator, as if they never existed. The American people deserve answers for millions of immigration status revocations and a collapse in citizenship approvals. And Congress must hold accountable everyone responsible, including the ICE and Border Patrol agents who carried out unlawful, cruel, and deadly actions across America. The people have demanded that it stop.

Third, reclaim Congress’s Article I authority as a co-equal branch of government. For too long, Congress looked away and let Trump rule by executive order and social media posts. Those days must end. Trump may keep abusing executive power. But if he does, he will do so in open defiance of the clear will of the American people who have demanded that Congress end Trump’s chaos and restore the rule of law.

Due process is not a Democratic value or a Republican value. It is an American value: the promise that no government stands above the law and no person falls beneath its protection. Everyone facing arrest, detention, or deportation deserves a fair hearing before a judge and a real chance of getting a lawyer. Without that, no one should be locked away or banished to a country they barely remember or have never seen.

On Tuesday, the American people threw out the enablers of a vicious out of control anti-immigrant ICE machine. Congress’s job now is simple and urgent: end Trump’s lawlessness and restore accountability, order, and, above all, human decency; make sure the Constitution still means something for everyone within our borders, and that cruelty ends now.

The American people have spoken.

text:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy is in federal custody after showing up for a scheduled immigration appointment earlier this week.

The incident was documented on video Wednesday by Karen Pohl, a volunteer immigration court observer with the group Detention Resistance. She said she’s never seen someone that young being detained before.

“It was just — I couldn't believe what I was seeing because I had never watched a child by himself get detained in that manner,” Pohl said.

The incident was upsetting to watch, she said.

“This is kind of like war,” Pohl, a retired Navy veteran, said. “And you just do what you got to do and deal with the emotion later because these people need us. There’s nobody else that’s witnessing how they’re being targeted and abused.”

The boy had been living with his uncle in City Heights after his father was deported in March 2025.

According to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, the uncle did not have legal custody.

In accordance with the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, the spokesperson said the boy was considered an unaccompanied minor.

“Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement,” the spokesperson said.

Cody Petterson, a board trustee with the San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD), said the uncle was designated on school records as an authorized caregiver.

“I am not surprised ICE would say just about anything to justify their actions,” he said.

While he does not know the full details on who has legal custody of the boy, he said the uncle was someone the father entrusted his child to.

“This is a classic case of legalized lawlessness, where these agencies will attempt to use the law to actually further what is essentially a lawless activity,” Petterson said. “There is no question that the best place for this child was with the uncle that their father had designated as the guardian.”

In a three-page letter to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., SDUSD and other local officials are demanding the federal government release the boy back to his uncle’s custody so that he could continue his education with familiar “schools, teachers, classmates and support systems.”

“We demand the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) and the ORR change its policies and procedures affecting school-aged children who enter government custody or placement,” the letter said. “At a minimum, greater consideration should be given to the educational continuity of these students.”

Wister Gaetan, the co-founder of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said the boy should be doing what boys his age are doing, going to school and playing with other kids. He said the boy should be returned to his family.

“This kid was in a setting that provided him with love, (brought) him to school and a path to education,” Gaetan said. “Sitting behind bars with the U.S. government is purely unacceptable, a violation of his due process rights and civil liberty.”

San Diego City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera, who also posted the information on Instagram on Thursday, is calling for the restoration of temporary protected status for Haitians.

“We're in this situation because of a decision to end a program that did not need to be ended, that should not have been ended,” he said.

The family is working on resolving the custody issue.

Meanwhile, the district said it will provide crisis counselors for students at Fay Elementary School, where the boy attended.

text:
By Gabrielle Caumon

Reporting Texas

Rafael, a former Austin middle school theater teacher, heard last year that some of his students from first-generation immigrant families had seen Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids at their apartment complex.

Fear, Rafael told them, should not stand in the way of their future. So he shared his story.

Rafael, 33, told the students that he is a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient who came to Texas from Mexico at age 6. The DACA program, created in 2012 by the Obama administration, provides eligible immigrants who came to the U.S. as children with temporary protection from deportation and allows them to obtain work authorization.

“I wanted to show my students: Look, if I did, you can do it,” said Rafael, who spoke on the condition that only his first name be published. “That was something really special; they were able to see someone like them teaching them, going through this entire path and being able to work because of DACA.”

But Rafael, like other DACA recipients and immigration lawyers, is fearful in the current immigration climate. Recipients are navigating a precarious legal status in the U.S. immigration system as court rulings reshape the legal landscape and deepen uncertainty.

Austin immigration attorney Jason Finkelman said DACA continues to face legal challenges. Texas and other states have argued that the DACA program conflicts with federal immigration law, he said, and that the Obama administration exceeded its authority when it created the program.

Courts have upheld parts of those challenges, Finkelman said, but current DACA recipients can still renew their status and work authorization every two years. However, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has been barred from approving new DACA applications since July 16, 2021.

In January 2025, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found parts of DACA to be illegal but allowed it to remain in place while the litigation continues. The court upheld DACA’s protections against deportation of DACA recipients, but the ruling could prevent DACA recipients from obtaining work permits.

The constant changes affect more than recipients’ immigration status. It can also shape the decisions about careers, finances and families.

“If you don’t know if you’re going to be able to work and make a living, are you going to buy a home? Are you going to save for retirement? Can you support your children?” Finkelman said. “So when this work authorization is temporary, and these renewals are unpredictable, that uncertainty can impact a family’s financial security in this country.”

Criminal defense attorney Pedro Villalobos, the first DACA recipient licensed to practice law in Texas, said DACA recipients must keep moving forward despite the instability of their status.

“You’ve got to keep trying to achieve your goals, try to get an education, try to advance your career professionally, and do your best because you can’t view that as an impediment,” Villalobos said. “It’s a hurdle, but not an impediment.”

Born in Mexico, Villalobos arrived in Texas at 3 and graduated from the University of Texas School of Law in 2016.

Villalobos, now a lawful permanent resident, has more comfort and security than he did under DACA, when renewal issues could upend his life at any moment. He said, however, that he remains vigilant given the current climate.

Rafael, meanwhile, said he has always been confused about where his status stands and how much longer he has in the country.

“As soon as DACA gets cancelled or stopped, obviously my name is now on a list,” Rafael said. “They have my address. They have all my information. They can just come pick me up. It’s one of those things where the future is just so blurry.”

The risks are real. In January 2025, the Department of Homeland Security rescinded restrictions on immigration enforcement in sensitive locations, including schools.

The fear Rafael sees in his students is one he remembers from his own childhood, when he worried whether his parents would still be home when he returned from school.

“Seeing my own students living with that is a really heartbreaking experience,” Rafael said. “At the end of the day, as teachers, we are supposed to be protecting these kids, and it’s really hard when both the students and the faculty are scared because you never know what’s gonna happen.”

Rafael has since moved to a different school district, where he teaches students from more privileged backgrounds. He has not shared his immigration status with those students.

When Rafael’s family arrived in Texas, his father hoped he and his sister would have opportunities beyond working in construction or at a fast-food restaurant. Their parents emptied their savings account to help Rafael and his sister obtain their DACA status.

“With my dad giving us this opportunity, I get to have a car, travel, teach; I get to do what I love; my sister gets to buy a car, a house and create a family — and it’s all because of DACA.”

But even after building a career, Rafael said he does not know how long that stability will last.

“DACA doesn’t prevent anyone from entering a career, but what its effect is, is on the ability to maintain that work authorization,” Finkelman said.

Filing a renewal application on time does not automatically extend work authorization. If a work permit expires before a new one arrives, recipients generally must stop working, Finkelman said, even if their DACA status remains valid.

“Someone may have a college degree and experience and a great employment record, but if they don’t have that work permit or they have to plan around getting a work permit every two years, that creates a lot of uncertainty,” Finkelman said.

Recent renewal delays have added to those concerns. Some recipients are waiting more than six months for their renewal, compared with an average of 15 days in fiscal 2025. Finkelman said the reason for the longer delays remains unclear.

Rafael said he was “lucky” with his latest renewal. After seeing warnings about delays on TikTok and Reddit, he applied earlier than planned, moving up his renewal from its January 2027 expiration date. He submitted his application on Aug. 16 and received approval on Sept. 15.

One of his friends, however, had to start a GoFundMe in April after a delay in his renewal application, which he had submitted Dec. 5, cost him his job. His application was approved at the end of July, and his employer rehired him.

For Rafael, the risks extend beyond his ability to work. Last year, before going to work, he said he stopped at a Circle K near his school, in a predominantly Latino community in Austin. An ICE agent came in.

“My heart is beating at a thousand miles an hour, but I’m making sure that I have my teacher’s ID on me, that I have my wallet with me, that I have my work permit with me,” Rafael said. “Just making sure that I have a way to actually show them like, ‘Hey, I am here, I can legally be here.’”

He has stopped going to that convenience store.

“We have to be the perfect model citizens,” Rafael said. “We have to respect everything and be careful — because one mistake, and our entire life goes away.”

Lasting security for DACA recipients would require congressional action, Finkelman said, including legislation that creates a pathway to permanent residence for people brought to the U.S. as children.

“We’re not asking for a free ride; we’re not asking for special privileges,” Villalobos said. “We’re only asking to give us a chance to prove ourselves and show you that we can succeed, that we can make something of ourselves.”

Rafael said he wants to live somewhere where he no longer has to worry about his future because of his immigration status.

“I need to move to a place where I know I’m going to be safe, where I am no longer going to be treated like a pawn,” Rafael said — “like Texas treats DACA recipients.”

text:
The Justice Department on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.

The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.

The case was at the forefront of the Trump administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Mr. Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.

On Monday, on the eve of Election Day, the Supreme Court rejected an emergency appeal from the Justice Department to require California to separate mail ballots received from the approximately 20,000 people it alleged were noncitizens.

The Supreme Court rejected the appeal in a one-line, unsigned order.

The Justice Department remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what it says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial lawsuit it filed in Alaska at Mr. Trump's direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state's Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."

"The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary," the motion said.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after Election Day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.

Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to "safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election."

"We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later," he said outside of court the week before the election.

The United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of California referred all questions to the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., which did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday evening.

California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections.

The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year.

Miller, long a member of Trump’s tight inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday's midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president's executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Wiles gave Trump her resignation Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told The Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Miller is tied to immigration policies that voters said went too far

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoting unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.

He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that "Stephen has been with me from the beginning.

"He gets it; very good politically," Trump said as he departed the White House. "He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely associated with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

In a statement, Garcia added, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign

Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.”

But he added, “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.

She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.

Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear.

In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.

Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for Florida governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.

Wiles once said Trump had ‘an alcoholic’s personality'

But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.

The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”

Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.

In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
