text:
President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. Wiles, a steely political operator and the first woman to serve in the post, was Trump’s longest-serving White House chief of staff and his longtime adviser.

A handful of remaining Senate and House races still to be called by The Associated Press will determine the strength of Democrats’ majority in Congress. Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate next year and as many as 56 depending on final results in Alaska and Mississippi — where contests remain narrow with votes still outstanding.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who is likely to return as majority leader next year, promised in an interview with the AP that Democrats will prevent the Republican president from installing a “right-winger” on the Supreme Court or “crappy nominees” elsewhere in the federal judiciary or in Trump’s Cabinet.

The Latest:

Trump says he expects ‘very little’ staffing changes to his administration

Speaking to reporters on the tarmac after he landed in Palm Beach, Trump was asked if he expected more departures in coming months after Wiles left as chief of staff.

“Very little,” he said, adding “We have a great cabinet.”

In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” taped before he left for Florida, Trump suggested at least some staff turnover, saying of his Cabinet, “I think they’re good. But I’ll do — be doin’ maybe a few changes.”

He declined to say who, while also defending Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hegseth could face impeachment by the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress.

US Department of Justice drops lawsuit over 20,000 California ballots

The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that aimed to stop California from processing up to 20,000 ballots it suspected were mailed to noncitizens.

The federal government’s decision comes before a scheduled hearing next week where a special master was to evaluate the list’s accuracy. California officials and a federal judge have said the list is outdated and includes legitimate voters.

The lawsuit was part of the Trump administration’s effort to stop alleged illegal voting.

▶ Read more

Trump say he’s planning ‘maybe a few changes’ to his Cabinet, but defends Hegseth

In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes,” the president said, “I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good. But I’ll do — be doin’ maybe a few changes. I don’t wanna mention who.”

An excerpt released Friday night by CBS also showed Trump being asked if he has confidence in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Trump responded, “I do.”

The defense secretary could face impeachment after Democrats take control of Congress in January, following their big midterm election wins on Tuesday.

The full interview is set to air during “60 Minutes” on Sunday.

Democrat Nancy Lacore wins election to US House in South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District

Lacore is a former Navy vice admiral who served as chief of the Navy Reserve before Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired her last year without explanation, part of a series of steps targeting military leaders during President Donald Trump’s second term.

She defeated Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt. Honeycutt is an attorney and a member of the Charleston County Council.

The winner succeeds Rep. Nancy Mace, the Republican vacating the seat after unsuccessfully running for governor. The Associated Press declared Lacore the winner at 6:51 p.m. EST.

After Democrats flip Texas House, state’s longest-serving Black lawmaker says she has support for speaker

Rep. Senfronia Thompson would be the first Black lawmaker and first woman elevated to Texas House speaker in the state’s history. The 87-year-old Democrat was first elected in 1972.

Democrats won a majority in the state House for the first time since 2002 as part of their sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The next House speaker will be elected by majority vote of the 150-member chamber next January. Thompson will have to hold together the coalition she claims until then.

US coordinates with Canada to target Iranian digital asset providers

The Treasury Department on Friday targeted several firms exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for allegedly helping Tehran evade sanctions and fund its proxies.

Some of the providers dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges already sanctioned by Washington.

The latest targets were coordinated with the Canadian government as several of the individuals and entities named are based in Vancouver and Toronto.

“Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

The actions are part of the Trump administration’s economic campaign to cripple the various financial networks that help sustain Iran as the longtime adversaries struggle to find a diplomatic resolution to a more than eight-month long conflict.

Ukraine welcomes more help from Melania Trump in the future

Ukrainian officials have praised first lady Melania Trump for her role in a humanitarian ceasefire in the besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky and hope for more of her help going forward.

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of Zelenskyy’s party, and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, spoke to reporters in Washington a day after a White House event recognizing the recent six-day truce between Russia and Ukraine in Oleshky.

Lubinets says he thinks of the first lady “as a heavyweight” in negotiations, saying her office was instrumental in getting the Russians to open negotiations.

Asked about a greater role for Melania Trump in talks between Russia and Ukraine, Arakhamia said, “we would appreciate it.” He says he wants to expand the ability to get truces in other parts of the war-torn country.

Ukraine expects to see more support from US after midterms

A Ukrainian official says with Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterm elections, they expect American support to surge next year.

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of Zelenskyy’s party, told reporters in Washington that he sees “the chances for us to get better U.S. support” financially and generally is “at least double” with the new Congress.

Arakhamia said he and other Ukrainian officials know newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller “well” and were broadly optimistic about his new role.

But before the congressional changes, “we have the hardest winter ever,” Arakhamia said.

Russia has been targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. He said the country’s supply of missile interceptors is all but depleted.

Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair says promoting Miller is ‘putting lipstick on a pig’

Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York said Trump’s decision to name Miller the White House chief of staff “is a desperate and irresponsible cry for attention.”

He said Miller has been the architect of Trump’s immigration policies and voters have “rejected mass deportations, the targeting of Latino communities.”

To give Miller “a fancier title is just putting lipstick on a pig,” he said.

‘I wanted to make a change,’ Trump says, explaining chief of staff shakeup

Trump praised both Wiles and Miller to reporters but said it was time for a change.

“Susie has done a very good job. Great job,” Trump said as he left the White House to travel to Florida. But he said, “We’ve got to make moves sometimes.”

Trump said Miller is great.

“He gets it” and is “very good politically. And he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job, great manager,” Trump said.

House Oversight’s Garcia warns Stephen Miller: ‘Lawyer up’

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is in line to become chairman of the Oversight Committee, said Trump is “doubling down” on the administration policies that voters just rejected in the midterm election.

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families,” said Garcia of California.

Garcia said the committee continues to investigate Miller “for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts.”

Wiles is the first woman to ever serve as White House chief of staff

Announcing her departure on social media, Wiles called serving Trump “the honor of a lifetime.”

“I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” she wrote. “More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside.

“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” Wiles said.

Wiles steered Trump’s 2024 comeback campaign. She has long been seen as a check on some of his most destructive impulses.

Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new chief of staff

He’s one of Trump’s most loyal and longest-serving advisers. He came aboard Trump’s longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter and has remained in the president’s orbit.

Miller, 41, currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff and, though his portfolio is wide-ranging, Miller is most closely aligned with Trump’s actions and rhetoric on immigration.

He’s a former Capitol Hill staffer who worked for former Sen. Jeff Sessions, an Alabama Republican who was Trump’s first attorney general.

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media. He also promoted unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke

Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy says he will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital Friday after suffering a stroke.

Murphy said the doctors are encouraged by the progress he’s made and the time at the rehabilitation center will help him get back to work on the quickest timeline possible. He expects to miss the next several weeks of votes as he continues his recovery.

“I want to be direct with you,” Murphy said in a statement. “So here is my diagnosis. Last Saturday afternoon, I felt something was not right with my body and called 9-1-1 out of an abundance of caution, and I’m glad I did. I was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain.”

Murphy says he’s staying engaged with his colleagues and staff remotely to ensure the work of his office continues.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to embark on his first post-midterm foreign trip to attend a Group of 7 foreign ministers meeting in France next week.

He’ll likely face questions about the Trump administration’s policies, namely in Iran, after huge Republican losses in elections that gave Democrats control of Congress.

The State Department said Friday that Rubio would travel to Paris to meet his counterparts from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan on Monday and Tuesday.

The G7 nations will confront a number of unresolved world crises, including the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars. They must also cope with Trump’s often antagonistic approach to allies and concerns that the election results may harden his attitude.

Rubio is often seen as presenting a gentler side to Trump’s belligerence in foreign policy. He may get questions about speculation he might leave the administration to prepare for a 2028 presidential run, which he has adamantly denied.

Susie Wiles, Trump’s longest-serving White House chief of staff, is leaving the administration

President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.

On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post.

Wiles’ departure comes almost immediately after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Trump.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Democrats win the Arizona House, Senate and governor’s office for the first time since 1966

Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor’s office, giving the party its first trifecta in the state since 1966 as Democrats made major gains nationwide in this week’s elections and took control of both chambers of Congress.

In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she’s looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state’s school voucher program.

The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. There have not been major disputes or disruptions this year.

In Arizona, Republicans have held the House for 60 years and the Senate since the early 1990s.

Trump says he wants Gruters to stay on as head of RNC, despite losses

In a Truth Social post, Trump is praising “MAGA Warrior Joe Gruters” and says Gruters should continue to serve as chairman of the Republican National Committee.

“As Chairman, Joe turned the RNC into an efficient, focused, and powerful machine that will continue to empower the America First Agenda for many years to come,” Trump writes, endorsing him for a second term.

“Joe Gruters should return as Chairman of the RNC to continue to build our Party, and be a trusted partner as we MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, and ensure Free and Fair Elections,” he says.

“Joe is 100% America First, the Grassroots LOVES him, and I know he will do an incredible job in 2028, and secure Great Success for Republicans all across our Country. Joe has my Complete and Total Endorsement.”

Beijing confirms it’s discussing a Xi-Trump-Putin summit

Beijing confirmed for the first time that it’s discussing a possible meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Mao Ning, spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a regular briefing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state.”

The three-leader meeting would be historic if it happens during a regional economic summit this month in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. But experts say the trio may not agree on what to discuss when their interests are at odds.

Trump has said he wants to discuss nuclear arms control, while Putin is interested in discussing the war with Ukraine without Kyiv at the table.

If it happens, the meeting is certain to upset Europe, while China hopes to score a diplomatic win by facilitating the summit.

Amazon releases trailer for the follow-up to Melania Trump’s documentary about herself

The minute-long trailer promoting the two-part series features Melania Trump in never-before-seen moments in her roles as wife, mother and first lady.

It will be available on Nov. 20. Amazon Prime Video also produced “Melania,” the documentary, which was in theaters in January.

The first lady said in a September interview on Fox News Channel’s “Fox & Friends” that “Melania: The Series” is different from the documentary “because it’s more conversation, one on one with me.”

She said the docuseries will have some surprises, too.

“So when I was traveling and doing all of the filming, the director was asking me questions, and there are some private questions that I will answer that people never heard before. So it’s kind of exciting,” Melania Trump said.

Houston mayor signs order to limit cooperation with ICE, says ‘elections matter’ after Democrats win

The mayor of Houston on Friday said the city would limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, heralding “a new model” of immigration enforcement after Democrats swept statewide offices in Texas.

Mayor John Whitmire said the city would go after immigrants “that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education.”

“Traffic incident will not even ... you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way. No contact with (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses. It reduces the fear and anxiety.”

Details of the change were to be spelled out in an executive order but the move by the nation’s fourth-largest city is one of the first steps to curb ICE’s powers since Tuesday’s election.

DHS says it acted lawfully in talks with Iran on deportations

Court documents Thursday showed that the Trump administration held secret talks with Iran to deport Iranians during the war.

In its first comments since the revelation, the Department of Homeland Security justified the ongoing contacts in a statement Friday, saying that it’s common practice for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to work with countries to get travel documents.

It said it follows all “established protocols” to allow people to meet with consular officials from their country.

“As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to execute the largest deportation operation in history,” the department said.

The judge in a lawsuit challenging the deportations questioned how the U.S. could send people back to a country where they could face a “serious threat of certain death.”

DHS did not respond to a question about the potential danger the deportees might face.

title: How Stephen Miller appointment shows Trump hasn't learned his lesson on immigration
description:
On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets.

text:
On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets.

But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff.

It was never likely that Trump – who rose to political prominence on the promise that he would expel immigrants en masse from the US – would dampen his agenda, even after voters rejected Republican candidates up and down the ballot, near and far from the southern border, in blue and deep-red states.

But the elevation of Miller – a zealous, anti-immigrant crusader who has been by Trump’s side since the president’s first term – is an ominous signal that the deportation machine that Trump has built up over the past two years will be driving ahead at full speed.

Miller more than any single other person is responsible for unleashing a series of violent immigration raids across US cities this year and last, for sending hordes of masked agents in military gear through residential streets to round up undocumented immigrants. He has pushed the administration to all but shut down legal immigration as well. In his previous roles – as a deputy chief of staff and policy adviser – he has stuck close to Trump’s side and stoked the president’s most extreme instincts.

“The elevation of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff signals a doubling down on the administration’s cruelest impulses,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. “Miller’s promotion guarantees an acceleration of mass deportations and of brute force unleashed within our neighborhoods.”

After immigration agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a nurse, amid immigration raids in Minneapolis, it was Miller, according to the Wall Street Journal, who raised the idea that Trump could invoke the Insurrection Act to send in military troops.

It was Miller who came up with the legal framework of using the Alien Enemies Act to cast Venezuelan immigrants – including asylum seekers – as foreign terrorists associated with the Tren de Aragua cartel, and using that reasoning to expel them to a Salvadorian megaprison and to strike small Venezuelan boats.

During the first Trump administration, it was Miller who devised the “Muslim ban” restricting travel from Muslim-majority countries. It was he who designed the now-notorious zero tolerance policy of the first Trump administration – which separated more than 5,600 children from their parents and caregivers at the US-Mexico border. More recently, he’s pushed the administration to accelerate the deportation of undocumented children.

Miller, 41, who is himself the descendant of Jewish immigrants to the US and grew up in liberal Santa Monica, California, came to reject his home town, viewing California as a failed state that had been perverted by mass immigration. Eventually, he came to see immigration as a leftwing plot to undermine his vision of a traditional United States.

In more than a decade by Trump’s side, Miller has worked with the president to wrest extreme executive authority, to undermine Congress and the judiciary and defy oversight – in large part to advance his anti-immigrant campaign.

“He never backs down,” said Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth in a congratulatory social media post, calling Miller a true patriot.

Democratic lawmakers who’ve re-taken control of Congress, governor’s offices and statehouses may have to spend much of the next two years bringing Miller’s ambitions to heel. Human rights activists and advocates on behalf of immigrants are immediately calling on congressmembers to do everything they can to stop Miller.

US representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is poised to lead the House oversight committee next year, warned that Miller “should lawyer up” – promising to investigate him and his involvement in the administration’s mass deportation scheme.

Senator Alex Padilla said that if Trump was doubling down, “so will we”, promising to use “every tool at our disposal – oversight, investigations, subpoenas, and our leverage over federal funding – to expose this administration’s abuse of power and hold those responsible accountable”.

But even with full control of Congress, Democrats will likely have a limited ability to rein in the administration’s immigration enforcement agencies – which are bloated with $70bn in funding through 2029. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is poised to massively expand its workforce. Immigration arrests and detentions are already at an all-time high.

Miller, meanwhile, has shown a unique unwillingness to concede – in 2018, he reportedly sank a deal that would have gotten Trump $25bn funding for a border wall in exchange for a provision that would have provided permanent protection for undocumented immigrants who had come to the US as children.

It hasn’t seemed to faze him that the administration’s policies have alienated the coalition of voters who elected Trump into office in 2024 – including a large contingency of Latino voters. And he is unlikely to be moved by voters’ backlash against the Trump administration’s most extreme policies.

“This puts him in a position of greater power to wreak havoc,” Al-Juburi said.

title: Montana Supreme Court sides with Bozeman County attorney in legal scuffle with state
authors: Zeke Lloyd | Montana Free Press, Zeke Lloyd, Montana Free Press

Cromwell’s office advised county records personnel that ICE was not entitled to the information without a court order.

text:
The Montana Supreme Court sided unanimously with Gallatin County Attorney Audrey Cromwell in her case against Attorney General Austin Knudsen on Friday, ruling that Knudsen exceeded his authority when he attempted to take control of Cromwell’s local responsibilities. The court did not decide the question underlying Knudsen’s attempted takeover of Cromwell’s office, which relates to how much county governments must cooperate with U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The conflict began in October 2025 when Gallatin County records personnel sought Cromwell’s legal advice about an ICE request for confidential criminal justice information. Law enforcement agencies generally exchange such information with one another, but members of the public, including the media, must go through an onerous process to obtain it. (The information sought in this instance, for example, remains publicly unavailable.) Cromwell’s office advised county records personnel that ICE was not entitled to the information without a court order.

In April, Knudsen exercised supervisory powers — “the power to order and direct county attorneys in all matters pertaining to the duties of their office,” according to Montana code — over the Gallatin County Attorney’s Office. Exercising that control of Cromwell’s office, Knudsen ordered Cromwell to fulfill ICE requests.

Cromwell issued the memorandum that Knudsen demanded, but noted to her staff that she could not “vouch for the accuracy of the legal analysis underlying the directive.”

She also filed a petition with the Montana Supreme Court arguing that ICE shouldn’t have automatic access to confidential criminal justice information for civil immigration purposes and that Knudsen had overstepped his authority by exercising supervisory powers over her office.

On Friday, the court ruled that Knudsen did not have legal authority to take supervisory control of Cromwell’s office. Justice James Shea wrote the unanimous opinion.

Shea wrote that a county attorney has responsibility to two entities: the state and the county. Montana’s attorney general, Shea ruled, can exercise supervisory control only over a county attorney’s state-related responsibilities, like “prosecuting criminal laws and on occasion instituting or defending a civil suit in the name of the state.”

In this situation, because Cromwell was acting in her capacity as a legal adviser to Gallatin County, Shea ruled that Knudsen can’t force her to change course.

“The AG does not have supervisory authority over a county attorney when the county attorney acts as legal advisor to the county and its subdivisions,” Shea wrote.

Knudsen’s Supreme Court filings also argued that the case was beyond judicial review, positing that the dispute was an internal executive-branch matter to which Cromwell was a subordinate party. Shea rejected that argument, ruling that Cromwell had independent responsibility as a county official and a right to dispute Knudsen’s interference with her duties. Shea’s opinion, and a concurring opinion by Chief Justice Cory Swanson, rejected that argument.

The state Supreme Court also made plans to hear additional arguments about two underlying questions: Does ICE qualify as a criminal justice agency under Montana law? And does a criminal justice designation alone entitle an entity to confidential information, regardless of whether the request was for civil or criminal purposes?

The court asked both Knudsen and Cromwell to file briefs by Dec. 7, 2026.

------

Zeke Lloyd |zlloyd@montanafreepress.org

text:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump’s last two years in office.

Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump’s controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government’s immigration policies.

“It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff,” Miller said on X later Friday.

“The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” he said.

Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post, praising his longtime aide as “one of my most trusted advisors.”

Wiles, “who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” the president wrote.

Asked about the move later Friday afternoon, Trump said, “I wanted to make a change.”

“I think Susie’s done a very good job, great job. But I just wanted to make it,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House for an event in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

“Stephen’s been great,” Trump said, adding, “Sometimes in life you have to make moves.”

Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP’s huge election losses, “let me make this easy on you — I am going to resign,” MS NOW reported.

“Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff,” Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime.”

“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” she wrote.

Senior administration officials were quick to congratulate Miller.

“Patriots in control,” read an X post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose job security has come into question after some Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the midterm results on the Iran war.

Vance also praised Miller on X, saying he “will do great things.”

The official X account for Trump’s political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, “It’s Miller time.”

Democrats and other critics, meanwhile, filed in to denounce the pick.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who could be elected House speaker next year, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.”

“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries wrote on X.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote that Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way,” Schumer wrote.

Others took Miller’s promotion as a sign that Trump, who seemed to express some willingness to negotiate with a blue Congress, will instead remain combative.

“For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water,” wrote David Axelrod, a former senior advisor to President Barack Obama.

The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ’s civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump’s foes.

Wiles oversaw Trump’s winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued “retribution” as president and that he had an “alcoholic’s personality.”

Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.

While Wiles is not fully leaving Trump’s orbit, her resignation follows a pattern of other top female officials who have left or been fired from Trump’s second administration, and then replaced by men.

text:
The Montana Supreme Court sided unanimously with Gallatin County Attorney Audrey Cromwell in her case against Attorney General Austin Knudsen on Friday, ruling that Knudsen exceeded his authority when he attempted to take control of Cromwell’s local responsibilities. The court did not decide the question underlying Knudsen’s attempted takeover of Cromwell’s office, which relates to how much county governments must cooperate with U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The conflict began in October 2025 when Gallatin County records personnel sought Cromwell’s legal advice about an ICE request for confidential criminal justice information. Law enforcement agencies generally exchange such information with one another, but members of the public, including the media, must go through an onerous process to obtain it. (The information sought in this instance, for example, remains publicly unavailable.) Cromwell’s office advised county records personnel that ICE was not entitled to the information without a court order.

In April, Knudsen exercised supervisory powers — “the power to order and direct county attorneys in all matters pertaining to the duties of their office,” according to Montana code — over the Gallatin County Attorney’s Office. Exercising that control of Cromwell’s office, Knudsen ordered Cromwell to fulfill ICE requests.

Cromwell issued the memorandum that Knudsen demanded, but noted to her staff that she could not “vouch for the accuracy of the legal analysis underlying the directive.”

She also filed a petition with the Montana Supreme Court arguing that ICE shouldn’t have automatic access to confidential criminal justice information for civil immigration purposes and that Knudsen had overstepped his authority by exercising supervisory powers over her office.

On Friday, the court ruled that Knudsen did not have legal authority to take supervisory control of Cromwell’s office. Justice James Shea wrote the unanimous opinion.

Shea wrote that a county attorney has responsibility to two entities: the state and the county. Montana’s attorney general, Shea ruled, can exercise supervisory control only over a county attorney’s state-related responsibilities, like “prosecuting criminal laws and on occasion instituting or defending a civil suit in the name of the state.”

In this situation, because Cromwell was acting in her capacity as a legal adviser to Gallatin County, Shea ruled that Knudsen can’t force her to change course.

“The AG does not have supervisory authority over a county attorney when the county attorney acts as legal advisor to the county and its subdivisions,” Shea wrote.

Knudsen’s Supreme Court filings also argued that the case was beyond judicial review, positing that the dispute was an internal executive-branch matter to which Cromwell was a subordinate party. Shea rejected that argument, ruling that Cromwell had independent responsibility as a county official and a right to dispute Knudsen’s interference with her duties. Shea’s opinion, and a concurring opinion by Chief Justice Cory Swanson, rejected that argument.

The state Supreme Court also made plans to hear additional arguments about two underlying questions: Does ICE qualify as a criminal justice agency under Montana law? And does a criminal justice designation alone entitle an entity to confidential information, regardless of whether the request was for civil or criminal purposes?

The court asked both Knudsen and Cromwell to file briefs by Dec. 7, 2026.

text:
Members of San Diego's congressional delegation and California's senators Friday demanded answers from the Trump Administration in the death of an immigrant detainee who died last month at Otay Mesa Detention Center.

Guillermo Pascual Verganza, 42, was found unconscious and unresponsive in his single-occupant cell at the Department of Homeland Security penitentiary near the U.S.-Mexico border on Saturday, according to the San Diego County Medical Examiner's Office.

Prison staff members and paramedics tried in vain to revive Pascual Verganza before pronouncing him dead at the scene shortly before 12:30 p.m., the county agency reported.

Democrat representatives from San Diego including Juan Vargas, Scott Peters, Sara Jacobs and from San Juan Capistrano Mike Levin, and Democrat senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff wrote a letter to demand an investigation into the death.

The letter, addressed to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director David Venturella, read:

As members of the San Diego Congressional delegation, we write to express our grave concern following the latest death of an individual in ICE custody at Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego, California, operated by the for-profit prison corporation CoreCivic.

Any death in federal custody is a tragic reminder of the serious responsibility entrusted to DHS, ICE and their contracted detention facilities to safeguard the lives of those in their care.

A thorough investigation is all the more important in light of previously documented concerns regarding delayed access to medical care, subpar detention conditions and compliance with public health reporting requirements.

We further request that the department regularly update members of Congress as the investigation progresses. Without complete and accurate information, Congress cannot fully assess whether existing policies, procedures and safeguards are sufficient to protect individuals in federal custody.

In the week following Varganza's death, CoreCivic, the Tennessee-based firm that runs the facility in the 7400 block of Calzada De La Fuente, released a statement confirming the in-custody death.

"We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care," the company stated. "Our government partners at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement ... were notified immediately."

ICE did not respond to a request for comment about the death.

Pascual Verganza, a Guatemalan national, had been taken into custody in Escondido in early October, according to news accounts.

During a news conference on Tuesday afternoon, San Diego County Supervisors Paloma Aguirre and Terra Lawson-Remer called on the Trump administration and CoreCivic to cooperate with county investigators and clear the way for ongoing inspections.

"Earlier this year, we took ICE to federal court for blocking public health inspections amid disturbing reports of unsafe conditions at Otay Mesa (Detention Center)," Lawson-Remer said. "Now a man has died inside that facility. When the federal government flouts due process and shuts the door on independent health inspectors, we cannot look away. We need answers, accountability and the ability to protect the health and safety of everyone held inside."

The lawsuit "wasn't a political exercise - it was a necessary step to protect human lives," Aguirre said.

"Ensuring basic human rights, medical oversight and safety within our borders is non-negotiable," she said. "ICE and CoreCivic must be held accountable for these failures right now, before another family is forced to suffer this same unimaginable grief."

After ICE denied supervisors access to the detention center, the county sued and secured a federal court order allowing an inspection in June.

That scrutiny identified failures to promptly report suspected tuberculosis cases, a lack of vaccines in stock and delays in providing necessary medical equipment, according to the supervisors. In September, the county issued another notice of noncompliance after a suspected tuberculosis case allegedly went unreported for about three weeks.

The county's public health officer is evaluating additional oversight measures, including follow-up inspections. Litigation over the county's ongoing inspection authority remains unresolved.

While exact numbers of such fatalities are elusive, the ACLU reported last month that at least 57 people had died while in U.S. immigration detention since the start of President Donald Trump's second term - more than double the number of deaths recorded from the previous four years combined.

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in June, the mortality rate of ICE detainees - based on 52 known deaths at the time - had reached its highest level in over a decade and more than doubled since Trump's current term began. The rate at that time was nearly four times that of the Biden administration, and more than 2.5 times as high as that of the first Trump administration, the watchdog organization reported.

"Urgent action is needed to address this crisis and prevent further deaths," the report concluded.

The Lone Star State swung blue for the first time since its new senator-elect, James Talarico, was born, and Houston Mayor John Whitmire wasted no time Friday announcing new restrictions on cooperation with ICE.

Whitmire told The New York Times that city police are not permitted to notify ICE if they encounter an illegal immigrant in "nonviolent contacts" like traffic stops or minor offenses.

'WE DIDN'T EXPECT THIS': TEXAS DEMOCRATS STUNNED AS BLUE WAVE TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLD

"If they’re charged with a new crime, we’ll let ICE know as we get them to the jailhouse," he told the paper Friday.

Abbott lost his bid for a fourth term Tuesday, and Talarico flipped one of the state’s Senate seats blue for the first time since Clinton Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen won his final re-election bid in 1988 — seven months before the current senator-elect was born.

Texas’ most recent Democratic governor, Ann Richards, the mother of former longtime Planned Parenthood president Cecile Richards, was elected shortly thereafter in 1990.

Whitmire did not respond to a request for comment but signaled to the Times that he made the decision at least in part because Abbott’s order requiring DHS contact caused "anxiety" among Houstonians.

In a statement put out Friday afternoon, Whitmire said, "I have signed an executive order directing HPD to no longer contact ICE for nonviolent offenses, helping reduce fear in our communities. Thank you to Chief Diaz, our state and local leaders for their collaboration. A step toward building a stronger Houston. Let’s Go to Work."

He also acknowledged Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa won’t take office until January but characterized his decision as "responsible" and "more effective policy."

A DHS spokesperson responded to Whitmire's move in comments to Fox News Digital.

"We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities," the spokesperson said.

"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities.

The spokesperson pointed to some recent criminal illegal aliens captured by ICE in Houston – including Alexander Montano of Cuba, convicted of willful homicide, burglary and forced entry into a residence.

Vietnamese national Ding Nguyen, also convicted of homicide, along with Guatemalan national Julio Camey, convicted of sex offense against a child, were also mentioned by the spokesperson.

"You write a citation or you warn them, and they go about their way. No contact with [ICE] over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses," Whitmire told the AP.

A previous policy enacted in March by Whitmire and Police Chief Noe Diaz stipulated that if a background check revealed an immigration-related warrant, a sergeant would be called to oversee ICE involvement, according to Houston’s FOX affiliate.

The policy also said that if ICE could not make it to the stop within half an hour, the subject would be released.

text:
Federal immigration agents have detained a 21-year-old Wisconsin State Patrol trooper who has a valid work permit and a pending asylum case, according to his attorney.

The trooper, Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, came to the U.S. from South Africa with his family on visas at age 14, said attorney Marc Christopher. His family has been waiting seven years for their asylum case to be heard.

Christopher slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for detaining a Wisconsin law enforcement officer who has permission to work, saying he was "flabbergasted" by the agents' decision to use its resources to target Van Der Merwe.

"I almost can't even believe that they would be so brazen as to do this. But they are," Christopher said. "There's no reason for them to detain him other than to indiscriminately pick up as many people as they can."

Van Der Merwe, who lived in New Mexico with his family, wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but could not because he was not a permanent resident, Christopher said. He graduated with a degree in criminal justice in New Mexico, then researched states where he could do similar work with his status and found Wisconsin.

Van Der Merwe was living in Onalaska and working in Tomah for Wisconsin State Patrol over the last year. His work authorization is valid until 2030.

Attorney disputes ICE's assertion about legal status

ICE's argument is that Van Der Merwe – as a teenager in the U.S. with his family – overstayed his visitor's visa.

"He entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019. In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement. "Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S."

Christopher pushed back on that assertion.

"That is just absurd and ridiculous," Christopher said. "They've been here lawfully. They have been waiting for their application to be adjudicated and to be decided by immigration."

The family, who are white South Africans, had applied for asylum on the grounds they were persecuted. A family member had been attacked, Christopher said.

Van Der Merwe did not decide to come to the U.S. himself, as he was brought by his parents, and he chose a career in law enforcement to serve the U.S., Christopher said.

ICE agents detained him Nov. 5 at the Dane County Regional Airport just after he went through security, Christopher said. He was traveling to visit his family in New Mexico. Agents handcuffed him, shackled his legs and put him in a van and drove him to Dodge County Jail, which holds ICE detainees.

ICE's detainee locator confirmed Van Der Merwe remains detained at Dodge County Jail as of Nov. 6.

Christopher said it seems that the Transportation Security Administration tipped off ICE when he bought his ticket, and agents met Van Der Merwe at the airport. Christopher has heard of ICE making arrests at the Milwaukee and Appleton airports through similar tip-offs, he said.

Bond process to leave detention could take weeks

Van Der Merwe likely will be able to secure and post bond to leave immigration detention, Christopher said, because he will be able to prove he is not a flight risk or a public safety threat. But he first will have to get a immigration court date and go in front of a judge to ask for bond to be set. That could take two weeks or more.

"There is no way that any competent official could look at this case and view him as either a flight risk or a danger," Christopher said. "In fact, he's the antithesis. He's the person who we rely on to uphold our laws and to protect us."

Under the Trump administration, ICE has not been setting bond for detainees voluntarily unless a judge orders it. Trump administration policy changes have made many detainees ineligible to even seek bond and leave detention.

Christopher said he hopes Wisconsin's congressional delegation takes note of the case and institutes changes to the way ICE can operate. He was critical that ICE would use its resources to arrest Van Der Merwe, then hold him in custody.

"You're going to use your resources to go after this guy? You're going to use our tax dollars to detain this guy? It doesn't make any sense," Christopher said.

As part of its summer surge in street arrests in Milwaukee, ICE arrested a 20-year-old Milwaukee man, Giovanni Sosa, who had lived in the U.S. since age 4. In detaining him, ICE gave him paperwork that said – at age 4 – he had overstayed his visa. Sosa spent a month in detention at the Dodge County Jail as he waited for the chance to post bond.

text:
WASHINGTON —

President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, one of the architects of his administration's hardline immigration policies, as his new White House chief of staff, elevating a key adviser as the administration faces new political challenges following Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Miller, currently the White House deputy chief of staff, will replace Susie Wiles on Monday, Nov. 9. Wiles will transition to Trump's political operation.

When asked about the change, Trump told reporters, “I just wanted to make a change.”

The leadership shakeup comes as Vice President JD Vance raises the possibility of shifting immigration enforcement priorities toward businesses that employ undocumented immigrants.

In a post reflecting on Tuesday's election losses, Vance said he is open to changing immigration enforcement by focusing more on businesses employing undocumented workers.

The idea was previously discussed by border czar Tom Homan in July, when he proposed using private contractors to expand workplace audits.

Federal contracting records show Immigration and Customs Enforcement has already awarded millions in contracts supporting such efforts.

In September, the agency awarded a five-year contract worth up to approximately $21.5 million to a Maryland company to help investigate employment records and business documents.

Amy Peck, a workplace immigration compliance attorney based in Omaha, Nebraska, said she expects workplace audits to increase.

“I speak with them every day. Businesses are very concerned. The government hasn’t made it easy for employers to be 100% compliant because of the difficulty maneuvering through the regulations,” Peck said.

Meanwhile, Miller's promotion comes as Democrats prepare to use their incoming congressional majorities to investigate ICE's enforcement tactics and spending.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, who is in line to lead the House Homeland Security Committee, has demanded that the Department of Homeland Security preserve its records and respond to outstanding requests for documents.

While Democrats can investigate ICE, they cannot directly dictate how the agency carries out day-to-day immigration enforcement, authority that remains with the Trump administration.

Despite the looming investigations, Trump and some incoming Democrats have expressed openness to discussing immigration legislation.

Trump said he has long believed immigration is an area where compromise is possible. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico also expressed interest in working with the president on border security and expanding legal immigration.

“He entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019,” the spokesperson said in the statement. “In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission. This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

“This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” the spokesperson said.

Attorney Marc Christopher, who represents Van Der Merwe, said in a statement that the arrest was “inhumane and despicable.”

“Putting a Wisconsin State Trooper behind bars while his asylum case sits unresolved does not make our communities safer,” he said.

In another statement, Christopher said, “Wisconsin trusts Carel to protect the public.”

“DHS owes his family and our community an explanation of why keeping him behind bars is necessary,” he said.

text:
The mayor of Houston on Friday said the city would limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, heralding “a new model” of immigration enforcement after Democrats won power in Texas for the first time in decades.

Houston’s mayor, John Whitmire, said the city would go after immigrants “that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education”.

A traffic incident “will not even [trigger immigration enforcement] … You write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way. No contact with [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses. It reduces the fear and anxiety.”

The move by the nation’s fourth-largest city is one of the first steps to curb ICE’s powers since Tuesday’s midterm elections.

In July, ICE agents shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston while reportedly looking for other individuals.

The shooting rattled residents of the Magnolia Park neighborhood in Houston, where the shooting occurred. It was also another blow to the embattled housing construction industry in Texas, which has been losing skilled, experienced workers at a high volume and high rates.

“We feel it on a level we can’t even describe,” a neighbor who declined to share his name for fear of retaliation told the Guardian in July. “Everybody knows that what happened is wrong. How will we not stand with our people, stand behind them, especially when something so vicious and ugly happened?”

Under the mayor’s new directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if the person it stops is arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing or if ICE issues an administrative warrant, which is an order signed by a senior ICE official indicating that the person is wanted by immigration officials.

“The fact that a person is, or is suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement shall not, by itself, be a basis to contact ICE, to prolong any detention, or to take any person into or hold any person in custody,” the two-page order states.

Spokespersons for ICE did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the mayor’s announcement.

In October, an ICE agent struck an individual with their vehicle during a pursuit of a different suspect whose family noted he died years ago.

A grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Prosecutors say Morales intentionally rammed his car into Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video.

Despite a one-time $75bn infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements – many in Texas – to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests.

Texas’s governor, Greg Abbott, has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. He lost his bid for a fourth term to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Fiel, an immigrant-rights group in Houston that has been working with the family of Parra Hernandez, planned to hold a press conference on Friday afternoon in light of the announcement.

“Today Houston won. The Houston city council had already decided this months ago,” said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of Fiel Houston, adding that it was time to follow through.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

text:
SAN ANTONIO – Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas filed 237 new immigration and immigration-related criminal cases from Oct. 31 through Nov. 5, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons. Charges were brought against alien smugglers and illegal aliens with past convictions for numerous DWIs, thefts, multiple prior removals, and violent crimes to include aggravated battery on a pregnant victim.

Among the new cases, two U.S. citizens and an illegal alien from Mexico are charged with alien smuggling after a joint law enforcement operation interdicted a tractor trailer carrying 53 illegal aliens in El Paso. On Oct. 28, Horizon Police Department officers initiated a traffic stop on a semi-truck driven by U.S. citizen Miguel Angel Debruhl. U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted an immigration inspection inside the truck’s cab and allegedly discovered a backpack containing a large number of cell phones. Debruhl was placed under arrest.

Simultaneously, a second semi-truck was pulled over by a Texas Department of Public Safety trooper. The truck was driven by U.S. citizen Alan Montelongo, who allegedly consented to an inspection of the semi-truck’s cab and trailer. A criminal complaint alleges that the inspection led to the discovery of 53 illegal aliens sitting along both sides of the trailer. Further investigation allegedly revealed that Montelongo had agreed to transport the illegal aliens through the I-25 Border Patrol checkpoint in Las Cruces and would be paid approximately $16,000 to split with Debruhl.

U.S. Border Patrol continued surveillance at a suspected stash house where, according to the criminal complaint, Abel Delval-Dominguez, an illegal alien from Mexico, was seen loading groceries and several full black trash bags into a pickup truck. The complaint alleges that agents had previously seen Delval-Dominguez and the pickup transporting aliens between the stash house and the truck yard from which Debruhl and Montelongo departed on Oct. 28. Delval-Dominguez was arrested and charged for alien smuggling along with Debruhl and Montelongo.

Edgar Villanueva-Garcia, an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested in El Paso on Oct. 28 and charged with illegal re-entry. He was recently deported for the fourth time through Dallas on Oct. 6, following a conviction for his second DWI. Villanueva-Garcia has also been previously convicted for improper entry by an alien and for bail jumping.

In Del Rio, Gregorio Zamano-Ortiz, an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested and charged with illegal re-entry. Zamano-Ortiz was previously convicted in New York for third-degree assault and first-degree sexual abuse.

Illegal alien from Mexico Paulin Balderas-Mejia was arrested near Carrizo Springs and charged with illegal re-entry. In December 2019, he was convicted of harboring aliens and sentenced to more than three years in prison. He was deported for the second time on Nov. 16, 2022.

Manuel Guadalupe Armenta-Ortega, also an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry after being deported for the fourth time on Sept. 21. Prior to his September removal, Armenta-Ortega was arrested for his second DWI. A felon, Armenta-Ortega has been convicted of deadly conduct discharge of a firearm as well as assault causing bodily injury to a family member.

An illegal alien from Nicaragua was also arrested near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry. Eling Francisco Briceno-Vidaurre has been previously deported six times, the last being in March 2025. He has been convicted of illegal re-entry twice as well as possession of a weapon and possession of an unregistered firearm.

Antonio Vargas-Colindres, an illegal alien from Honduras, was arrested near Eagle Pass on Nov. 1. Vargas-Colindres, who has been previously deported five times, was charged with his second illegal re-entry. He was convicted of illegal re-entry in Miami, Florida, in July 2023 and sentenced to one day in prison. The following month, Vargas-Colindres was convicted in Miami for aggravated battery on a pregnant victim, cruelty toward a child and cocaine possession.

Also an illegal alien from Honduras, Mainor Castillo-Reyes was arrested in Austin and booked in the Travis County Jail on Oct. 28 for unauthorized use of a motor vehicle. He was transferred to ICE custody and now faces an illegal re-entry charge. Castillo-Reyes was convicted of indecency with a child in 2017 and sentenced to four years in state prison. He was deported in August 2019.

Jose Medardo Anariba-Cruz, an illegal alien from Honduras, is charged in Austin with illegal re-entry. He was arrested for this third DWI in December 2025 and convicted of fleeing from police and reckless driving. He’s been previously removed from the U.S. three times.

In San Antonio, Geovani Lizbeth Rodriguez-Delgado, an illegal alien from Mexico, was released from the Bexar County Jail and transported to ICE custody after being convicted of assault causing bodily injury. Rodriguez-Delgado had been previously removed from the U.S. to Mexico in September 2025. In 2009, she was convicted and sentenced to four years in state prison for robbery.

Another illegal alien from Mexico, Juan Vincente Romero-Trejo, was transferred into ICE custody from the Bexar County Jail on Wednesday. Romero-Trejo had been arrested on Oct. 1 for assault causing bodily injury to a family member. He’s been previously removed from the U.S. four times and has three convictions in the South District of Texas for illegal re-entry.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas comprises 68 counties located in the central and western areas of Texas, encompasses nearly 93,000 square miles and an estimated population of 7.6 million people. The district includes three of the five largest cities in Texas—San Antonio, Austin and El Paso—and shares 660 miles of common border with the Republic of Mexico.

Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

These cases are part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Mayor John Whitmire said Friday that he will direct the Houston Police Department to limit when its officers’ contact federal immigration agents after Democrats swept Texas’ statewide offices in Tuesday’s midterm election.

The change is a reversal in how the city works with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a central fight that has embroiled the city council over the last year and sparked numerous public protests, and an early window into Houston’s place within the soon-to-be Democratic-led state.

Whitmire, who had repeatedly turned back calls to restrict HPD’s interactions with ICE, citing the risk of angering Gov. Greg Abbott and other state leaders, said Friday’s action is possible now that Abbott and other state Republicans have been swept out of office.

“It’s to reduce the fear and anxiety, not just in some of our communities but across Houston,” Whitmire said at a Friday press conference.

The new executive order, dated Friday, says HPD will contact ICE “only if that person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants.”

Previously officers were directed to call ICE anytime they encountered someone with one of the 700,000 civil “administrative” ICE warrants President Donald Trump’s administration added to a national law enforcement database at the outset of his immigration crackdown last year.

Article continues below this ad

Officers were then directed to wait a “reasonable amount of time” for an ICE agent to reach the scene, though that sometimes resulted in officers waiting more than an hour.

READ MORE: Inside the collapse of Houston’s ICE policy

The change comes just two days after Whitmire defended HPD’s existing practice in a written statement as “good policy,” though the mayor on Friday denied saying that.

Several other city leaders, including Controller Chris Hollins and Council Member Alejandra Salinas, had said at Wednesday’s council meeting that they would push to limit ICE cooperation following Abbott’s defeat. The governor, who is leaving office in January, had successfully stopped similar efforts earlier this year in Houston after threatening to revoke state funding.

Whitmire on Friday argued he’d walked a political tightrope with the city’s ICE policies, helping Houston avoid the worst of Trump’s immigration crackdown that some other cities have experienced.

Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, senior policy attorney for the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, argued the mayor was rewriting history, pointing out that ICE agents killed Houstonian Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July and have injured other residents. None of that was enough to convince Whitmire to limit police involvement with the federal agency, she said.

“Even though this is a win for the community, it’s only because advocates have been continuously showing up, applying pressure and reminding him this community deserves protection,” she said. “He’s only doing this now, when it’s politically feasible.”

INVESTIGATION: HPD quietly ended automatic probes of federal police shootings before ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado

Salinas agreed that months of public activism helped spur Friday’s announcement, but also commended Whitmire and Police Chief Noe Diaz for making it.

“This is a critical step toward protecting Houstonians’ constitutional rights and reducing the fear and anxiety too many families have carried that calling for help or being pulled over for a routine traffic stop could lead to them or a loved one being detained by ICE,” she said. “This progress belongs to the families who bravely shared their stories, advocates who tirelessly kept organizing, and hundreds of Houstonians who returned to City Hall again and again, even when change felt out of reach.”

Immigration advocates, who have questioned whether the city’s policy violated the U.S. Constitution by directing officers to detain people based solely upon civil warrants and not criminal charges, celebrated Whitmire’s decision, calling it overdue.

“This is what needed to happen since day 1,” Cesar Espinosa of FIEL Houston said in a statement. “Now it is time to follow (through).”

Whitmire said he hoped the new policy would be a model for other Texas cities under the state’s new Democratic leaders. Travis Fife, an attorney for the Texas Civil Rights Project, said immigration advocates in every city from which Abbott threatened to pull funding were exploring what changes might be possible after Tuesday’s elections.

Hours after Whitmire's announcement, leaders in Austin said they planned to discuss how they might also change their ICE-related policies in light of the election, according to a news report.

Under HPD’s prior policy, which the city negotiated with Abbott’s office, local police handed 17 people to immigration authorities from July through September, according to city data.

Another 13 people were charged with crimes and transferred to county jail, where they are likely to be released to ICE. That group would not be affected by the policy, Whitmire said.

text:
LANSING, Iowa (WKBT) -- The Mississippi River bridge at Lans…

GREEN BAY — Kevin Zeitler gets it.



ONALASKA, Wis. (WKBT) — A 21-year-old Wisconsin State Trooper who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will be released from ICE custody, according to his attorney.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who lives in Onalaska and works out of the Tomah post, was detained by ICE agents at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison on Nov. 5 while waiting to board a domestic flight. His attorney Marc Christopher claims when Van Der Merwe showed agents his federal work permit and explained he had a pending asylum application, they told him they "did not care," before detaining and taking him to the Dodge County detention facility.

According to Van Der Merwe's attorney, he will be released shortly and will be placed on an order of supervision which requires Van Der Merwe to meet with ICE regularly and to be monitored by an electronic device. However, his attorney says 'our fight is not over.'

"His release does not erase what he and his family have been through," the office stated. "There is still no explanation why DHS detained him or why exactly he is now being released. Those are the answers we seek and Carel and his family, and work community deserves.  We continue to stress how DHS’s own agency, USCIS, authorized him to work. He used that authorization to serve and protect Wisconsin communities. Yet that same agency, detained him. We hope DHS will provide an explanation."

ICE's detainee locator previously showed a Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, born in South Africa, was in ICE custody at the Dodge Detention Facility in Wisconsin. Van Der Merwe no longer appears on this site.

In a statement to News 8 Now, ICE said it arrested Van Der Merwe on Nov. 5 during a targeted enforcement operation at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. ICE says Van Der Merwe entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019 but overstayed his admission. ICE added that Van Der Merwe will receive due process and remain in custody pending removal proceedings. ICE also noted that work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States.

The Wisconsin State Patrol confirmed Van Der Merwe's employment in a statement to News 8 Now, saying it is aware of the situation and that Van Der Merwe has been employed with the State Patrol since July 13, 2025.

Van Der Merwe came to the United States legally from South Africa as a child. His family claims they have followed the legal immigration process and waited seven years for an asylum interview. He is listed on his father's pending asylum application and holds a federal work authorization card through 2030, according to Christopher. Wisconsin State Patrol hiring rules allow noncitizens with valid work authorization to serve as troopers.

"Carel came here legally as a child. His family pursued asylum through the legal process. He holds federal work authorization and serves Wisconsin as a State Trooper," Christopher said. "Now the same government that authorized him to work has locked him up."

According to a statement, Van Orden, who represents Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, contacted DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin directly after learning of Van Der Merwe's detention.

"As soon as Congressman Van Orden became aware of the situation, he contacted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to discuss the trooper's case. The trooper will be released immediately and will be responsible for working with the appropriate authorities to resolve his outstanding immigration paperwork and address his legal status. Congressman Van Orden appreciates Secretary Mullin's attention to this matter."

Congresswoman-elect Rebecca Cooke (D-WI), who will represent Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District in January, released a statement on the detention prior to Van Orden's announcement.

"I am disturbed at reports that a valued member of our Wisconsin community, Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, was unjustly detained by ICE. If these reports are true, ICE's behavior is unacceptable. This is a public servant who puts his life in danger to keep Wisconsinites safe. And it comes after ICE has repeatedly put our communities in danger by violating fundamental rights. I will investigate this incident and demand an explanation from ICE officials about why a member of Wisconsin law enforcement is being treated this way - and I will stand up for him until he is released."

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.
